docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Step-by-Step Introduction to the [ASP.NET Core MVC] Web Framework

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude at the request of Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course shows, step by step, how to build an MVC web application with ASP.NET Core MVC (.NET 10) and the C# language. The HTML pages are generated by the server with Razor views, with no JavaScript framework in the browser.

It has two parts. First come 28 small examples, each focused on a single concept: controllers, actions and routing; binding, converting and validating the parameters of an action; Razor views, layout, partial views, helpers and Tag Helpers; forms, validation and the Post / Redirect / Get pattern with TempData; internationalization; data scopes (Singleton, Scoped, Transient) and cookies; the request life cycle with middleware, filters and error pages; JWT authentication in a cookie, roles, captcha and rate limiting; and finally a layered web / business / DAO architecture with Entity Framework Core and MySQL.

Then comes a complete case study, RdvMedecins: an appointment-booking application for a medical practice, with three roles (administrator, doctors, patients), available in French and English, in which every file is commented.

Prerequisites: the basics of web programming (HTTP, HTML) and of the C# language. The tools used are the .NET 10 SDK, Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit extension, MySQL and curl. Every example is commented line by line, with the URL to test.

This course belongs to a series that covers the same 28 examples, number by number, with other frameworks: NestJS, Spring MVC, Flask, Laravel, Symfony and Django. The frameworks can thus be compared example by example, but this course can be read on its own.

All courses by Serge Tahé

docs.title: 13.1. Installing SDK and NET
docs.text:
SDK [.NET] 10 can be downloaded from dotnet.microsoft.com/download: Select version 10 (LTS), then the installer for your system ([Windows] x64, [macOS], [Linux]). With [Windows], you can also use the package manager [winget]:

winget install Microsoft.DotNet.SDK.10

For [Linux] ([Ubuntu], for example), the package [dotnet-sdk-10.0] is available in the distribution’s or Microsoft’s repositories. Verify the installation in a console ([PowerShell] or command prompt):

dotnet --version

which should display a version number starting with 10. The SDK package contains everything you need: the [C#] compiler, the [ASP.NET Core] framework, and the [dotnet] tool ([dotnet new], [dotnet build], [dotnet run], [dotnet watch]...). The additional libraries ([NuGet] packages) are automatically downloaded from nuget.org the first time a project that declares them is compiled: an Internet connection is required for this.

docs.title: 13.2. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text: [Visual Studio Code] is downloaded from code.visualstudio.com. Add the Microsoft extension [C# Dev Kit] (View > Extensions menu, then search for “C# Dev Kit”): This extension provides syntax highlighting and code completion for [C#] and [Razor], a list of projects in a solution (the “Solution Explorer” view), and the debugger. Open the [examples] folder or the case study folder (File menu / Open Folder); the integrated terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal) allows you to run [dotnet] commands without leaving the editor. The F5 key runs the application under the debugger’s control.

docs.title: 13.3. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] (laragon.org) installs a ready-to-use [MySQL] server (or [MariaDB]) ready for use, along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the "Start All" button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the default values for the connection strings in Example 28 and the case study;
  • the "Database" button opens [HeidiSQL], where the File / Run File SQL runs the scripts [dbpersons.sql] (Example 28) and [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] (case study).

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and run the scripts using the command-line client [mysql]. With [MariaDB], specify its version in [appsettings.json] (key [MySql:ServerVersion], for example, [10.11.0-mariadb]).

docs.title: 13.4. Installing curl
docs.text: [curl] is included with [Windows] 10 and 11, [macOS], and most [Linux] distributions. On [PowerShell], you must type [curl.exe], not [curl]: In older versions of [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which has different options.

docs.title: 8. Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Two distinct questions arise for each request:

  • Who is the user? This is authentication: the user has identified themselves with a username and password, and each subsequent request must prove that it comes from them;
  • Does the user have permission to access this page? This is authorization: in the case study, only a user with the role ADMIN manages doctors and clients.

Since the server is stateless (Chapter 6), proof of identity must be included with every request. A token JWT ([JSON Web Token]) is used: after login, the server generates a token containing the user’s identity and signs it with a secret key. The token is stored in a cookie; the browser sends it back with every request; the server verifies the signature. The user can read their token but cannot modify it: any modification invalidates the signature.

[ASP.NET Core] clearly distinguishes between the two issues:

  • authentication is handled by middleware ([UseAuthentication]) and an authentication scheme: in this case, the [JwtBearer] scheme, provided by the [NuGet] [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer] package. For each request, it looks for a token, verifies it, and derives the user from it, [HttpContext.User];
  • Authorization is handled by the [[Authorize]] attribute, verified by the [UseAuthorization] middleware: it compares the action’s requirements with what is known about the user.

The examples in this chapter use two [NuGet] packages: [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer] and [BCrypt.Net-Next] (password hashing). They are declared in the project file; the command [dotnet build] (or [dotnet run]) downloads them from nuget.org during the first compilation: an Internet connection is therefore required.

docs.title: 8.1. Example 25: Login, Token, Protected Page
docs.text:
25-jwt/
├── Auth/
│   ├── AuthService.cs
│   └── UsersService.cs
├── Controllers/
│   ├── AuthController.cs
│   └── ProfileController.cs
├── Views/
│   ├── Auth/
│   │   └── Login.cshtml
│   ├── Profile/
│   │   └── Profile.cshtml
│   ├── Shared/
│   │   └── _Layout.cshtml
│   ├── _ViewImports.cshtml
│   └── _ViewStart.cshtml
├── appsettings.json
├── Example25.csproj
└── Program.cs

The file [Example25.csproj]:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- JWT token authentication (token verification) -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer" Version="10.0.0" />
    <!-- password hashing (bcrypt) -->
    <PackageReference Include="BCrypt.Net-Next" Version="4.0.3" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • Lines 5–7: the [NuGet] packages used, and their versions. The elements common to all examples (version of [.NET]...) are in the file [Directory.Build.props] in the [examples] folder.

The [appsettings.json] file:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"
    }
  },
  "AllowedHosts": "*",
  "Jwt": {
    "Secret": "a-secret-key-of-at-least-32-characters-for-example-25",
    "DurationMinutes": 60
  }
}
  • Lines 9–11: an application-specific configuration section: the key used to sign tokens and their lifetime. Anyone who knows the key can generate valid tokens: in production, it is not stored in a project file; instead, it is provided by an environment variable ([Jwt__Secret]) or a secret vault. The algorithm used (HMAC-SHA256) requires a key of at least 32 bytes.

The file [Auth/UsersService.cs]:

namespace Example25.Auth;

public record User(string Login, string Name, string Role, string PasswordHash);

// the users, in memory (the next chapter will put them in a database)
public class UsersService
{
    private readonly List<User> users =
    [
        // a password is NEVER kept, only its hash
        Create("marie", "Marie Pélissier", "USER", "marie"),
        Create("admin", "Administrator", "ADMIN", "admin"),
    ];

    public User? Find(string login) =>
        users.Find(u => u.Login == login);

    // bcrypt, with a cost of 10: 2^10 rounds of computation, deliberately slow
    private static User Create(string login, string name, string role, string password) =>
        new(login, name, role, BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.HashPassword(password, 10));
}
  • line 3: a user, along with their role;
  • lines 10–12: a password is never stored; only its hash is retained—a fingerprint calculated by a one-way function. It is possible to verify that a password matches a fingerprint, but not to recover the password from the fingerprint;
  • lines 19–20: [BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.HashPassword(password, 10)] calculates the hash using the [bcrypt] algorithm. The 10 represents the “cost”: [bcrypt] is intentionally slow (2¹⁰ calculation cycles) to discourage anyone from trying millions of passwords. Two hashes of the same password are different (a random “salt” is added): [BCrypt.Verify] is responsible for verifying them.

The file [Auth/AuthService.cs]:

using System.Text;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;

namespace Example25.Auth;

public class AuthService(UsersService users, IConfiguration configuration)
{
    // the name of the cookie that carries the token
    public const string Cookie = "token";

    // the key that signs the tokens, read from appsettings.json (Jwt section)
    public static SymmetricSecurityKey Key(IConfiguration configuration) =>
        new(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(configuration["Jwt:Secret"]!));

    // null if the login is unknown or the password wrong
    public User? Validate(string? login, string? password)
    {
        var user = users.Find(login ?? "");
        if (user is null || password is null)
        {
            return null;
        }
        return BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.Verify(password, user.PasswordHash) ? user : null;
    }

    // the user's JWT token, signed with the secret key
    public string CreateToken(User user)
    {
        var descriptor = new SecurityTokenDescriptor
        {
            // the content of the token: the "claims" (statements about the user)
            Claims = new Dictionary<string, object>
            {
                ["sub"] = user.Login,
                ["name"] = user.Name,
                ["role"] = user.Role,
            },
            Expires = DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes(configuration.GetValue<int>("Jwt:DurationMinutes")),
            SigningCredentials = new SigningCredentials(Key(configuration), SecurityAlgorithms.HmacSha256),
        };
        return new JsonWebTokenHandler().CreateToken(descriptor);
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 10: the name of the cookie that carries the token;
  • Lines 13–14: The signature key, generated from the text of [appsettings.json]. [IConfiguration] provides access to the configuration; ["Jwt:Secret"] refers to the [Secret] property in the [Jwt] section. The same key is used to sign and verify tokens (symmetric algorithm);
  • lines 17–24: verification of the username and password;
  • lines 33–37: the token’s content, the claims (statements about the user). [sub] ([subject]) is the conventional name for the user’s identifier. We include what the pages need (name, role) so we don’t have to query the database with every request;
  • line 39: the token’s expiration date;
  • line 40: the signature key and algorithm;
  • line 42: the class [JsonWebTokenHandler] (package [Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens], provided by [JwtBearer]) generates the signed token.

The file [Program.cs]:

using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Example25.Auth;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews();
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));
builder.Services.AddSingleton<UsersService>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<AuthService>();

// authentication: a JWT token, verified at each request
builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.MapInboundClaims = false; // keep the claim names as they are ("sub", "role"...)
        options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
        {
            ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,
            IssuerSigningKey = AuthService.Key(builder.Configuration), // the signature must be ours
            ValidateLifetime = true,                                   // the token must not be expired
            ValidateIssuer = false,
            ValidateAudience = false,
            NameClaimType = "name", // User.Identity.Name
            RoleClaimType = "role", // [Authorize(Roles = ...)], User.IsInRole(...)
        };
        options.Events = new JwtBearerEvents
        {
            // 1. the token is read from the cookie (and not from the Authorization header)
            OnMessageReceived = context =>
            {
                context.Token = context.Request.Cookies[AuthService.Cookie];
                return Task.CompletedTask;
            },
            // 2. protected page without a valid token: off to the login page
            OnChallenge = context =>
            {
                context.HandleResponse(); // we build the response ourselves (no 401)
                context.Response.Redirect("/login");
                return Task.CompletedTask;
            },
        };
    });
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});
app.UseAuthentication(); // who is it? -> HttpContext.User
app.UseAuthorization();  // is it allowed? -> [Authorize]

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 16–17: We declare the [JwtBearer] authentication schema and set it as the default schema;
  • line 19: By default, [JwtBearer] renames certain claims using long names inherited from Microsoft technologies ([role] would become [http://schemas.microsoft.com/ws/2008/06/identity/claims/role]). We retain the token names;
  • Lines 20–26: The checks performed on each token: the signature (using our key) and the expiration date. Our tokens do not specify either the issuer ([issuer]) or the recipient ([audience]), so we do not verify them;
  • lines 27–28: which claim contains the user’s name ([User.Identity.Name]), and which one contains their role ([[Authorize(Roles = ...)]], [User.IsInRole(...)]);
  • lines 33–36: the events from [JwtBearer] allow its behavior to be customized. By default, it looks for the token in the [Authorization: Bearer ...] header of the request: this is how a [JavaScript] client or a mobile app operates. A browser does not add this header on its own: the token is retrieved from the cookie;
  • lines 39–42: the challenge occurs when a protected page is requested without a valid token. By default, the response is a 401 error with no content: useful for a [JavaScript] client, but confusing for a user. The user is redirected to the login page. [HandleResponse()] tells [JwtBearer] that the response is being handled;
  • lines 56–57: the two middleware components, in this order: first determine who the user is, then verify their permissions.

The file [Controllers/AuthController.cs]:

using Example25.Auth;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example25.Controllers;

public class AuthController(AuthService auth, IConfiguration configuration) : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Home() => Redirect("/profile");

    [HttpGet("login")]
    public IActionResult Form() => View("Login");

    [HttpPost("login")]
    public IActionResult Login(string? login, string? password)
    {
        var user = auth.Validate(login, password);
        if (user is null)
        {
            // a deliberately vague message: we do not say whether it is the login or the password
            ViewData["Error"] = "Incorrect login or password.";
            ViewData["Login"] = login;
            return View("Login");
        }
        // the token, in a cookie that the page's JavaScript cannot read
        Response.Cookies.Append(AuthService.Cookie, auth.CreateToken(user), new CookieOptions
        {
            HttpOnly = true,
            SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax,
            MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(configuration.GetValue<int>("Jwt:DurationMinutes")),
        });
        return Redirect("/profile");
    }

    // logging out changes the user's state: it is a POST
    [HttpPost("logout")]
    public IActionResult Logout()
    {
        Response.Cookies.Delete(AuthService.Cookie);
        return Redirect("/login");
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 14–23: the login. If the login fails, the form is redisplayed with a deliberately vague message: saying “this login does not exist” would help an attacker find valid logins;
  • lines 26–32: if successful, the token is stored in an [HttpOnly] cookie; the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it, which protects the token if a malicious script were to execute on the page. [SameSite = Lax]: The cookie is not included in POST requests sent from another site, which protects against request forgery ([CSRF]). The cookie’s lifetime matches that of the token;
  • Lines 36–40: Logging out deletes the cookie ([Cookies.Delete]). This is a POST: it changes the user’s status (see Example 21).

The file [Controllers/ProfileController.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example25.Controllers;

// [Authorize]: reserved for authenticated users
[Authorize]
public class ProfileController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("profile")]
    public IActionResult Profile()
    {
        // User: the user authenticated by the token (HttpContext.User)
        return View(User.Claims.Select(c => (c.Type, c.Value)).ToList());
    }
}
  • Line 7: The [[Authorize]] attribute, set on the controller, restricts all its actions to authenticated users. This is an authorization filter (see Chapter 7). Without a valid token, it triggers the challenge, resulting in a redirect to [/login];
  • Line 14: [User] (the [HttpContext.User] from the request) is the user established by [JwtBearer] based on the token. [User.Claims] is the list of its claims; this is converted into a list of (type, value) pairs for the view.

The file [Views/Profile/Profile.cshtml]:

@model List<(string Type, string Value)>
<h1 class="h3">Hello @User.Identity!.Name</h1>
<p>Your role: <b>@(User.IsInRole("ADMIN") ? "administrator" : "user")</b>.</p>
<p>The content of your token:</p>
<table class="table table-sm w-auto">
  @foreach (var (type, value) in Model)
  {
    <tr><td><code>@type</code></td><td>@value</td></tr>
  }
</table>
@* logging out: a POST form reduced to its button *@
<form method="post" action="/logout">
  <button class="btn btn-outline-secondary" type="submit">Log out</button>
</form>
  • line 2: the property [User] is also accessible in a view. The name is the claim [name] (see [NameClaimType]);
  • line 3: [IsInRole] tests the claim [role] (see [RoleClaimType]);
  • line 6: the loop breaks down each pair into two variables;
  • line 12: logout via a POST form.

The file [Views/Auth/Login.cshtml]:

<h1 class="h3">Login</h1>
<form method="post" action="/login">
  <div class="mb-2">
    <label class="form-label" for="login">Login</label>
    <input class="form-control" id="login" name="login" value="@ViewData["Login"]" required>
  </div>
  <div class="mb-3">
    <label class="form-label" for="password">Password</label>
    <input class="form-control" type="password" id="password" name="password" required>
  </div>
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Log in</button>
</form>
@if (ViewData["Error"] is string error)
{
  <div class="alert alert-danger mt-3">@error</div>
}
<p class="text-muted small mt-3">Test accounts (password = login): marie (USER), admin (ADMIN).</p>

docs.title: 8.1.1. Execution
docs.text:
Without a cookie, the protected page redirects to the login page:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Location: /login

An incorrect password:

Successful login, as seen by [curl]:

curl -i -c cookies.txt -d "login=marie&password=marie" http://localhost:5000/login

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Location: /profile
Set-Cookie: token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJleHAiOjE3OTAzMzU1MzgsInN1YiI6Im1hcmllIiwibmFtZSI6Ik1hcmllIFDDqWxpc3NpZXIiLCJyb2xlIjoiVVNFUiIsImlhdCI6MTc5MDMzMTkzOCwibmJmIjoxNzkwMzMxOTM4fQ.uAKi5OB-jReuSrQR12_AWdiLR1l6ZLORBYSfHwg99xk; max-age=3600; path=/; samesite=lax; httponly

The token consists of three parts separated by periods: a header, the content, and the signature. The first two are simply encoded as [base64url]. The decoded header:

{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}

(the signature algorithm and the token type). The decoded content:

{
  "exp": 1790335538,
  "sub": "marie",
  "name": "Marie Pélissier",
  "role": "USER",
  "iat": 1790331938,
  "nbf": 1790331938
}

We find the claims generated by [CreateToken], plus three fields added by [JsonWebTokenHandler]: [exp] (the expiration date), [iat] ([issued at], the creation date), and [nbf] ([not before], the date from which the token is valid), in seconds since January 1, 1970. The token is not encrypted: it does not contain any confidential information. In the browser, at the URL http://localhost:5000/profile:

Now let’s try modifying the token to assign ourselves the role ADMIN: we decode the content, replace [USER] with [ADMIN], and re-encode it… but we can’t recalculate the signature without the secret key:

curl -i -b "token=eyJhbGciOi...(modified content)...(old signature)" http://localhost:5000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Location: /login

The signature no longer matches the content: the token is rejected, the user is not authenticated, and [[Authorize]] redirects to the login page. Logout:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -X POST http://localhost:5000/logout

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Location: /login
Set-Cookie: token=; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; path=/

The server deletes the cookie by resetting it—empty—with an expired expiration date.

docs.title: 8.2. Example 26: Roles
docs.text:
Example 26 builds on Example 25 and adds a page reserved for the role ADMIN. With [ASP.NET Core], there is almost nothing to write: the role is a claim in the token, and [[Authorize]] knows how to verify it. The [Controllers/AdminController.cs] file:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example26.Controllers;

// the whole controller is reserved for the ADMIN role: one must be authenticated
// AND have the "role" claim equal to "ADMIN" (see RoleClaimType in Program.cs)
[Authorize(Roles = "ADMIN")]
public class AdminController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("admin")]
    public IActionResult Admin() => View();
}
  • Line 8: The entire controller is reserved for the role ADMIN. The filter first checks that the user is authenticated (if not: challenge, i.e., the login page), then that the user has the requested role (if not: 403 response, “access denied”). [Roles = "ADMIN,DOCTOR"] would accept either of these roles.

The file [Program.cs] has only one additional line:

var app = builder.Build();

// 403 (insufficient role), 404...: an error page
app.UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/error/{0}");
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});
app.UseAuthentication(); // who is it? -> HttpContext.User
app.UseAuthorization();  // is it allowed? -> [Authorize]

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
  • Line 4: The 403 response has no content; it is rendered as a page by the [ErrorController] controller (see Example 24).

User [marie] (role USER) is attempting to open the administration page from their profile:

The same attempt by [admin]:

With [curl], we see a 403 error:

curl -i -c cookies.txt -d "login=marie&password=marie" http://localhost:5000/login
curl -i -b cookies.txt http://localhost:5000/admin

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Authentication</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 34rem">
    <div class="alert alert-danger">
  <h1 class="h4">Error 403</h1>
  <p class="mb-0">Access denied: this page is reserved for administrators.</p>
</div>
<p><a href="/profile">Back to the profile</a></p>

  </div>
</body>
</html>

The case study has three roles (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER) and uses exactly these attributes: [[Authorize]] on all page controllers, [[Authorize(Roles = "ADMIN")]] for doctor and client management, and [[Authorize(Roles = "USER")]] for the patient area. The 403 page is translated there.

docs.title: 8.3. Example 27: CAPTCHA and attempt limits
docs.text:
A login page attracts bots: programs that try thousands of login/password combinations. Two complementary safeguards:

  • a CAPTCHA: an image of distorted characters that a human can easily read but that a simple bot cannot decipher;
  • an attempt limit: after a few failed attempts, the address IP is blocked for a while.

Example 27 adds these two safeguards to Example 25. The file [Auth/CaptchaService.cs]:

using System.Collections.Concurrent;

namespace Example27.Auth;

// a captcha: its identifier, and its image (SVG)
public record Captcha(string Id, string Svg);

// singleton: the pending captchas are kept in memory by the server
public class CaptchaService
{
    private static readonly TimeSpan Lifetime = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10);

    // identifier -> (expected answer, expiry date).
    // ConcurrentDictionary: a dictionary usable by several simultaneous requests
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, (string Text, DateTime Expires)> pending = new();

    public Captcha Generate()
    {
        var text = CaptchaDrawing.RandomText(5);
        var id = Guid.NewGuid().ToString(); // a random identifier, impossible to guess
        pending[id] = (text, DateTime.UtcNow + Lifetime);
        return new Captcha(id, CaptchaDrawing.Svg(text));
    }

    // the captcha is CONSUMED in every case: an image is used only once
    public bool Check(string? id, string? input)
    {
        if (id is null || input is null || !pending.TryRemove(id, out var expected))
        {
            return false;
        }
        return expected.Expires > DateTime.UtcNow
            && string.Equals(expected.Text, input.Trim(), StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 15: the expected responses are stored by the server under a random identifier. The page contains only the image and the identifier: the response never leaves the server. The service is a singleton, used by concurrent requests: [ConcurrentDictionary] is a dictionary designed for this purpose;
  • lines 17–22: a five-character text string is randomly selected, stored, and drawn as an image. The drawing is handled by the class [CaptchaDrawing] (file [Auth/CaptchaDrawing.cs], taken from the case study and commented on line by line): each character is a set of lines that is enlarged, tilted, and randomly distorted, and the image is blurred by three curves. Characters that are easily confused (0 and O, 1, I and L) are excluded;
  • lines 26–33: the verification process consumes the CAPTCHA ([TryRemove] removes it from the dictionary): an image is used only once; a bot cannot reuse a solution it has already found. Uppercase letters do not count.

The file [Auth/LimiterService.cs]:

namespace Example27.Auth;

// singleton: counts the login failures of each IP address
public class LimiterService
{
    private const int MaxFailures = 3;
    private static readonly TimeSpan BlockDuration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);

    private class Counter
    {
        public int Failures;
        public DateTime BlockedUntil;
    }

    private readonly Dictionary<string, Counter> counters = [];
    private readonly Lock padlock = new(); // several simultaneous requests: one access at a time

    // the number of remaining blocking seconds (0: not blocked)
    public int BlockedSeconds(string ip)
    {
        lock (padlock)
        {
            if (!counters.TryGetValue(ip, out var c)) return 0;
            var remaining = c.BlockedUntil - DateTime.UtcNow;
            return remaining > TimeSpan.Zero ? (int)Math.Ceiling(remaining.TotalSeconds) : 0;
        }
    }

    public void Failure(string ip)
    {
        lock (padlock)
        {
            if (!counters.TryGetValue(ip, out var c))
            {
                c = new Counter();
                counters[ip] = c;
            }
            c.Failures++;
            if (c.Failures >= MaxFailures)
            {
                c.BlockedUntil = DateTime.UtcNow + BlockDuration;
                c.Failures = 0; // after the block, we start again from zero
            }
        }
    }

    public void Success(string ip)
    {
        lock (padlock)
        {
            counters.Remove(ip);
        }
    }
}
  • lines 6–7: three failed attempts block the address IP for one minute;
  • line 16: the counter dictionary is shared by all queries. The instruction [lock (padlock) { ... }] ensures that only one query at a time executes the block: two simultaneous failures cannot be lost (see [Interlocked], Chapter 6). [Lock] is the lock type for [.NET] 9 and later versions;
  • lines 19–25: the remaining lock time;
  • lines 29–42: a failure is counted; on the third failure, the address is blocked;
  • lines 47–51: a success resets the counter to zero.

The file [Controllers/AuthController.cs]:

using Example27.Auth;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example27.Controllers;

public class AuthController(AuthService auth, CaptchaService captchas, LimiterService limiter,
    IConfiguration configuration) : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Home() => Redirect("/profile");

    [HttpGet("login")]
    public IActionResult Form() => LoginPage(null, null);

    [HttpPost("login")]
    public IActionResult Login(string? login, string? password, string? captchaId, string? captcha)
    {
        // the client's IP address
        var ip = HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "?";

        // 1. a blocked address is not even listened to
        var seconds = limiter.BlockedSeconds(ip);
        if (seconds > 0)
        {
            return LoginPage(login, $"Too many attempts: try again in {seconds} s.");
        }
        // 2. the captcha first (cheap), the password (bcrypt, expensive) next
        if (!captchas.Check(captchaId, captcha))
        {
            limiter.Failure(ip);
            return LoginPage(login, "The image code is incorrect.");
        }
        var user = auth.Validate(login, password);
        if (user is null)
        {
            limiter.Failure(ip);
            return LoginPage(login, "Incorrect login or password.");
        }
        limiter.Success(ip);
        Response.Cookies.Append(AuthService.Cookie, auth.CreateToken(user), new CookieOptions
        {
            HttpOnly = true,
            SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax,
            MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(configuration.GetValue<int>("Jwt:DurationMinutes")),
        });
        return Redirect("/profile");
    }

    [HttpPost("logout")]
    public IActionResult Logout()
    {
        Response.Cookies.Delete(AuthService.Cookie);
        return Redirect("/login");
    }

    // each display of the form builds a NEW captcha
    private ViewResult LoginPage(string? login, string? error)
    {
        ViewData["Login"] = login;
        ViewData["Error"] = error;
        return View("Login", captchas.Generate());
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 19: the client’s address, IP, provided by the network connection;
  • lines 22–25: A blocked address isn’t even listened to;
  • lines 28–31: the CAPTCHA is verified first, then the password (a computationally expensive [bcrypt] operation) only if the CAPTCHA is correct. An incorrect CAPTCHA counts as a failure;
  • lines 57–61: Each time the form is displayed, a new CAPTCHA is generated, which becomes the view’s template.

The file [Views/Auth/Login.cshtml]:

    <label class="form-label" for="captcha">Copy the code of the image</label>

  • line 15: the image SVG is text (from XML): it is inserted into the page as-is. [Html.Raw] is legitimate here: it is HTML generated by the server, not user input;
  • Line 17: The CAPTCHA ID is passed in a hidden field; the response, however, remains on the server.

The login page, at URL http://localhost:5000/login:

An incorrectly entered CAPTCHA:

After three failed attempts, even the correct password is rejected for one minute:

docs.title: 11.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The RdvMedecins application manages appointments for a medical practice. Each doctor has time slots (from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. in 20-minute increments, for example); an appointment consists of a day, a time slot, and a client (a patient). This is the exact implementation, in [ASP.NET Core MVC], of the [NestJS] application from the previous lesson: same database, same business rules, same pages, same translation dictionaries. The HTML pages are generated by the server using [Razor] views.

Three user roles share the application:

RoleWhoWhat it can doADMINThe administrator ([admin])View schedules, make and cancel appointments for any patient; manage (list, add, edit, delete) doctors and clientsDOCTORDoctorsView schedules, make appointments, and cancel appointments for any patientUSERclients (patients)view schedules without seeing other patients’ names; book an appointment for themselves; cancel their appointment; manage their account; create an account

Key management rules:

  • No appointments in the past;
  • a time slot can only be booked once per day;
  • a patient may have only one upcoming appointment at a time;
  • Two doctors (or two clients) cannot have the same first and last names, and a login belongs to only one account;
  • A doctor with appointments cannot be deleted; A client is deleted along with their appointments;
  • the login page is protected against bots (CAPTCHA, limited attempts), and creating a client account requires first solving the CAPTCHA on that page.

docs.title: 11.4. The application architecture
docs.text:
• [Program.cs] configures the application: services (dependency injection), middleware (static files, error pages, language, authentication), controllers;
  • [Auth]: connection, JWT tokens, roles, CAPTCHA, and attempt limits;
  • [Controllers]: web layer controllers. They all pass through a single service, [ApplicationModel] (folder [Web]), which stores the lists of doctors and clients in memory and forwards other requests to the business layer;
  • [Web]: Common elements of the web layer: translation, flash messages, validation, view parent class, exception filter; [Models]: Form and view templates;
  • [Business]: business rules;
  • [Repositories]: the DAO layer, one class per table; [Data]: the [DbContext] layer of EF Core;
  • [Entities]: the EF Core entities; [Domain]: the calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [Views]: the views [Razor]; [i18n]: dictionaries; [wwwroot]: the style sheet, the page script, and [Bootstrap].

The suite comments on all files, from the lower layers (database) to the upper layers (views).

docs.title: 11.5. The database
docs.text: The [dbrdvmedecins2] database is created by the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script, which is run in the same way as in Example 28 (the [HeidiSQL] tool from [Laragon], or the [mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] command). It is, word for word, the script for the [NestJS] application: both applications can work on the same database, and one can replace the other without making any changes.

docs.title: 11.5.1. database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Evolution of [dbrdvmedecins]:
--   1. the [doctors] and [clients] tables get a [user] column,
--      foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--      now also a user able to log in;
--   2. a third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--   3. the script creates a [users] row for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--      and for each client (role USER):
--        - login        = last name in lower case
--        - password     = last name in lower case, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--        - display name = first name + last name
--
--   4. uniqueness constraints, all NAMED (the application recognizes
--      the name of the violated constraint in the MySQL error message):
--        - unq_users_login                   : a login belongs to one account only;
--        - unq_doctors_first_name_last_name  : two doctors cannot have the
--                                              same first and last names;
--        - unq_clients_first_name_last_name  : same for the clients.
--      Beware: the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares regardless of
--      case and accents - "Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--      are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The [users] table must now be created BEFORE [doctors] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and dropped AFTER them.
-- =========================================================================

-- we start again from an empty database on each run of the script (handy in development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- drop order: from the "child" tables to the "parent" tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS appointments;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slots;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS doctors;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: the users allowed to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login identifier
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HASHED password (bcrypt) - never in clear
  name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- name displayed once logged in
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR' or 'USER'
  -- a login can belong to one account only
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [doctors]: the doctors of the practice
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE doctors (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,            -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,              -- Melle, Mme, Mr
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_doctors_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two doctors cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: the doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per client, and one client per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [slots]: the time slots of each doctor
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE slots (
  id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  doctor_id    INT NOT NULL,                     -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  start_hour   INT NOT NULL,                     -- start hour of the slot
  start_minute INT NOT NULL,                     -- start minute of the slot
  end_hour     INT NOT NULL,                     -- end hour of the slot
  end_minute   INT NOT NULL,                     -- end minute of the slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY (doctor_id) REFERENCES doctors(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [appointments]: the appointments booked by the clients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE appointments (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  day        DATE NOT NULL,                      -- day of the appointment
  slot_id    INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> slots(id)
  client_id  INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> clients(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_slot   FOREIGN KEY (slot_id)   REFERENCES slots(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_client FOREIGN KEY (client_id) REFERENCES clients(id),
  -- the same slot, on the same day, can be booked only once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- the users: passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds)
--   admin/admin (ADMIN)
--   one DOCTOR account per doctor, one USER account per client
--   (the user/user demo account is gone: a USER account is
--   now ALWAYS a client's account, who can book and manage the account)
--   (login = password = last name in lower case)

  ('admin',     '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrator',    'ADMIN'),
  -- doctors

  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already booked, to see an occupied slot right away in the schedule
INSERT INTO appointments (day, slot_id, client_id) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);

Let’s go over this script:

  • Line 30: The database is created if it does not yet exist, using the character set [utf8mb4] and the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci], as in Example 28: string comparisons are case-insensitive and ignore accents. This also applies to uniqueness constraints: [Hélène DUPONT] and [helene dupont] are, for [MySQL], two instances of the same person;
  • Lines 34–38: The script starts with an empty database on each execution. Tables are deleted from the “child” tables to the “parent” tables: a table referenced by a foreign key ([users], for example, referenced by [doctors] and [clients]) cannot be deleted as long as another table still references it. Tables are created in the reverse order;
  • lines 43–52: user accounts. Each table begins with a primary key [id], assigned by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]), and a column [version], which is set to 0 when the row is created;
  • rows 46–49: the login, password, display name after logging in, and role ([ADMIN], [DOCTOR], or [USER]). The [password] column never contains the password itself, but rather its hash, [bcrypt] (see Example 25): 60 characters, hence the column width;
  • Line 51: A login belongs to only one account. As in Example 28, the constraint is named: when [MySQL] rejects a write operation, its error message specifies the name of the violated constraint, and the business layer uses this to select the message to display (see [Business/BusinessService.cs]);
  • lines 57–69: doctors: title, last name, first name;
  • Line 59: The column [version] is used for optimistic locking (see Example 28): it is incremented each time the row is modified, which makes it possible to detect whether another user has modified the row between the time it was read and the time it was written. As in Example 28, the application increments this value (see [DbContext], below);
  • lines 63–64: Each doctor has an account: the column [user] is a foreign key referencing [users(id)]. The database rejects a value that does not refer to any account, and refuses to delete an account that is still referenced by a doctor. Since [user] is a reserved word in [MySQL], the column name is enclosed in backticks;
  • line 66: an account belongs to only one doctor: the relationship between [doctors] and [users] is a “one-to-one” relationship;
  • line 68: Two doctors cannot have the same first and last names. The constraint applies to the pair of columns: two doctors can have the same last name if they do not have the same first name;
  • Lines 74–86: Clients (patients), following the same pattern: one account per client (foreign key [fk_clients_user], uniqueness constraint [unq_clients_user]); no two clients can have the same first and last names;
  • rows 91–100: each doctor’s time slots (foreign key [doctor_id]): start hour and minute, end hour and minute. A time slot does not have a date; it repeats every day;
  • lines 105–115: appointments: a date (type [DATE], without a time), a time slot, and a client, identified by two foreign keys;
  • line 114: the same time slot can only be booked once per day. The database itself enforces this rule: if two users book the same time slot at the same time, the second [INSERT] is rejected, regardless of what the application verified just before;
  • Lines 127–137: Demo accounts: the administrator, three doctors (role [DOCTOR]), and four clients (role [USER]). Each user’s password is their login ([admin] / [admin], [pelissier] / [pelissier]...). The hashes begin with [$2b$10$]: the algorithm [bcrypt], with a cost of 10 (see Example 25); the application’s library [BCrypt.Net-Next] knows how to verify them;
  • lines 141–144: each doctor’s [user] column is retrieved via a subquery on the login, rather than assuming the identifiers assigned by the database to the accounts;
  • lines 146–150: clients are handled in the same way;
  • lines 153–157: twelve 20-minute time slots, from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., for Dr. PELISSIER. Here, the doctor’s ID (1) is hard-coded: the table [doctors] has just been created, so its IDs start at 1;
  • lines 160–164: twelve time slots, from 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM, for Dr. TATOU. Dr. DUPONT has no time slots: his schedule is empty;
  • lines 167–168: an appointment has already been scheduled for Brigitte BISTROU (client #3) during the second time slot of Dr. PELISSIER (8:20 a.m.). [CURDATE()] is the date the script is run: upon the first login, today’s calendar shows a slot that is already booked.

docs.title: 11.6.1. RdvMedecins.csproj
docs.text:
<!--
  =========================================================================
  RdvMedecins.csproj - the project file (the equivalent of package.json).

  Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web: the SDK of ASP.NET Core applications. On its own it
  brings the whole web framework (MVC, Razor views, authentication,
  localization, static files...): only the libraries
  EXTERNAL to the framework are listed below (PackageReference), and
  downloaded from nuget.org by [dotnet restore] / [dotnet build].
  =========================================================================
-->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <!-- .NET 10, LTS version (long-term support) -->
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <!-- "nullable" reference types: the compiler reports the risks of
         NullReferenceException (the equivalent of strictNullChecks in TypeScript) -->
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <!-- implicit usings: System, System.Linq, System.Threading.Tasks... -->
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <RootNamespace>RdvMedecins</RootNamespace>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- Entity Framework Core + its MySQL / MariaDB provider.
         Pomelo itself pulls Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore (and MySqlConnector,
         the ADO.NET driver) in the version that matches it. -->
    <PackageReference Include="Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql" Version="9.0.0" />
    <!-- JWT token authentication (reading and verifying the token) -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer" Version="10.0.0" />
    <!-- password hashing (bcrypt), compatible with the
         $2b$ hashes of the SQL script -->
    <PackageReference Include="BCrypt.Net-Next" Version="4.0.3" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the translation dictionaries are read at startup. The Web SDK
         already puts all .json files among the files to publish (Content):
         we simply specify to always copy them (dotnet publish) -->
    <Content Update="i18n\*.json" CopyToPublishDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
    <!-- the SQL script does not need to be published -->
    <Content Remove="database\**" />
    <None Include="database\**" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Let’s go over this file:

  • line 12: the SDK for web applications, as in all the examples (see introduction);
  • lines 14–23: the settings that the examples found in the shared file [examples/Directory.Build.props]: [.NET] 10, “nullable” reference types, [using] implicit. The case study is a standalone project: it writes these files itself. [RootNamespace] is the project’s root namespace, the one that [Visual Studio Code] proposes for a new file;
  • line 29: the [MySQL] provider from EF Core, which includes EF Core and the [MySqlConnector] driver (see Example 28);
  • lines 31–34: the two authentication packages, already used in Chapter 8: JWT token verification and password hashing;
  • line 41: the translation dictionaries [i18n/*.json] are read from disk at startup. When preparing the application for a production server (command [dotnet publish]), they must be copied along with it: this is what [CopyToPublishDirectory] does;
  • Lines 43–44: The script SQL is not an application file; it is excluded from the published files, as shown in Example 28.

docs.title: 11.6.2. appsettings.json
docs.text:
The file [appsettings.json] serves the same purpose as the file [.env] in the [NestJS] application. One important difference: the file [.env] was never shared, and a file named [.env.example] served as its template. Here, [appsettings.json] is part of the project; machine-specific values (such as a password) can be provided in another way, without modifying it (see below).

// =========================================================================
// appsettings.json - the configuration of the application (the equivalent of
// the .env file of the NestJS project). ASP.NET Core accepts comments
// in this JSON file.
//
// The sensitive values (MySQL password, JWT secret) can be
// replaced without touching this file: environment variables or
// "user secrets" (see README.md, Configuration section).
// =========================================================================
{
  // listening port. The JSON server already listens on 8080: we choose another
  // port to be able to run both at the same time.
  "Urls": "http://localhost:8081",

  // connection to the MySQL database [dbrdvmedecins2] (script: database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql)
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "RdvMedecins": "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbrdvmedecins2;User=root;Password=;"
  },
  "MySql": {
    // server version, so that EF Core generates the right SQL dialect:
    // "8.0.0-mysql" for MySQL 8, "10.11.0-mariadb" for MariaDB 10.11...
    "ServerVersion": "8.0.0-mysql"
  },

  // authentication (see Auth/)
  "Auth": {
    // secret key of the JWT tokens: at least 32 characters (HMAC-SHA256).
    // Must absolutely be changed in production (long random string).
    "JwtSecret": "change-me-to-a-long-random-string",
    // validity duration of a token, in seconds (7200 s = 2 h); the cookie
    // that carries the token has the same lifetime
    "JwtExpiresInSeconds": 7200,
    // true in production (site served over HTTPS): the authentication cookie
    // is then never sent over an unencrypted connection
    "CookieSecure": false
  },

  // protection against robots (see Auth/AttemptLimiterService.cs)
  "Protection": {
    // login: failures allowed for the same login from the same IP address...
    "LoginMaxFailures": 5,
    // ... before a block of this duration (the whole IP address is also
    // blocked if it accumulates 5 times more failures, all logins combined)
    "LoginBlockMinutes": 15,
    // client account creation: at most this many accounts created per hour and per
    // IP address. In a classroom, all the computers often go out through the
    // same address: increase if needed.
    "RegistrationMaxPerHour": 10
  },

  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning",
      "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore": "Warning"
    }
  },
  "AllowedHosts": "*"
}

Let’s go over this file:

  • lines 1–9: Unlike the standard JSON, [ASP.NET Core] allows comments in its configuration files;
  • line 13: the address and listening port. The examples listened on port 5000, the default port; the application listens on port 8081, like the [NestJS] version;
  • lines 16–18: the connection string to the [dbrdvmedecins2] database, using the default values from [Laragon] (username [root], no password); see Example 28;
  • lines 19–23: the server version, which tells the provider [Pomelo] which dialect SQL to generate (see Example 28);
  • lines 26–36: the authentication section: the secret key that signs the tokens (at least 32 characters; must be replaced in production), the token’s lifetime (two hours), and the [Secure] option in the cookie that carries it. In production, the site is served as HTTPS, and the cookie must never travel over an unencrypted connection: the option is set to [true];
  • lines 39–49: bot protection thresholds (see Example 27): number of allowed failed login attempts and duration of the resulting block; number of customer accounts created per hour from the same IP address IP;
  • lines 51–57: logging levels (see introduction). Messages from EF Core are only displayed starting at level [Warning]: SQL commands, which are at level [Information], do not appear (see Example 28);
  • Line 58: All domain names are accepted.

The sections [Auth] and [Protection] are interpreted as typed classes (see [Config/AuthOptions.cs], below). Each value is designated by its path, with the levels separated by [:]: [Auth:JwtSecret], [ConnectionStrings:RdvMedecins], [MySql:ServerVersion]. [ASP.NET Core] reads the configuration from several successive sources, each of which can override the values from the previous ones: [appsettings.json], then [appsettings.{environment}.json] (see the next file), then, in development, “user secrets” (values stored outside the project, in the user’s profile), then environment variables, and finally command-line arguments. A password can thus be provided via an environment variable, where [:] is written as [__]:

export ConnectionStrings__RdvMedecins="Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbrdvmedecins2;User=root;Password=myPassword;"

The application’s [README.md] file details these options.

docs.title: 11.6.3. appsettings.Development.json
docs.text:
// Override of appsettings.json in development (ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=
// Development, see Properties/launchSettings.json): we display in the
// console the SQL queries generated by EF Core - as the
// logging: true option of TypeORM did.
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning",
      "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command": "Information"
    }
  }
}
  • Line 10: [ASP.NET Core] knows the environment in which the application is running: [Development], [Production]... It reads this from the environment variable [ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT] (see the following file); otherwise, it uses [Production]. After [appsettings.json], it reads the file [appsettings.{environment}.json], if it exists, and merges the two: the keys present in the second file replace those in the first, while the others are retained. During development, we therefore add the level [Information] for the category [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command]: the more specific rule takes precedence over the more general one for [appsettings.json] ([Warning] for any [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore]), and every SQL command sent to the database is displayed in the console. This is equivalent to the [logging] option of [TypeORM], which the [NestJS] version enabled outside of production. All other values (connection, authentication, etc.) remain the same as in [appsettings.json].

docs.text:
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/launchsettings.json",
  "profiles": {
    "http": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "dotnetRunMessages": true,
      "launchBrowser": true,

        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
