docs.title: 11.12.4.1. The descriptors
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Business/BusinessService.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Implementation of the business layer.
//
// The management of the doctors and clients obeys three business rules:
//
//   1. a person (doctor or client) and their user account go
//      ALWAYS together: they are created, updated and deleted together, in
//      the same TRANSACTION - either everything succeeds, or nothing is written;
//   2. the login is unique in the whole application, and two doctors (or
//      two clients) cannot have the same first and last names;
//   3. deletion:
//      - a DOCTOR who has appointments cannot be deleted (their
//        patients would lose their appointment without being warned): they must
//        first be cancelled. Their time slots disappear with them;
//      - a CLIENT, on the other hand, disappears with ALL their appointments (past and
//        future) - whether the deletion comes from the ADMIN or from the patient
//        themselves.
//
// And two rules for booking appointments, whatever the role of
// the one who books (ADMIN, DOCTOR or the patient themselves):
//   4. no appointment in the past;
//   5. a patient has only ONE upcoming appointment at a time.
//
// Doctors and clients follow exactly the same rules: the common code
// is written ONCE (generic private methods XxxPersonAsync<T>), and
// parameterized by a small "descriptor" that says which type of person we are
// dealing with.
// =========================================================================

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using MySqlConnector;
using RdvMedecins.Data;
using RdvMedecins.Domain;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;
using RdvMedecins.Repositories;

namespace RdvMedecins.Business;

public class BusinessService : IBusiness
{
    // number of bcrypt salting rounds - the same as in the SQL script ($2b$10$...)
    private const int BcryptRounds = 10;

    // everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client for the business rules.
    // "where T : Person, new()": T is a Person, and we can write new T().
    private record PersonDescriptor<T>(
        PersonRepository<T> Dao,
        Role Role, // DOCTOR or USER
        string NotFoundKey, // message if the person does not exist
        string AlreadyExistsKey, // message if the same first and last names already exist
        // optional: if present, the deletion is REFUSED as long as the
        // person has appointments (CountAppointments > 0), with the message HasAppointmentsKey
        Func<int, Task<int>>? CountAppointments = null,
        string? HasAppointmentsKey = null,
        // optional: what must be deleted BEFORE the person (the rows that
        // reference it through a foreign key)
        Func<int, Task>? BeforeDelete = null) where T : Person, new();

    private readonly RdvMedecinsDbContext db;
    private readonly DoctorRepository doctorRepository;
    private readonly ClientRepository clientRepository;
    private readonly SlotRepository slotRepository;
    private readonly AppointmentRepository appointmentRepository;
    private readonly UserRepository userRepository;
    private readonly PersonDescriptor<Doctor> doctorDescriptor;
    private readonly PersonDescriptor<Client> clientDescriptor;

    // all the dependencies are provided by the dependency injection
    // of ASP.NET Core (see Program.cs). The DbContext is used here ONLY to open
    // transactions - the queries themselves remain in the DAO layer.
    public BusinessService(
        RdvMedecinsDbContext db,
        DoctorRepository doctorRepository,
        ClientRepository clientRepository,
        SlotRepository slotRepository,
        AppointmentRepository appointmentRepository,
        UserRepository userRepository)
    {
        this.db = db;
        this.doctorRepository = doctorRepository;
        this.clientRepository = clientRepository;
        this.slotRepository = slotRepository;
        this.appointmentRepository = appointmentRepository;
        this.userRepository = userRepository;

        doctorDescriptor = new PersonDescriptor<Doctor>(
            doctorRepository,
            Role.DOCTOR,
            "ERRORS.DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND",
            "ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS",
            CountAppointments: appointmentRepository.CountByDoctorAsync,
            HasAppointmentsKey: "ERRORS.DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS",
            // a doctor without appointments may still have time slots:
            // they no longer make sense without them, we delete them with the doctor (otherwise
            // the foreign key slots.doctor_id would forbid the deletion)
            BeforeDelete: slotRepository.DeleteByDoctorAsync);

        clientDescriptor = new PersonDescriptor<Client>(
            clientRepository,
            Role.USER,
            "ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND",
            "ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS",
            // no CountAppointments: the deletion of a client is never refused;
            // their appointments (past and future) are deleted with them (otherwise
            // the foreign key appointments.client_id would forbid the deletion)
            BeforeDelete: appointmentRepository.DeleteByClientAsync);
    }
  • lines 6–29: The header comment summarizes the five business rules applied by the class;
  • line 34: the [MySQL] driver (see Chapter 9): the class uses its [MySqlException] exception to detect violations of uniqueness constraints;
  • line 42: the class implements the interface; it must provide all of its methods;
  • line 45: the cost of [bcrypt] (see Example 25), which is the same as that of the passwords in the SQL script (prefix [$2b$10$]);
  • lines 49–60: everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client in terms of business rules: their DAO, their account role ([DOCTOR] or [USER]), their error messages, and what happens when they are deleted. Since doctors and clients follow the same rules, the code for these rules is written only once, in generic methods (parameterized by a [T] type) that accept a descriptor. The constraint [where T : Person, new()] requires that [T] inherit from [Person] (we could read [LastName], [FirstName], [User]...) and have a parameterless constructor (we could write [new T()]). [Func<int, Task<int>>] is the type of a function that takes a [int] and returns a [Task<int>]; [Func<int, Task>] is the type of an asynchronous function that returns nothing. These parameters have a default value ([= null]): they are optional;
  • lines 62–69: the class fields: the [DbContext], the five DAO, and the two descriptors. [readonly] prevents them from being modified after the constructor;
  • lines 74–87: all dependencies are provided by dependency injection. The [DbContext] is used here only to open transactions: the requests remain in the DAO layer. As in Example 28, DAO and the business layer receive the same [DbContext] during a query, and thus the same connection and the same transaction;
  • Lines 89–99: the doctor descriptor. The named arguments ([CountAppointments:], [HasAppointmentsKey:]...) refer to a parameter by name, which allows optional parameters to be skipped (the client descriptor, further down, thus omits [CountAppointments] and [HasAppointmentsKey]). [appointmentRepository.CountByDoctorAsync] is not called here: the method itself is passed, and it will be called later (a method can thus serve as a value of type [Func]). Deleting a doctor will be denied as long as they have appointments; their time slots, however, will be deleted before the doctor is deleted;
  • Lines 101–109: The client descriptor. No [CountAppointments]: Deleting a client is never denied, and its appointments (past and future) are deleted before the client itself; otherwise, the foreign key [appointments.client_id] would prevent the deletion.

    // same algorithm as the JSON server (and as the original Spring project)
    public async Task<DoctorDaySchedule?> GetDoctorDayScheduleAsync(int doctorId, DateOnly day)
    {
        var doctor = await GetDoctorByIdAsync(doctorId);
        if (doctor is null)
        {
            return null;
        }
        var timeSlots = await GetAllSlotsAsync(doctorId);
        var bookings = await GetDoctorDayAppointmentsAsync(doctorId, day);
        // slot no. -> appointment booked on this slot
        var bookingsBySlot = bookings.ToDictionary(booking => booking.SlotId);
        var doctorDaySlots = timeSlots
            .Select(slot => new DoctorDaySlot(slot, bookingsBySlot.GetValueOrDefault(slot.Id)))
            .ToList();
        return new DoctorDaySchedule(doctor, day, doctorDaySlots);
    }

[Select] transforms each item in a list (see [LINQ], Chapter 9). The result is a [DoctorDaySchedule] object in the [Domain] folder, which the calendar view will display.

docs.text:
// =======================================================================
    // appointments
    // =======================================================================

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // booking of an appointment, in a transaction:
    //   1. no appointment in the past;
    //   2. we LOCK the row of the patient (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): if the
    //      same patient books two slots at the same instant (two tabs,
    //      double click...), the second transaction waits for the end of the
    //      first one - and then sees the appointment it has just created;
    //   3. a single upcoming appointment per patient;
    //   4. finally the insertion. If the slot has just been taken by ANOTHER
    //      patient, it is the SQL constraint unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) that
    //      refuses the insertion - translated into a BusinessException by TransactionAsync.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public Task<Appointment> AddAppointmentAsync(DateOnly day, Slot slot, Client client) =>
        TransactionAsync(async () =>
        {
            var today = Dates.Today();
            if (day < today)
            {
                throw new BusinessException("ERRORS.PAST_DATE");
            }
            if (await clientRepository.LockAsync(client.Id) is null)
            {
                throw new BusinessException("ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND");
            }
            if (await appointmentRepository.CountUpcomingByClientAsync(client.Id, today) > 0)
            {
                throw new BusinessException("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT");
            }
            // we fill in the foreign keys: no need to attach the
            // Slot and Client objects themselves to write the [appointments] row
            var appointment = new Appointment { Day = day, SlotId = slot.Id, ClientId = client.Id };
            return await appointmentRepository.SaveAsync(appointment);
        });

    public Task DeleteAppointmentAsync(Appointment appointment) => appointmentRepository.DeleteByIdAsync(appointment.Id);
  • lines 17–18: The entire booking takes place within a single transaction: the method passes an asynchronous anonymous function, [async () => { ... }], to [TransactionAsync] (see below), which performs the task;
  • lines 20–23: no appointments in the past. The rule is verified here regardless of the role of the person making the reservation (ADMIN, DOCTOR, or the patient), even if the web layer has already hidden the “Book” buttons for past dates: a request can be created manually;
  • lines 25–27: the patient’s record is locked: [LockAsync] executes [SELECT * FROM clients WHERE id = ... FOR UPDATE] (see [Repositories/PersonRepository.cs]). This is a pessimistic lock: it is acquired before processing begins, assuming a potential conflict, and remains in place until the end of the transaction. Without it, two reservations for the same patient sent at the exact same time (two tabs, a double-click) could both pass the following test before either one has written its appointment to the database. With this lock, the second transaction waits for the first to finish, then sees the appointment it created. A patient who cannot be found (deleted in the meantime) is rejected;
  • lines 29–31: only one upcoming appointment per patient;
  • lines 35–36: the insertion. Only the foreign keys [SlotId] and [ClientId] are specified: there is no need to link the objects [Slot] and [Client] to write the row [appointments]. If another patient has just booked the same time slot, the lock did not prevent it (the lock applies to the patient’s row): it is the database’s [unq1_appointments (day, slot_id)] uniqueness constraint that rejects the insertion, and [TransactionAsync] translates the error into [BusinessException] with the key [ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED];
  • Line 39: Cancellation of an appointment: a simple [DELETE], with no specific rules.

// =======================================================================
    // doctors and clients - the public methods delegate to the common
    // private methods, with the right descriptor
    // =======================================================================

    public Task<Doctor> AddDoctorAsync(PersonData data) => AddPersonAsync(doctorDescriptor, data);

    public Task<Doctor> EditDoctorAsync(int id, PersonData data) =>
        EditPersonAsync(doctorDescriptor, id, data);

    public Task DeleteDoctorAsync(int id) => DeletePersonAsync(doctorDescriptor, id);

    public Task<Client> AddClientAsync(PersonData data) => AddPersonAsync(clientDescriptor, data);

    public Task<Client> EditClientAsync(int id, PersonData data) =>
        EditPersonAsync(clientDescriptor, id, data);

    // the client, their account AND all their appointments (ADMIN, or the patient
    // themselves from "Manage my account": same method, same rule)
    public Task DeleteClientAsync(int id) => DeletePersonAsync(clientDescriptor, id);

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // creation: the user account first (the person references it),
    // then the person - all in ONE transaction.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private Task<T> AddPersonAsync<T>(PersonDescriptor<T> d, PersonData data) where T : Person, new()
    {
        var lastName = data.LastName.Trim().ToUpperInvariant();
        var firstName = data.FirstName.Trim();
        // the rules of the dbrdvmedecins2 database: login = last name in lower case,
        // password = login - unless the ADMIN has typed other ones
        var login = (string.IsNullOrEmpty(data.Login) ? lastName : data.Login).ToLowerInvariant();
        var password = string.IsNullOrEmpty(data.Password) ? login : data.Password;

        return TransactionAsync(async () =>
        {
            await CheckPersonUniqueAsync(d, firstName, lastName, null);
            await CheckLoginFreeAsync(login);

            var user = new User
            {
                Login = login,
                Password = BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.HashPassword(password, BcryptRounds),
                Name = $"{firstName} {lastName}",
                Role = d.Role,
            };
            await userRepository.SaveAsync(user);

            var person = new T { Title = data.Title, LastName = lastName, FirstName = firstName, User = user };
            return await d.Dao.SaveAsync(person);
        });
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // update: the person AND their account (the display name "firstName LASTNAME"
    // must follow; the login and the password only change if they have been
    // typed).
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private Task<T> EditPersonAsync<T>(PersonDescriptor<T> d, int id, PersonData data)
        where T : Person, new() =>
        TransactionAsync(async () =>
        {
            var person = await d.Dao.FindByIdAsync(id) ?? throw new BusinessException(d.NotFoundKey);

            // optimistic lock: if the version in the database is no longer the one of the
            // form, someone has modified this record in the meantime - we refuse
            // rather than silently overwrite their changes.
            // (If the concurrent update happens AFTER this read, it is
            // the "WHERE version = ..." clause of the UPDATE that detects it.)
            if (data.Version is not null && data.Version != person.Version)
            {
                throw new BusinessException("ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE");
            }

            // we merely modify the objects: the DbContext, which tracks them,
            // will send the necessary UPDATEs at the next SaveChangesAsync
            person.Title = data.Title;
            person.LastName = data.LastName.Trim().ToUpperInvariant();
            person.FirstName = data.FirstName.Trim();
            await CheckPersonUniqueAsync(d, person.FirstName, person.LastName, id);

            var user = person.User;
            user.Name = $"{person.FirstName} {person.LastName}";
            if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(data.Login) && data.Login.ToLowerInvariant() != user.Login)
            {
                var login = data.Login.ToLowerInvariant();
                await CheckLoginFreeAsync(login);
                user.Login = login;
            }
            if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(data.Password))
            {
                user.Password = BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.HashPassword(data.Password, BcryptRounds);
            }
            await userRepository.SaveAsync(user);
            return await d.Dao.SaveAsync(person);
        });

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // deletion, in ONE transaction, in the order imposed by the foreign
    // keys:
    //   1. possible refusal if appointments remain (doctor);
    //   2. what references the person (slots of a doctor, appointments
    //      of a client);
    //   3. the person (it references its account);
    //   4. its account.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private Task DeletePersonAsync<T>(PersonDescriptor<T> d, int id) where T : Person, new() =>
        TransactionAsync(async () =>
        {
            var person = await d.Dao.FindByIdAsync(id) ?? throw new BusinessException(d.NotFoundKey);
            if (d.CountAppointments is not null && await d.CountAppointments(id) > 0)
            {
                throw new BusinessException(d.HasAppointmentsKey ?? "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
            }
            if (d.BeforeDelete is not null)
            {
                await d.BeforeDelete(id);
            }
            await d.Dao.DeleteByIdAsync(id);
            await userRepository.DeleteByIdAsync(person.UserId);
            return true; // TransactionAsync expects a result: we do not need one here
        });

    // refuses first and last names already used by ANOTHER person of the same type
    // (currentId: the person being updated, who obviously has the
    // right to keep their own first and last names; null for a creation)
    private static async Task CheckPersonUniqueAsync<T>(PersonDescriptor<T> d, string firstName, string lastName, int? currentId)
        where T : Person, new()
    {
        var namesake = await d.Dao.FindByFirstNameLastNameAsync(firstName, lastName);
        if (namesake is not null && namesake.Id != currentId)
        {
            throw new BusinessException(d.AlreadyExistsKey);
        }
    }

    private async Task CheckLoginFreeAsync(string login)
    {
        if (await userRepository.FindByLoginAsync(login) is not null)
        {
            throw new BusinessException("ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN");
        }
    }
  • Lines 6–20: The six public methods delegate to the three private generic methods, using the correct descriptor. The compiler infers [T] from the descriptor: [Doctor] for [doctorDescriptor], [Client] for [clientDescriptor];
  • Lines 26–50: Creating a person and their account;
  • lines 28–33: data preparation, outside of a transaction. [Trim] removes leading and trailing spaces from the string; the name is capitalized. By default, the login is the same as the name and is always in lowercase; by default, the password is the same as the login: these are the account rules for the SQL script;
  • lines 37–38: within the transaction, the two uniqueness rules: no duplicate names, and a free choice of login. These are checked before writing to the database to provide a clear message (see Example 28);
  • lines 40–47: The user account is created first, since the person references it (foreign key). The password is never stored in plain text: [BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.HashPassword] calculates its hash (see Example 25). [$"{firstName} {lastName}"] is an interpolated string: the displayed name of the account;
  • Lines 49–50: Then, based on the constraint [new()], the person uses [new T] to generate either [Doctor] or [Client]. If this second write operation fails, the transaction also rolls back the first one: an account can never exist without a person;
  • lines 59–95: modifying the person and their account in a single transaction;
  • line 63: a person not found is a [BusinessException], with the descriptor key. [?? throw] was seen in Example 28;
  • lines 70–72: the optimistic lock (see Example 28): the form has carried over the version of the record read to its display; if the version in the database is different, someone has modified the record in the meantime, and the system rejects the update rather than silently overwriting their work. Unlike the pessimistic lock used for reservations, nothing is blocked: we assume that conflicts are rare, and we simply detect them. If the concurrent modification occurs after this read, it is the condition [WHERE version = ...] of [UPDATE] that will detect it (see [TranslateDatabaseError], below);
  • Lines 77–80: The read object is simply modified: the subsequent [DbContext] will send the necessary [UPDATE] to the next [SaveChangesAsync]. The name check transmits the person’s identifier: they are, of course, entitled to keep their own first and last names;
  • lines 82–88: the account follows the person (navigation property [User], loaded by DAO): their displayed name is recalculated. The login changes only if it has been entered and differs from the current one; in that case, it must be available;
  • lines 90–92: The password changes only if it has been entered; it is then hashed;
  • lines 94–95: saving the account and the person. Our [DbContext] increments the version number of each modified entity (see [Data/RdvMedecinsDbContext.cs]);
  • lines 107–121: deletion, within a single transaction, in the order dictated by the foreign keys;
  • lines 111–113: potential rejection: a doctor with scheduled appointments cannot be deleted (their patients would lose their appointments without being notified). [d.CountAppointments(id)] calls the function stored in the descriptor;
  • lines 115–117: deletion of what references the person: a doctor’s time slots, a client’s appointments;
  • lines 119–120: the person, then their account, which the person was referencing;
  • line 121: [TransactionAsync] expects a function that returns a result: one is returned, but no one will use it;
  • lines 127–133: a homonym is rejected, unless it is the person currently being edited ([currentId], [null] for a new creation). The method is [static]: it does not use any fields from the object;
  • Lines 137–141: A login name already in use—by a doctor, a client, or the administrator—is rejected.

docs.title: 11.12.4.5. Transactions and uniqueness constraints
docs.text:
// -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // runs [work] in a transaction:
    //   BeginTransactionAsync -> START TRANSACTION;
    //   CommitAsync            -> COMMIT, if everything went well;
    //   if an exception is thrown (BusinessException included), we do not commit:
    //   "await using" closes the transaction on leaving the block, and a
    //   transaction closed without COMMIT is cancelled (ROLLBACK).
    //
    // The "login free" and "unique first + last names" checks are made BEFORE
    // the write, to give a clear message. But two ADMINs could
    // save the same login (or the same doctor) at the same instant: in this
    // rare case, it is an SQL uniqueness constraint that refuses the second
    // write - we then translate this SQL error into the same BusinessException.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private async Task<R> TransactionAsync<R>(Func<Task<R>> work)
    {
        await using var transaction = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
        try
        {
            var result = await work();
            await transaction.CommitAsync();
            return result;
        }
        catch (Exception e)
        {
            // on failure, the DbContext "forgets" everything it was tracking: an
            // entity left in the Added state would otherwise be sent again to the database at the
            // next SaveChangesAsync of the same request
            db.ChangeTracker.Clear();
            if (TranslateDatabaseError(e) is { } businessError)
            {
                throw businessError;
            }
            throw; // "throw;" rethrows the original exception, with its call stack intact
        }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Database errors -> BusinessException
    //
    // - DbUpdateConcurrencyException: the UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..."
    //   modified no row (optimistic lock, see AbstractEntity);
    // - DbUpdateException whose cause (InnerException) is the MySQL error
    //   ER_DUP_ENTRY (no. 1062): a UNIQUE constraint refused the write. Its
    //   message quotes the NAME of the constraint:
    //     Duplicate entry 'marie-pelissier' for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name'
    //   (MySQL 8 prefixes the name with that of the table, MariaDB does not). That is
    //   why the SQL script NAMES all its constraints.
    // Any other error is a real anomaly: we return null (not translated).
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private static readonly Dictionary<string, string> ConstraintMessages = new()
    {
        ["unq_users_login"] = "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN",
        ["unq_doctors_first_name_last_name"] = "ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS",
        ["unq_clients_first_name_last_name"] = "ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS",
        ["unq1_appointments"] = "ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED",
    };

    private static BusinessException? TranslateDatabaseError(Exception e)
    {
        // beware of the order: DbUpdateConcurrencyException inherits from DbUpdateException
        if (e is DbUpdateConcurrencyException)
        {
            return new BusinessException("ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE");
        }
        // "pattern matching": is e a DbUpdateException
        // whose InnerException is a MySqlException with code DuplicateKeyEntry?
        if (e is DbUpdateException { InnerException: MySqlException { ErrorCode: MySqlErrorCode.DuplicateKeyEntry } sqlError })
        {
            // "... for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name'" -> "unq_doctors_first_name_last_name"
            var match = Regex.Match(sqlError.Message, @"for key '(?:[^'.]*\.)?([^']+)'");
            if (match.Success && ConstraintMessages.TryGetValue(match.Groups[1].Value, out var key))
            {
                return new BusinessException(key);
            }
        }
        return null;
    }
}
  • line 15: all multi-step entries go through this generic method: [R] is the type of the result of the operation ([Appointment], [Doctor], [Client], [bool]), and [Func<Task<R>>] is the type of a parameterless asynchronous function that returns a [R]. This is the [TransactionAsync] method from Example 28, expanded;
  • line 17: [BeginTransactionAsync] opens a transaction ([START TRANSACTION]). [await using var] declares a variable that will be automatically closed upon exiting the block that contains it, regardless of what happens (normal termination or exception); the version [await] allows for asynchronous closure. A transaction that is closed without having been committed is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]);
  • Lines 20–22: The task is executed; if it succeeds, [CommitAsync] commits the transaction ([COMMIT]). If an exception is thrown—including [BusinessException]—[CommitAsync] is never reached: everything that has been written is rolled back;
  • line 24: Example 28 caught two specific types of exceptions; here, we catch all exceptions to clean up before restarting them;
  • line 29: the cleanup. The database has rolled back everything, but the [DbContext] is still tracking entities that no longer correspond to anything: for example, the doctor whose insertion failed remains in the [Added] state. Since the [DbContext] persists throughout the entire query, it would be sent back to the database with the next [SaveChangesAsync] for that query. [ChangeTracker.Clear()] causes the [DbContext] to forget all the entities it was tracking;
  • lines 30–32: if the error is a known database error, the corresponding [BusinessException] is raised instead. [is { } businessError] is a pattern filter: it checks that the value is not [null] and stores it in the variable [businessError];
  • line 34: otherwise, the original exception is rethrown as-is. [throw;] alone, within a [catch], keeps its call stack intact (the one that indicates where the error occurred), whereas [throw e;] would reset it. A [BusinessException] raised by the job is thus passed back, unchanged, to the controller; any other error is an anomaly, which will generate a 500 error page;
  • lines 51–56: for each named uniqueness constraint in the SQL script, its translation key. This is why the script SQL names all its constraints. [new()] without a type name is allowed when the type is already specified on the left; [["key"] = value] populates the dictionary;
  • lines 59–77: translation of a database error into [BusinessException], or [null] if the error is not recognized;
  • lines 62–64: [UPDATE ... WHERE id = ... AND version = ...] did not modify any lines: EF Core raises a [DbUpdateConcurrencyException] (optimistic lock; see Example 28). This test comes first because [DbUpdateConcurrencyException] inherits from [DbUpdateException]: if placed later, the following test would have intercepted it;
  • line 68: a uniqueness constraint violation. The error [MySQL] (code [DuplicateKeyEntry], No. 1062) occurs nested within a [DbUpdateException], in its property [InnerException]. Pattern filtering checks everything in a single expression, on two levels: [e] is a [DbUpdateException], whose [InnerException] is a [MySqlException], which is a [ErrorCode] that equals [DuplicateKeyEntry]; this [MySqlException] is contained within [sqlError]. The [NestJS] version also tested the [ER_DUP_ENTRY] code of a [QueryFailedError];
  • line 71: the error message lists the constraint name, for example, [Duplicate entry 'marie-pelissier' for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name']. The regular expression extracts it: [(?:[^'.]*\.)?] skips the optional prefix [doctors.] (written by [MySQL] 8, not by [MariaDB]), and the group [([^']+)] captures the name up to the apostrophe. The [@] at the beginning of the string makes it a verbatim string, where [\] is not an escape character;
  • Lines 72–74: If the name was found and is listed in the dictionary, [TryGetValue] stores the translation key in [key], and the error becomes [BusinessException]. Any other error, including a violation of a constraint not present in the dictionary, is left untranslated: this is a true anomaly.

docs.title: 11.13. Authentication
docs.text: The [Auth] folder includes, in a more comprehensive form, examples 25 through 27: the JWT token in a cookie, roles, CAPTCHA, and attempt limits. It also includes a “pass” for creating a customer account. The [AuthController] controller, discussed at the end of this section, brings these components together for the login page.

docs.title: 11.13.1. Auth/ConnectedUser.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Auth/ConnectedUser.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// What the JWT token contains, and how to read it back.
//
// In ASP.NET Core, the user of the request is a ClaimsPrincipal
// (User property of a controller, HttpContext.User elsewhere): a list of
// "claims", type / value pairs - exactly the
// fields of the JWT token once verified. The authentication middleware
// fills it on EVERY request (see Program.cs, UseAuthentication).
//
// The claims of our tokens (see AuthService.SetToken):
//   sub   : the id of the user account (JWT convention: "subject")
//   login : the login
//   name  : the display name ("Marie PELISSIER"), for the navigation bar
//   role  : ADMIN, DOCTOR or USER
// =========================================================================

using System.Security.Claims;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Auth;

public static class JwtClaims
{
    public const string Sub = "sub";
    public const string Login = "login";
    public const string Name = "name";
    public const string Role = "role";
}

// the connected user, in a typed form
public record ConnectedUser(int UserId, string Login, string Name, Role Role);

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// An "extension method": it is called as if it were part of
// ClaimsPrincipal (User.CurrentUser()), whereas it is defined here.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
public static class ClaimsPrincipalExtensions
{
    // the connected user, or null if the request is not authenticated
    public static ConnectedUser? CurrentUser(this ClaimsPrincipal principal)
    {
        if (principal.Identity?.IsAuthenticated != true
            || !int.TryParse(principal.FindFirstValue(JwtClaims.Sub), out var userId)
            || !Enum.TryParse<Role>(principal.FindFirstValue(JwtClaims.Role), out var role))
        {
            return null;
        }
        return new ConnectedUser(
            userId,
            principal.FindFirstValue(JwtClaims.Login) ?? "",
            principal.FindFirstValue(JwtClaims.Name) ?? "",
            role);
    }
}
  • lines 24–29: the names of the token claims, grouped into constants: a typo in [JwtClaims.Name] is flagged by the compiler, whereas an error in the string ["name"] would only be discovered at runtime;
  • line 33: the user logged in using a typed form: an integer identifier, a role of type [Role] (the enumeration ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER from the [Entities] folder), instead of the list of string pairs that constitute the claims. This is equivalent to the [req.user] object created by the [Passport] strategy of the [NestJS] project;
  • lines 39–42: an extension method (see Example 06) on ***[ClaimsPrincipal], the type of the ***[User] property of controllers and views (see Example 25). The pages simply write [User.CurrentUser()];
  • lines 44–48: the method returns [null] if the request is not authenticated, or if the claims are not as expected. [Identity?.IsAuthenticated] is equal to [null] if [Identity] is missing: the [!= true] comparison treats this case as “unauthenticated.” [int.TryParse] and [Enum.TryParse<Role>] attempt a conversion and return [false] if the conversion fails, rather than throwing an exception; the result is stored in the variable declared by [out var];
  • lines 50–54: [FindFirstValue] returns the value of the first claim of the requested type, or [null]; the operator [??] then replaces it with an empty string.

docs.title: 11.13.2. Auth/AuthService.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Auth/AuthService.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The authentication logic:
//   - ValidateUserAsync()      : checks a login / password pair;
//   - SetToken()               : builds the JWT token of a validated user
//                                and stores it in a cookie;
//   - ClearToken()             : deletes this cookie (logout).
//
// Where does the JWT token travel?
// With the Angular client, it was the JavaScript code of the client that kept the
// token and added it itself to each request ("Authorization:
// Bearer ..." header). A browser that displays ordinary HTML pages cannot
// do that: for it to present the token on its own with each request,
// it must be stored in a COOKIE. The options of this cookie matter for
// security:
//   - HttpOnly : the JavaScript of the page cannot read the cookie (an
//     injected script could therefore not steal the token);
//   - SameSite=Lax : the browser does NOT send the cookie with a POST coming
//     from another site. As all the actions that modify data are
//     POSTs, a booby-trapped page on another site cannot book or
//     delete anything by impersonating the user
//     (so-called CSRF attack);
//   - Secure : in production (HTTPS), the cookie never travels in clear;
//   - MaxAge : the cookie disappears at the same time as the token expires.
// =========================================================================

using System.Text;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;
using RdvMedecins.Config;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;
using RdvMedecins.Repositories;

namespace RdvMedecins.Auth;

public class AuthService(UserRepository userRepository, IOptions<AuthOptions> options)
{
    // the name of the cookie that carries the token
    public const string JwtCookie = "rdvmedecins_jwt";

    private readonly AuthOptions auth = options.Value;

    // the signing key of the tokens, built from the secret of
    // appsettings.json. Also used to VERIFY the tokens (see Program.cs).
    public static SymmetricSecurityKey SigningKey(AuthOptions auth)
    {
        var bytes = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(auth.JwtSecret);
        if (bytes.Length < 32)
        {
            // HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits: we say so
            // clearly at startup rather than at the first login
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Auth:JwtSecret must be at least 32 characters long (see appsettings.json).");
        }
        return new SymmetricSecurityKey(bytes);
    }

    // null if the login does not exist or if the password is wrong.
    // BCrypt.Verify hashes the typed password with the "salt" contained in the
    // stored hash, then compares the two results.
    public async Task<User?> ValidateUserAsync(string login, string password)
    {
        var user = await userRepository.FindByLoginAsync(login);
        if (user is null)
        {
            return null;
        }
        return BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.Verify(password, user.Password) ? user : null;
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // builds the JWT token of [user] and puts it in a cookie.
    // The token is SIGNED (HMAC-SHA256) with the secret key: the browser
    // can read it (it is not encrypted), but not modify it - any
    // modification would make the signature invalid.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public void SetToken(HttpResponse response, User user)
    {
        var descriptor = new SecurityTokenDescriptor
        {
            Claims = new Dictionary<string, object>
            {
                [JwtClaims.Sub] = user.Id,
                [JwtClaims.Login] = user.Login,
                [JwtClaims.Name] = user.Name,
                [JwtClaims.Role] = user.Role.ToString(),
            },
            Expires = DateTime.UtcNow.AddSeconds(auth.JwtExpiresInSeconds),
            SigningCredentials = new SigningCredentials(SigningKey(auth), SecurityAlgorithms.HmacSha256),
        };
        var token = new JsonWebTokenHandler().CreateToken(descriptor);

        response.Cookies.Append(JwtCookie, token, new CookieOptions
        {
            HttpOnly = true,
            SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax,
            Secure = auth.CookieSecure,
            MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(auth.JwtExpiresInSeconds),
            Path = "/",
        });
    }

    public static void ClearToken(HttpResponse response) =>
        response.Cookies.Delete(JwtCookie, new CookieOptions { Path = "/" });
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 38: the service receives, via injection, the DAO containing user accounts ([UserRepository], discussed with the DAO layer) and the authentication configuration. [IOptions<AuthOptions>] provides the [Auth] section of [appsettings.json] in the form of a [AuthOptions] object ([Config] folder): its [Value] property contains the secret key, the token lifetime, and the [CookieSecure] option. The service is registered as [Scoped] in [Program.cs], just like the DAO it uses (see Chapter 6);
  • line 41: the name of the cookie that carries the token;
  • lines 47–56: the signature key (see Example 25). New feature: a key that is too short is rejected with a clear exception. The method is static: it depends only on its parameter, and it is called when the application starts, by [JwtAuthentication] (next file), at a time when no services yet exist. Since the length check occurs at this point, an incorrect configuration prevents the application from starting, rather than causing the first connection to fail;
  • lines 62–69: the account if the username and password are correct; otherwise, [null] (see Example 25). The method is asynchronous: the account lookup is a database query (see Chapter 9);
  • lines 78–92: the token, generated as in Example 25. It contains the account ID, the username, the name displayed in the navigation bar, and the role; its lifetime is determined by the configuration (two hours by default);
  • Lines 94–100: the cookie, with the options from Example 25 ([HttpOnly], [SameSite = Lax]) and two additional ones: [Secure], enabled in production (the site is served with [HTTPS]), prevents the browser from sending the cookie over an unencrypted connection; [Path = "/"] ensures it is included with every request to the site. [MaxAge] deletes the cookie when the token expires;
  • lines 104–105: Logging out deletes the cookie. For the browser to recognize the cookie to be deleted, the path ([Path]) must be that of the storage location. The method is static: it is also used by the handler [JwtBearer] (next file) and the exception filter [HtmlExceptionFilter] (folder [Web]), which do not have an instance of [AuthService] available.

docs.title: 11.13.3. Auth/JwtAuthentication.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Auth/JwtAuthentication.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The configuration of JWT token authentication, called from
// Program.cs (builder.Services.AddJwtAuthentication(...)).
//
// The JwtBearer "handler" of ASP.NET Core does, on each request, what
// the Passport 'jwt' strategy and JwtAuthGuard did in NestJS:
//   1. find the token;
//   2. check its signature and its expiry date;
//   3. derive the user from it (HttpContext.User, see ConnectedUser.cs).
//
// Three adaptations to an HTML application, thanks to the "events" of the
// handler (functions that it calls at precise moments):
//   - OnMessageReceived : the token is read from a COOKIE, and not from
//     the "Authorization: Bearer ..." header;
//   - OnChallenge : when a protected page is requested without a valid token,
//     JwtBearer would answer 401 - which suits a JavaScript client. A
//     browser, however, must be SENT BACK to the login page;
//   - (403: insufficient role) nothing to do here: the empty 403 response is
//     turned into an error page by UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute
//     (see Program.cs and Controllers/ErrorController.cs).
// =========================================================================

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;
using RdvMedecins.Config;
using RdvMedecins.Web;

namespace RdvMedecins.Auth;

public static class JwtAuthentication
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddJwtAuthentication(this IServiceCollection services, AuthOptions auth)
    {
        services
            .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
            .AddJwtBearer(options =>
            {
                // we keep the claim names of the token as they are ("role", "sub"...)
                // instead of translating them into long Microsoft-style names
                options.MapInboundClaims = false;

                options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
                {
                    ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,
                    IssuerSigningKey = AuthService.SigningKey(auth),
                    ValidateLifetime = true,
                    // an expired token is refused immediately (by default, a
                    // tolerance of 5 minutes is granted for clock differences)
                    ClockSkew = TimeSpan.Zero,
                    // our tokens have neither issuer (iss) nor audience (aud)
                    ValidateIssuer = false,
                    ValidateAudience = false,
                    // which claim contains the name, and which one the role:
                    // [Authorize(Roles = "ADMIN")] compares the "role" claim
                    NameClaimType = JwtClaims.Name,
                    RoleClaimType = JwtClaims.Role,
                };

                options.Events = new JwtBearerEvents
                {
                    // 1. the token is in the cookie
                    OnMessageReceived = context =>
                    {
                        context.Token = context.Request.Cookies[AuthService.JwtCookie];
                        return Task.CompletedTask;
                    },

                    // 2. protected page without a valid token -> login page
                    OnChallenge = context =>
                    {
                        // HandleResponse(): "I take care of the response", JwtBearer
                        // will therefore not write its 401
                        context.HandleResponse();
                        // a cookie was present but is no longer valid: the session has expired
                        if (context.Request.Cookies.ContainsKey(AuthService.JwtCookie))
                        {
                            AuthService.ClearToken(context.Response);
                            Flash.Put(context.HttpContext, FlashType.Danger, "ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED");
                        }
                        context.Response.Redirect("/login");
                        return Task.CompletedTask;
                    },
                };
            });

        return services;
    }
}

In Example 25, the configuration for [JwtBearer] was written in [Program.cs]. Here, it is stored in an extension method, which [Program.cs] calls in a single line: [builder.Services.AddJwtAuthentication(authOptions)]. Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 32–34: the extension method (see Example 06). It directly receives a [AuthOptions] object, read from the configuration by [Program.cs]: when services are registered, dependency injection is not yet available, so we cannot request a [IOptions<AuthOptions>];
  • lines 37–42: the authentication schema [JwtBearer], which stores the token’s claim names (see Example 25);
  • lines 44–54: the checks performed on each token: the signature, using the key generated by [AuthService.SigningKey], and the expiration date. New feature compared to Example 25: [ClockSkew = TimeSpan.Zero]. By default, [JwtBearer] still accepts a token for five minutes after it expires, to account for a slight discrepancy between the clocks of the server that generates the token and the one that verifies it. Here, it is the same server: an expired token is rejected immediately;
  • lines 57–58: the claim [name] yields [User.Identity.Name], the claim [role] is the one verified by [[Authorize(Roles = "ADMIN")]] and [User.IsInRole] (see Example 26);
  • lines 64–67: the token is read from the cookie, not from the [Authorization] header (see Example 25);
  • lines 71–82: A request for a protected page without a valid token redirects to the login page (see Example 25). New feature (lines 77–80): If the request included a token cookie, it means the user was logged in, but their token has expired (or was tampered with). We delete this now-useless cookie and display a flash message (see Example 20; the [Flash] class is discussed with the [Web] folder): the login page will display “Your session has expired,” rather than leaving the user wondering why they are there. The message is a translation key (see Example 22).

A 403 Forbidden response (insufficient role) does not require an event: as in Example 26, the empty response is converted into an error page by [UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute]. In the [NestJS] project, this task was divided among the [Passport] and [jwt] strategies (read and verify the token), the guard [JwtAuthGuard] (require a token), and the exception filter (convert the denial to a redirect); here, the handler [JwtBearer], its events, and the attribute [[Authorize]] are sufficient.

docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Auth/InvalidSessionException.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The token is valid, but the account it designates no longer exists: it has been
// deleted since the login (by the patient themselves in another
// tab, or by the ADMIN). We treat this case as an expired session:
// HtmlExceptionFilter clears the cookie and sends back to the login page
// (the equivalent of NestJS's UnauthorizedException).
// =========================================================================

namespace RdvMedecins.Auth;

public class InvalidSessionException() : Exception("the account of the connected user no longer exists");
  • Line 13: A token may be valid (properly signed, not expired) even though the account it refers to has been deleted since the login. The patient’s pages detect this by searching for the client associated with the account (method [ConnectedPatientAsync] in file [Web/Utils.cs]) and then throw this exception; the exception filter [HtmlExceptionFilter] (see Example 24 for filters) intercepts it, deletes the cookie, and redirects to the login page with the message “session expired.” The class has a main constructor with no parameters, which passes its message to the constructor of the parent class [Exception].

docs.title: 11.13.5. Auth/CaptchaService.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Auth/CaptchaService.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A CAPTCHA ("test to tell a human from a robot") made by the
// server itself, without any external service: a few distorted characters,
// scrambled by strokes, in an SVG image. A human reads them without
// difficulty; a robot that merely sends forms in a loop
// cannot do it.
//
// The NestJS project used the svg-captcha library. Here, no
// library: the image is drawn by the CaptchaDrawing class (below)
// from a small hand-written vector "font". An important
// point: each character is drawn with STROKES (<path>), never
// written as text (<text>) - otherwise a robot would only have to read the source
// code of the image.
//
// How it works:
//   1. Generate() draws a random text, turns it into an image, and stores the
//      right answer IN THE SERVER'S MEMORY, under a random identifier;
//   2. the page displays the image and puts the identifier in a hidden field of the
//      form (the answer itself never leaves the server);
//   3. Verify(id, input) compares the input with the expected answer, then
//      FORGETS this captcha: each image is used only once, a robot cannot
//      replay an answer already found.
//
// SINGLETON service (a single instance for the whole server, see
// Program.cs), used by several requests IN PARALLEL: hence the
// ConcurrentDictionary, a dictionary that several threads can read
// and modify at the same time without corrupting it.
//
// Accepted limit: the memory of a single process. With several servers
// behind a load balancer, a shared storage would be needed.
// =========================================================================

using System.Collections.Concurrent;
using System.Globalization;
using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Text;

namespace RdvMedecins.Auth;

// Id : to put in the hidden "captchaId" field of the form
// Svg : the image, to insert as is in the page
public record Captcha(string Id, string Svg);

public class CaptchaService
{
    // validity duration of an image: you have 10 minutes to fill in the form
    private static readonly TimeSpan Lifetime = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10);

    // memory safeguard: beyond this, we forget the oldest captchas
    private const int MaxCaptchas = 10_000;

    // id -> (expected answer, expiry date)
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, (string Text, DateTime Expires)> pending = new();

    public Captcha Generate()
    {
        Purge();
        var text = CaptchaDrawing.RandomText(5); // 5 characters
        var id = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
        pending[id] = (text, DateTime.UtcNow + Lifetime);
        return new Captcha(id, CaptchaDrawing.Svg(text));
    }

    // true if [input] is the right answer to captcha [id] (regardless
    // of case). The captcha is consumed in all cases.
    // TryRemove is ATOMIC: if two requests present the same captcha at the
    // same instant, only one removes it - the other fails.
    public bool Verify(string? id, string? input)
    {
        if (id is null || input is null || !pending.TryRemove(id, out var expected))
        {
            return false;
        }
        return expected.Expires > DateTime.UtcNow
            && string.Equals(expected.Text, input.Trim(), StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    }

    private void Purge()
    {
        var now = DateTime.UtcNow;
        foreach (var (id, captcha) in pending)
        {
            if (captcha.Expires <= now || pending.Count >= MaxCaptchas)
            {
                pending.TryRemove(id, out _);
            }
        }
    }
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The drawing of the SVG image (150 x 50 pixels).
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
internal static class CaptchaDrawing
{
    private const int Width = 150;
    private const int Height = 50;

    // The "font": each character is a list of strokes, each stroke a
    // series of points (x, y) in a 4 x 6 grid (y pointing down).
    // Characters too easy to confuse with one another: excluded (0 O, 1 I L).
    private static readonly Dictionary<char, double[][]> Font = new()
    {
        ['A'] = [[0, 6, 2, 0, 4, 6], [0.8, 3.8, 3.2, 3.8]],
        ['B'] = [[0, 0, 0, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 0, 3], [0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3]],
        ['C'] = [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5]],
        ['D'] = [[0, 0, 0, 6, 2.5, 6, 4, 4.5, 4, 1.5, 2.5, 0, 0, 0]],
        ['E'] = [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6, 4, 6], [0, 3, 3, 3]],
        ['F'] = [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6], [0, 3, 3, 3]],
        ['G'] = [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 3.5, 2.5, 3.5]],
        ['H'] = [[0, 0, 0, 6], [4, 0, 4, 6], [0, 3, 4, 3]],
        ['J'] = [[4, 0, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
        ['K'] = [[0, 0, 0, 6], [4, 0, 0, 3.5], [1.3, 2.6, 4, 6]],
        ['M'] = [[0, 6, 0, 0, 2, 3.5, 4, 0, 4, 6]],
        ['N'] = [[0, 6, 0, 0, 4, 6, 4, 0]],
        ['P'] = [[0, 6, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3]],
        ['Q'] = [[1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5, 0, 1, 1, 0], [2.5, 4.5, 4, 6.3]],
        ['R'] = [[0, 6, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3], [2, 3, 4, 6]],
        ['S'] = [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
