docs.title: 5.1.1. Dictionaries
docs.text:
The file [i18n/fr.json]:

{
  "MENU": {
    "HOME": "Accueil",
    "PRODUCTS": "Produits"
  },
  "HOME": {
    "TITLE": "Bienvenue",
    "HELLO": "Bonjour {name} !",
    "DATE": "Nous sommes le {date}."
  },
  "PRODUCTS": {
    "TITLE": "Nos produits",
    "NAME": "Produit",
    "PRICE": "Prix",
    "COUNT": "{n} produit(s) au catalogue."
  }
}

The file [i18n/en.json]:

{
  "MENU": {
    "HOME": "Home",
    "PRODUCTS": "Products"
  },
  "HOME": {
    "TITLE": "Welcome",
    "HELLO": "Hello {name}!",
    "DATE": "Today is {date}."
  },
  "PRODUCTS": {
    "TITLE": "Our products",
    "NAME": "Product",
    "PRICE": "Price",
    "COUNT": "{n} product(s) in the catalogue."
  }
}
  • A dictionary is a JSON file, organized by page or by topic: The key [HOME.HELLO] refers to the text [HELLO] in section [HOME];
  • Line 8: A text may contain parameters, enclosed in curly braces, which are replaced during translation. Word order varies from one language to another: this is why a text is not created by simply concatenating translated segments.

docs.title: 5.1.2. The translation service
docs.text:
The file [Translation/Translator.cs]:

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

namespace Example22.Translation;

// the dictionaries, read ONCE at startup: the service is a singleton
public partial class Translator
{
    public static readonly string[] Languages = ["fr", "en"];
    public const string DefaultLanguage = "en";

    // language -> (full key "HOME.HELLO" -> text)
    private readonly Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, string>> dictionaries = [];

    public Translator(IWebHostEnvironment environment)
    {
        foreach (var language in Languages)
        {
            var path = Path.Combine(environment.ContentRootPath, "i18n", $"{language}.json");
            using var document = JsonDocument.Parse(File.ReadAllText(path));
            var dictionary = new Dictionary<string, string>();
            Flatten(document.RootElement, "", dictionary);
            dictionaries[language] = dictionary;
        }
    }

    // the language of the current request, set by the localization middleware
    public static string CurrentLanguage()
    {
        var language = CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.TwoLetterISOLanguageName;
        return Languages.Contains(language) ? language : DefaultLanguage;
    }

    // Translate("HOME.HELLO", { ["name"] = "Marie" }) -> "Hello Marie!"
    public string Translate(string? key, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>? parameters = null)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(key)) return "";
        // a missing key displays the key itself: an oversight shows on screen
        var text = dictionaries[CurrentLanguage()].GetValueOrDefault(key) ?? key;
        if (parameters is null) return text;
        // each {name} is replaced by the value of the parameter of the same name
        return Parameter().Replace(text, m => parameters.TryGetValue(m.Groups[1].Value, out var value) ? value : m.Value);
    }

    // { "MENU": { "HOME": "Home" } } -> { "MENU.HOME": "Home" }
    private static void Flatten(JsonElement node, string prefix, Dictionary<string, string> result)
    {
        foreach (var property in node.EnumerateObject())
        {
            var key = prefix == "" ? property.Name : $"{prefix}.{property.Name}";
            if (property.Value.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Object)
            {
                Flatten(property.Value, key, result);
            }
            else
            {
                result[key] = property.Value.GetString() ?? "";
            }
        }
    }

    // the {name} regular expression, compiled by the C# compiler
    [GeneratedRegex(@"\{(\w+)\}")]
    private static partial Regex Parameter();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 8: the keyword [partial] is required by the regular expression at the end of the file (see below);
  • lines 10–11: the supported languages and the default language;
  • line 14: for each language, a dictionary [C#] that associates each complete key ([HOME.HELLO]) with its text;
  • lines 16–24: the builder reads the JSON files. The [IWebHostEnvironment] service, provided by [ASP.NET Core], returns the project folder ([ContentRootPath]). [JsonDocument.Parse] parses the text JSON; [using var] releases the object at the end of the block. The service will be a singleton (see [Program.cs]): the files are read only once;
  • lines 29–32: the language of the current request. We will see that the localization middleware stores it in [CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture]. [TwoLetterISOLanguageName] returns its two-letter code ([fr], [en]);
  • Lines 36–43: the translation. The key is looked up in the dictionary of the current language; if it is not found, the key itself is displayed: an omission is immediately visible on the screen. The regular expression finds each [{name}] parameter in the text and replaces it with its value; a parameter without a value is left as is;
  • Lines 47–58: The function “flattens” the JSON: the object ["HOME": { "HELLO": "..." }] yields the key [HOME.HELLO]. It calls itself (recursive function) to traverse nested objects;
  • lines 64–65: the regular expression [\{(\w+)\}] (an opening curly brace, one or more word characters, captured, an closing curly brace). The attribute [[GeneratedRegex]] instructs the compiler to generate its parsing code once and for all during compilation. The method is declared as [partial]: its body is generated by the compiler.

docs.title: 5.1.3. Implementing in Views
docs.text:
A view could obtain the service using the [@inject Translator Translator] directive, then write [@Translator.Translate("MENU.HOME")]. This is time-consuming, and it would have to be repeated in every view. We take a different approach: each [Razor] view is compiled into a [C#] class, which by default derives from the framework’s [RazorPage<TModel>] class. We can insert our own class, which provides all views with the methods they need. The file [Translation/ViewPage.cs]:

using System.Globalization;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Razor;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Razor.Internal;

namespace Example22.Translation;

// the base class of all the views (see Views/_ViewImports.cshtml: @inherits)
public abstract class ViewPage<TModel> : RazorPage<TModel>
{
    // filled by dependency injection, as @inject would do in a view
    [RazorInject]
    public Translator Translator { get; set; } = null!;

    // @T("HOME.HELLO", ("name", "Marie")): the parameters are (name, value) pairs
    public string T(string? key, params (string Name, object? Value)[] parameters) =>
        Translator.Translate(key, parameters.ToDictionary(p => p.Name, p => p.Value?.ToString() ?? ""));

    // "fr" or "en"
    public string Language => Translator.CurrentLanguage();

    // a date in full words, in the current language
    public string LongDate(DateOnly date) => date.ToString("D", CultureInfo.CurrentCulture);

    // an amount in euros, in the format of the current language
    public string Money(decimal amount)
    {
        var format = (NumberFormatInfo)CultureInfo.CurrentCulture.NumberFormat.Clone();
        format.CurrencySymbol = "€";
        return amount.ToString("C", format);
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 8: a generic class—[TModel]—is the view model type, which is different for each view. The class is abstract: only the views inherit from it;
  • lines 11–12: the [[RazorInject]] attribute instructs [Razor] to populate the property via dependency injection: this is the equivalent of [@inject] for a class;
  • lines 15–16: The method [T] translates a key. Its parameters are [(name, value)] tuples: a compact syntax for writing value pairs, [("name", "Marie")]. The keyword [params] allows you to pass as many as you want, separated by commas. The method organizes them into a dictionary for the service. The rendered text is a string: [Razor] will escape it, just like any [@] expression;
  • line 19: the current language, [fr] or [en];
  • lines 22–29: dates and amounts are formatted according to the current culture, which is also set by the localization middleware (see Example 16).

The file [Views/_ViewImports.cshtml]:

@addTagHelper *, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.TagHelpers
@using Example22.Controllers
@using Example22.Translation
@* all the views derive from ViewPage: they have T(...), Language...;
   TModel denotes the model type of each view (@model ...) *@
@inherits ViewPage<TModel>
  • line 6: the directive [@inherits] specifies the parent class of the views. Placed in [_ViewImports.cshtml], it applies to all of them. Each view can now write [@T("MENU.HOME")].

docs.title: 5.1.4. Language Selection
docs.text:
The file [Program.cs]:

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Example22.Translation;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Localization;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews();
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));
// the dictionaries: a single instance, created when first needed
builder.Services.AddSingleton<Translator>();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles();
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});

// the language of each request: the cookie's, English otherwise
var cultures = Translator.Languages.Select(l => new CultureInfo(l)).ToList();
var localization = new RequestLocalizationOptions
{
    DefaultRequestCulture = new RequestCulture(Translator.DefaultLanguage),
    SupportedCultures = cultures,   // the languages of the formats (dates, numbers)
    SupportedUICultures = cultures, // the languages of the texts
};
// only the cookie decides (neither the browser language, nor a URL parameter)
localization.RequestCultureProviders = [new CookieRequestCultureProvider()];
app.UseRequestLocalization(localization);

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 12: the translation service, with a single instance;
  • lines 24–29: the localization middleware configuration. [.NET] distinguishes between two concepts: the culture ([CurrentCulture]), which defines the format of dates and numbers, and the interface culture ([CurrentUICulture]), which defines the language of the text. Both are assigned the same list of languages here; a language not on the list is rejected;
  • line 32: where to look for the request language. By default, the middleware checks, in order, a parameter from URL ([?culture=en]), a cookie, and then the [Accept-Language] header sent by the browser (its language). Only the cookie is retained: the user makes the selection using the FR / EN buttons;
  • Line 33: The middleware is added to the pipeline. For each request, it reads the cookie and sets [CultureInfo.CurrentCulture] and [CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture] for the duration of the request. If there is no cookie, the default language is English.

The [Controllers/LanguageController.cs] file:

using Example22.Translation;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Localization;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example22.Controllers;

public class LanguageController : Controller
{
    // GET /language/fr: stores the choice in a cookie, then goes back to the previous page
    [HttpGet("language/{language}")]
    public IActionResult Change(string language)
    {
        if (!Translator.Languages.Contains(language))
        {
            return NotFound();
        }
        Response.Cookies.Append(
            CookieRequestCultureProvider.DefaultCookieName,                              // the cookie name
            CookieRequestCultureProvider.MakeCookieValue(new RequestCulture(language)), // "c=fr|uic=fr"
            new CookieOptions { MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromDays(365), SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax, HttpOnly = true });
        return Redirect(OriginPage());
    }

    // the page we come from (Referer header), of which we keep only the path:
    // redirecting to a full address taken from the request would allow
    // sending the user to another site ("open redirect" vulnerability)
    private string OriginPage()
    {
        var referer = Request.Headers.Referer.ToString();
        if (!Uri.TryCreate(referer, UriKind.Absolute, out var url))
        {
            return "/";
        }
        return url.PathAndQuery;
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • lines 10–21: [GET /language/en] stores the selection in a cookie valid for one year, then redirects to the page the user came from. An unknown language results in a 404 error;
  • lines 17–20: [Response.Cookies.Append(name, value, options)] sets a cookie: the browser will send it back with every subsequent request. The name and format of its value are those expected by the localization middleware: we obtain them from the [CookieRequestCultureProvider] class, without having to write them ourselves. Options: [MaxAge] (lifetime), [HttpOnly] (the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it), [SameSite = Lax] (it is not sent by POST requests coming from other sites);
  • lines 27–34: The original page is specified by the [Referer] header, which the browser adds when a link is clicked. We retain only the path and parameters ([PathAndQuery]): redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow a malicious site to create a link that, after passing through our site, sends the user to the malicious site (a vulnerability known as [open redirect]).

docs.title: 5.1.5. The views
docs.text:
The file [Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml]:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="@Language">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  @* the title is a KEY, set by the view, translated by the layout *@
  <title>@T(ViewData["Title"] as string)</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    <partial name="_Navbar" />
    @RenderBody()
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 2: the page’s [lang] attribute reflects the selected language (useful for screen readers and spell-checkers);
  • line 6: the page title is a key, stored by the view in [ViewData], and translated by the template. [as string] converts the value (of type [object]) to a string, or to [null] if it is not one.

The [Views/Shared/_Navbar.cshtml] file:

<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <div class="navbar-nav me-auto">
    <a class="nav-link" href="/">@T("MENU.HOME")</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/products">@T("MENU.PRODUCTS")</a>
  </div>
  @* the current language is highlighted *@
  <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm">
    <a class="btn @(Language == "fr" ? "btn-primary" : "btn-outline-primary")" href="/language/fr">FR</a>
    <a class="btn @(Language == "en" ? "btn-primary" : "btn-outline-primary")" href="/language/en">EN</a>
  </div>
</nav>
  • Lines 8–9: two links (changing the language does not modify any application data: a GET is sufficient), with the current language highlighted.

The file [Views/Pages/Home.cshtml]:

@model HomeModel
@{
    ViewData["Title"] = "HOME.TITLE";
}
<h1>@T("HOME.TITLE")</h1>
<p>@T("HOME.HELLO", ("name", Model.Name))</p>
<p>@T("HOME.DATE", ("date", LongDate(Model.Today)))</p>
  • line 6: a parameter, passed as a tuple;
  • line 7: the date is first formatted by [LongDate], then passed as the parameter [date] to [T].

The [Views/Pages/Products.cshtml] file:

@model List<Product>
@{
    ViewData["Title"] = "PRODUCTS.TITLE";
}
<h1>@T("PRODUCTS.TITLE")</h1>
<table class="table table-sm w-auto">
  <thead><tr><th>@T("PRODUCTS.NAME")</th><th class="text-end">@T("PRODUCTS.PRICE")</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    @foreach (var product in Model)
    {
      <tr><td>@product.Name</td><td class="text-end">@Money(product.Price)</td></tr>
    }
  </tbody>
</table>
<p>@T("PRODUCTS.COUNT", ("n", Model.Count))</p>
  • line 11: the amount, formatted according to the language;
  • line 15: a numeric parameter; [T] converts it to a string.

The file [Controllers/PagesController.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example22.Controllers;

public record Product(string Name, decimal Price);

public record HomeModel(string Name, DateOnly Today);

public class PagesController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Home()
    {
        return View(new HomeModel("Marie", new DateOnly(2026, 9, 23)));
    }

    [HttpGet("products")]
    public IActionResult Products()
    {
        List<Product> products =
        [
            new Product("Keyboard", 25m),
            new Product("Mouse", 12.5m),
            new Product("Screen", 1149m),
        ];
        return View(products);
    }
}

Actions are language-agnostic: they provide data, and views translate and format it.

docs.title: 5.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
In English (no cookie yet), at URL http://localhost:5000/ and http://localhost:5000/products:

A click on FR, simulated with [curl] (the [-H] option adds the [Referer] header that the browser would have sent):

curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:5000/products" http://localhost:5000/language/fr

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Location: /products
Set-Cookie: .AspNetCore.Culture=c%3Dfr%7Cuic%3Dfr; max-age=31536000; path=/; samesite=lax; httponly

The server sets the [.AspNetCore.Culture] cookie, whose encoded value is [c=fr|uic=fr] (the culture and interface culture), and redirects to the original page, now in French:

An unsupported language:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/language/de

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Length: 0

The case study proceeds exactly this way, using more comprehensive dictionaries ([i18n/fr.json] and [i18n/en.json]): same service ([Translator]), same parent view class (with a few additional properties), same controller ([/language/{language}]), same cookie. There is only one difference: the error messages generated by the business and web layers are also keys, translated at the last moment by the view.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the document “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework” (2026), which itself adapted the document “Introduction to ASP.NET MVC by Example” (2013) to the [NestJS] framework. This document takes the reverse path and returns to the [.NET] platform, in its current version:

  • the [NestJS] framework and the [TypeScript] language are replaced by the [ASP.NET Core MVC] framework and the [C#] language;
  • the [Handlebars] views are replaced by [Razor] views;
  • ORM and [TypeORM] are replaced by ORM and [Entity Framework Core], still based on [MySQL].

The document closely follows the progression of the [NestJS] course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a single concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The examples have the same numbers and cover the same topics as in the [NestJS] course: a reader familiar with that course can compare the two frameworks example by example. However, this is not necessary: this document stands on its own and assumes no prior knowledge of [NestJS], nor, for that matter, of [ASP.NET]. The only prerequisites are a basic understanding of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) and the [C#] language.

docs.title: 1.1. The Role of ASP.NET Core MVC in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives requests HTTP from the browser and returns pages HTML to it. This is the layer that [ASP.NET Core MVC] helps us write;
  • The business layer contains the application’s business rules (for example, “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • The data access layer (layer [DAO], for [Data Access Object]) reads from and writes to the database. We will use the ORM [Entity Framework Core] ([Object Relational Mapper]), which maps the rows of the tables and objects in [C#].

The web layer itself follows the [MVC] ([Model – View – Controller]) model:

  • the controller (C) is a class whose methods—called actions—each handle a specific type of request (for example, [GET /schedule]). An action reads the request parameters, invokes the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view: a [C#] object;
  • the view (V) is a [Razor] file (extension [.cshtml]): from HTML, in which [C#] expressions—preceded by the character [@]—are replaced by data from the model.

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a HTTP request, for example, [GET /schedule?doctorId=1&day=2026-09-24];
  • 2: The web server [Kestrel], integrated with [ASP.NET Core], receives the request. It passes through a series of middleware components (cookie reading, authentication, static files, etc.), then [ASP.NET Core] selects the action responsible for handling this request: this is routing. Before reaching the action, the request may still pass through filters, which we’ll explore in later chapters;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer;
  • 4: It constructs the view template and designates the view that should display it;
  • 5: The [Razor] view engine renders the HTML page, which [ASP.NET Core] returns to the browser.

[ASP.NET Core] is the web framework for Microsoft’s [.NET] platform. Free and open-source, it runs on [Windows], [Linux], and [macOS]. It can create servers that return JSON to a [JavaScript] client ([Angular], [React], [Flutter]...) as well as traditional web applications, where the server generates the HTML pages and the browser simply displays them. It is this second use case—the MVC part of the framework—that this document examines. Like [NestJS], which drew heavily on it, [ASP.NET Core] is based on two ideas: attributes ([[HttpGet]], [[Route]], [[Authorize]]...) describe the roles of classes and methods, and dependency injection provides each object with the dependencies it needs.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • SDK [.NET] 10 ([Software Development Kit]), which contains the [C#] compiler, the [ASP.NET Core] framework, and the [dotnet] command-line tool. [.NET] 10 is the current LTS (Long-Term Support) version;
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor, with the [C# Dev Kit] extension;
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • the SGBD [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows], starting from the chapter on data access, and for the case study.

The [ASP.NET Core] framework is part of SDK: the examples do not require any additional libraries until Chapter 8. Examples 25 through 28 and the case study use three libraries, which are automatically downloaded from the [nuget.org] website during their first compilation (so you must be connected to the Internet on that day): [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer] (JWT tokens), [BCrypt.Net-Next] (password hashes), and [Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql] ([Entity Framework Core] for [MySQL]).

docs.title: 1.3. Run the case study
docs.text:
Reviewer’s note: I advise the reader to complete the case study immediately as described below. Once you fully understand the role of this appointment scheduling application, ask your favorite IA to modify the application as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own appointment slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons;

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. Ask IA to provide you with the new application code and the SQL script to create the new database. To do this, you’ll need to provide him with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database.

Also, I haven’t reviewed the course created by Claude. He had already produced a perfect [NestJS] course. I assumed the same was true for this one. If you run into a problem understanding something, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand. Claude, for example, is very good at this. You may need to “upload” the example you don’t understand to him.

End of note.

The case study at the end of this document is a complete application. Readers will likely want to see it in action before delving into the details of the framework: here’s how to run it. It’s located in the [rdvmedecins2-aspnetcore-mvc] folder, next to the [examples] folder:

aspnetcore-mvc-sept-2026/
├── examples/
└── rdvmedecins2-aspnetcore-mvc/

You must have installed SDK, [.NET] 10, [Visual Studio Code], and [MySQL] (see appendices). Then:

  • Create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database by running the [rdvmedecins2-aspnetcore-mvc/database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. With [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line:
mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
  • Check the database connection. The application connects to [MySQL] on [localhost], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password (the default settings for [Laragon]). If your [root] account has a password, enter it in the application’s [appsettings.json] file, at the end of the [ConnectionStrings:RdvMedecins] connection string ([...;User=root;Password=myPassword;]). For [MariaDB], also specify its version in the [MySql:ServerVersion] key (for example, [10.11.0-mariadb]);
  • Open the [rdvmedecins2-aspnetcore-mvc] folder in [Visual Studio Code] (File menu / Open Folder), then open a terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal);
  • Launch the application:
dotnet run
  • Upon first execution, [dotnet] downloads the libraries from [nuget.org], compiles the application, and then starts it. The console then displays the application’s address:
Using launch settings from Properties/launchSettings.json...
Building...
info: Microsoft.Hosting.Lifetime[14]
      Now listening on: http://localhost:8081

info: Microsoft.Hosting.Lifetime[0]

  • Open the address [http://localhost:8081] in a browser:

  • Log in with one of the demo accounts, whose password is the same as the username: [admin] (administrator), [pelissier], [tatou], [dupont] (doctors), [martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german] (patients). You must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase.

If the application closes immediately with the message [Unable to connect to any of the specified MySQL hosts], it means that [MySQL] has not been started; with [Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'], the connection string password is incorrect; with [Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'], the script SQL has not been executed. The application’s [README.md] file describes other scenarios. The application is stopped using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal.

The last chapter of the document explains how to use the application and then discusses each of its files.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in the [examples] folder, with one subfolder per example:

examples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routing/
├── ...
├── 28-layers/
├── common/
│   └── bootstrap/
├── Directory.Build.props
└── examples.slnx

Each example is an independent [.NET] project that can be compiled and run on its own. The file [examples.slnx] is a solution: a list of all these projects. When you open the [examples] folder in [Visual Studio Code], the [C# Dev Kit] extension finds the solution and loads all the projects (Solution Explorer pane): You then have access to syntax highlighting, code completion, and error reporting in each file.

The [common/bootstrap] folder contains the CSS and [Bootstrap] frameworks, shared by the examples that format their pages (starting with Example 15).

Each example has the structure of a [ASP.NET Core MVC] project:

13-first-view/
├── Controllers/
│   └── ViewsController.cs
├── Models/
│   └── PageModel.cs
├── Views/
│   ├── Views/
│   │   ├── Index.cshtml
│   │   └── Unknown.cshtml
│   └── _ViewImports.cshtml
├── appsettings.json
├── Example13.csproj
└── Program.cs
  • [Program.cs]: the application’s entry point—configuration, services, and server startup;
  • [Controllers]: the controllers;
  • [Models]: the classes that describe the models (actions and views);
  • [Views]: the views [Razor] (starting in Chapter 4);
  • [appsettings.json]: the application configuration (logging levels, and later, database connection, etc.);
  • [Example13.csproj]: the project file, which describes how to compile the application.

To run an example, open a terminal in its folder (in [Visual Studio Code]: right-click the example folder, then select “Open in the built-in terminal”) and type:

dotnet run

[dotnet run] compiles the project (in its [bin] folder), then runs the application. With [dotnet watch], the code is recompiled and the application is restarted whenever a file is modified. [.cs] or [.cshtml]:

dotnet watch

All examples listen on port 5000, the default port for [ASP.NET Core]: only one can be running at a time. Stop the server using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal. You can also compile all the examples at once from the [examples] folder to verify that the installation is complete:

dotnet build examples.slnx

The project file for an example is reduced to a single line. For example, [01-structure/Example01.csproj]:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
</Project>
  • Line 1: [Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web] is the SDK for web applications. It alone provides the entire [ASP.NET Core] framework: controllers, views, configuration, web server...

The settings common to all examples are written only once, in the [examples/Directory.Build.props] file, which the compiler automatically reads for any project located in the [examples] folder:

<!--
  Directory.Build.props: read automatically by ALL the projects located
  under this folder. The settings shared by the examples are therefore written
  only once, here, instead of being repeated in every .csproj file.
-->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <!-- .NET 10, LTS version (long-term support) -->
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <!-- the compiler reports the risks of NullReferenceException -->
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <!-- implicit usings: System, System.Linq, System.Threading.Tasks... -->
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

Let’s go over this file:

  • line 9: the target version of [.NET]: [.NET] 10;
  • line 11: “nullable” reference types. The compiler distinguishes between a variable of type [string], which must never be assigned the value [null], from a variable of type [string?], which can be set to that value, and issues a warning for any potential error involving [NullReferenceException];
  • Line 13: The most common namespaces ([System], [System.Linq], [System.Threading.Tasks], [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Builder]...) are automatically imported into each file: there is no need to write the corresponding [using] directives.

Finally, the file [appsettings.json] is the same for all examples up to Chapter 8:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"
    }
  },
  "AllowedHosts": "*"
}
  • Lines 4–5: logging levels. Application messages are displayed starting at level [Information]; those from [ASP.NET Core] itself—which are very numerous—are displayed only starting at level [Warning]. Thus, the console will display startup messages and errors, but not the details of each request;
  • Line 8: the domain names accepted in requests ([*]: all).

The document is organized as follows:

ChapterContentsExamplesControllers, actions,From the browser to the action: routes, responses, redirects, services01 through 06The Action ModelRequest parameters: binding, conversion, validation, forms POST07 to 12The view and its modelRazor, template, partial views, helpers, forms, validation, PRG13 to 21InternationalizationAn Application in French and English22Data Scopesapplication, query, client23The lifecycle of a requestmiddleware, authorization filters, action filters, exception filters, model binding24Authentication and authorizationJWT in a cookie, roles, CAPTCHA, attempt limits25–27Layered architectureWeb / Business Logic / DAO with Entity Framework Core and MySQL28Case StudyThe RdvMedecins application, explained file by file-

Each example introduces only a few new concepts, and the chapters build on one another: it is best to read them in order. The case study, meanwhile, draws on all the concepts from the previous chapters: whenever relevant, its commentary refers to the example where the concept was introduced.

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples kept their data in memory. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO ([Data Access Object]) layer: database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few details about it as possible: the web layer is unaware of SQL, and the business layer is unaware of HTML. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

Database access is handled by Entity Framework Core (EF Core), the ORM ([Object-Relational Mapper]) of [.NET]: it maps [C#] classes (the entities) to the database tables, translates queries written in [LINQ] into SQL, and transforms the retrieved rows into objects. EF Core communicates with each database type via a provider ([provider]): for [MySQL], the [NuGet] package, which includes [Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql], which in turn includes the EF Core and the [MySqlConnector] driver.

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The database [dbpersons] is created by a script named SQL. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersons.sql

The [database/dbpersons.sql] file:

-- database of example 28: a single table, [persons]
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersons;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersons CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersons;

CREATE TABLE persons (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  first_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  -- two persons cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_persons_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO persons (first_name, last_name, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The [utf8mb4] character set accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 8: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 14: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names. The name will be used to identify the error.

docs.title: 9.1.2. The configuration
docs.text:
The file [Example28.csproj]:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- Entity Framework Core and its MySQL / MariaDB provider -->
    <PackageReference Include="Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql" Version="9.0.0" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the SQL script is not an application file -->
    <Content Remove="database\**" />
    <None Include="database\**" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • line 5: the provider [MySQL] for EF Core;
  • Lines 10–11: The script SQL is not an application file: it is excluded from the published files.

The file [appsettings.json]:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning",
      "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command": "Warning"
    }
  },
  "AllowedHosts": "*",
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "DbPersons": "server=localhost;port=3306;database=dbpersons;user=root;password="
  },
  "MySql": {
    "ServerVersion": "8.0.30-mysql"
  }
}
  • line 6: EF Core logs every SQL command sent to the database at the [Information] level. The [Warning] level masks them; simply replace it with [Information] to view them in the console;
  • lines 10–11: the connection string: server, port, database, username, password. These are the default values for [Laragon] (username [root], no password);
  • line 14: the [MySQL] server version. The provider [Pomelo] adapts the SQL it generates to this version. For example, a version of [MariaDB] would be written as [10.11.0-mariadb].

The file [Program.cs]:

using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Example28.Dao;
using Example28.Data;
using Example28.Business;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// the database connection: connection string and server version, read from appsettings.json
var connectionString = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("DbPersons")!;
var version = ServerVersion.Parse(builder.Configuration["MySql:ServerVersion"]!);
// AddDbContext: one DbContext per request (Scoped lifetime)
builder.Services.AddDbContext<PersonsDbContext>(options => options.UseMySql(connectionString, version));

// the DAO and business layers: Scoped, like the DbContext they use
builder.Services.AddScoped<PersonsDao>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<PersonsBusiness>();

builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews(options =>
    options.ModelBindingMessageProvider.SetAttemptedValueIsInvalidAccessor((value, field) => $"The value [{value}] is not valid."));
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles();
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
  • line 12: [GetConnectionString("DbPersons")] reads the [DbPersons] property from the [ConnectionStrings] section;
  • line 15: [AddDbContext] saves [DbContext] (see below), with a lifetime of [Scoped]: one per request. [UseMySql] selects the provider [MySQL];
  • lines 18–19: the DAO and business layers, which also have a lifetime of [Scoped]: they use [DbContext], which cannot last longer than a single request (see Chapter 6);
  • line 22: a conversion error message (see Example 19).

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person Entity
docs.text:
The file [Entities/Person.cs]:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace Example28.Entities;

// a row of the [persons] table
[Table("persons")]
public class Person
{
    // the primary key: an integer key is, by convention, generated by the database
    // (AUTO_INCREMENT); EF Core reads its value back after each INSERT
    [Key]
    [Column("id")]
    public int Id { get; set; }

    // the optimistic lock: each UPDATE carries the condition "AND version = <value read>"
    [Column("version")]
    [ConcurrencyCheck]
    public int Version { get; set; } = 1;

    [Column("first_name")]
    [MaxLength(30)]
    public string FirstName { get; set; } = "";

    [Column("last_name")]
    [MaxLength(30)]
    public string LastName { get; set; } = "";

    [Column("age")]
    public int Age { get; set; }
}
  • line 7: the class [Person] corresponds to the table [persons]: each row of the table will be a [Person] object;
  • Lines 12–14: the primary key ([[Key]]). [[Column]] specifies the column name corresponding to each property;
  • lines 18–19: the version column. [[ConcurrencyCheck]] instructs EF Core to add the condition [AND version = <value read>] to each [UPDATE]: this is the optimistic lock, explained further below;
  • line 22: the other columns. [[MaxLength]] specifies the column size.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DbContext
docs.text:
The [Data/PersonsDbContext.cs] file:

using Example28.Entities;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Example28.Data;

// the DbContext: the connection to the database, and the tracking of the entities read
public class PersonsDbContext(DbContextOptions<PersonsDbContext> options) : DbContext(options)
{
    // the "table" of persons: it is queried with LINQ
    public DbSet<Person> Persons => Set<Person>();

    // just before each save: the version of every MODIFIED person
    // is increased by 1. The generated UPDATE compares the OLD value:
    //   UPDATE persons SET ..., version = 2 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 1
    public override Task<int> SaveChangesAsync(bool acceptAllChangesOnSuccess, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        foreach (var entry in ChangeTracker.Entries<Person>())
        {
            if (entry.State == EntityState.Modified)
            {
                entry.Entity.Version++;
            }
        }
        return base.SaveChangesAsync(acceptAllChangesOnSuccess, cancellationToken);
    }
}
  • line 7: DbContext is the central object of EF Core. It represents a work session with the database: it opens connections, sends queries, and tracks the entities it has read (it knows which ones have been modified);
  • Line 10: A [DbSet<Person>] represents the table: it is queried using [LINQ], and entities are added to it;
  • Lines 15–24: [SaveChangesAsync] sends all pending changes to the database. It is redefined to increment the version number for each modified person. [ChangeTracker] tracks the changes: for each tracked entity, it knows its status ([Added], [Modified], [Deleted], [Unchanged]). EF Core, unlike [TypeORM], does not manage an integer version column on its own: it is up to us to increment it.

docs.title: 9.1.5. The DAO layer
docs.text:
The [Dao/PersonsDao.cs] file:

using Example28.Data;
using Example28.Entities;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Example28.Dao;

// the DAO layer: queries, no business rule
public class PersonsDao(PersonsDbContext db)
{
    // SELECT ... FROM persons ORDER BY last_name, first_name
    public Task<List<Person>> ListAsync() =>
        db.Persons.AsNoTracking().OrderBy(p => p.LastName).ThenBy(p => p.FirstName).ToListAsync();

    // SELECT ... FROM persons WHERE id = @id LIMIT 1; null if missing
    public Task<Person?> ReadAsync(int id) =>
        db.Persons.FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == id);

    // a person with the same first and last names, other than [exceptId]
    public Task<Person?> NamesakeAsync(string firstName, string lastName, int exceptId) =>
        db.Persons.FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.FirstName == firstName && p.LastName == lastName && p.Id != exceptId);

    // INSERT if the person is new (Id = 0), UPDATE of the modified columns otherwise
    public async Task<Person> SaveAsync(Person person)
    {
        if (person.Id == 0)
        {
            db.Persons.Add(person);
        }
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        return person;
    }

    // DELETE FROM persons WHERE id = @id, without reading the person first
    public Task DeleteAsync(int id) =>
        db.Persons.Where(p => p.Id == id).ExecuteDeleteAsync();
}
  • line 8: DAO receives [DbContext] via injection;
  • Lines 11–12: A [LINQ] request, translated to SQL by EF Core. Nothing is sent to the database before the call to [ToListAsync], which executes the query and returns the list. [AsNoTracking()] indicates that these entities will not be modified: [DbContext] does not need to track them;
  • lines 15–16: the first function that checks the condition, or [null];
  • Lines 19–20: A person with the same first and last name, other than [exceptId]: useful for modifying a record, which must not conflict with itself. The comparison is performed by [MySQL], so according to the database’s collation: without regard to uppercase letters or accents;
  • Lines 23–30: A new person ([Id] set to 0) is added to [DbSet]; [SaveChangesAsync] then creates a [INSERT] and re-reads the identifier assigned by the database. A person read by this same [DbContext] and modified is detected by change tracking: [SaveChangesAsync] creates a [UPDATE] containing only the modified columns;
  • Lines 34–35: [ExecuteDeleteAsync] sends a [DELETE] directly to the database, without reading the records first.

The DAO layer contains no rules: only queries. These methods are asynchronous ([Task], [async] / [await]): while the database is processing, the thread is freed up and serves other requests.

docs.title: 9.1.6. The business layer
docs.text:
The file [Business/BusinessException.cs]:

namespace Example28.Business;

// a business rule rejects the operation: the message is intended for the user
public class BusinessException(string message) : Exception(message);

A [BusinessException] indicates that a business rule has rejected an operation. This is not a program error: the message is intended for the user.

The [Business/PersonsBusiness.cs] file:

using Example28.Dao;
using Example28.Data;
using Example28.Entities;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using MySqlConnector;

namespace Example28.Business;

public record PersonData(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age);

// the BUSINESS layer: the business rules, and only them
public class PersonsBusiness(PersonsDao dao, PersonsDbContext db)
{
    private const string Namesake = "A person already has these first and last names.";

    public Task<List<Person>> ListAsync() => dao.ListAsync();

    public async Task<Person> ReadAsync(int id) =>
        await dao.ReadAsync(id) ?? throw new BusinessException("This person does not exist (anymore).");

    public Task<Person> AddAsync(PersonData data) =>
        TransactionAsync(async () =>
        {
            // rule 1: no two persons with the same first and last names
            if (await dao.NamesakeAsync(data.FirstName, data.LastName, 0) is not null)
            {
                throw new BusinessException(Namesake);
            }
            var person = new Person { FirstName = data.FirstName, LastName = data.LastName, Age = data.Age };
            return await dao.SaveAsync(person);
        });

    public Task<Person> EditAsync(int id, int version, PersonData data) =>
        TransactionAsync(async () =>
        {
            var person = await ReadAsync(id);
            // rule 2: we do not modify a record modified meanwhile by someone else
            if (person.Version != version)
            {
                throw new BusinessException("This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.");
            }
            if (await dao.NamesakeAsync(data.FirstName, data.LastName, id) is not null)
            {
                throw new BusinessException(Namesake);
            }
            person.FirstName = data.FirstName;
            person.LastName = data.LastName;
            person.Age = data.Age;
            return await dao.SaveAsync(person);
        });

    public async Task<Person> DeleteAsync(int id)
    {
        var person = await ReadAsync(id);
        await dao.DeleteAsync(id);
        return person;
    }

    // [work] runs inside a transaction: COMMIT if it succeeds, ROLLBACK
    // if it throws an exception. The database errors become BusinessExceptions
    private async Task<R> TransactionAsync<R>(Func<Task<R>> work)
    {
        await using var transaction = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(); // START TRANSACTION
        try
        {
            var result = await work();
            await transaction.CommitAsync(); // COMMIT
            return result;
        }
        catch (DbUpdateConcurrencyException)
        {
            // the UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." modified no row
            throw new BusinessException("This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.");
        }
        catch (DbUpdateException e) when (e.InnerException is MySqlException { ErrorCode: MySqlErrorCode.DuplicateKeyEntry } sqlError
                                          && sqlError.Message.Contains("unq_persons_first_name_last_name"))
        {
            // two simultaneous additions: the uniqueness constraint of the database rejected the second
            throw new BusinessException(Namesake);
        }
        // any other exception goes on its way; the transaction, closed
        // without COMMIT by "await using", is cancelled (ROLLBACK)
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 9: a person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer;
  • line 12: the business layer uses DAO and [DbContext] to open transactions. Both are [Scoped] services: during a request, the DAO and the business layer receive the same [DbContext], and therefore the same connection and the same transaction. (With [TypeORM], the transaction object had to be passed to each method of DAO);
  • lines 18–19: An absent person is a [BusinessException]. The [??] operator provides a replacement value; [throw] can serve as a substitute;
  • lines 21–30: the addition, within a transaction. Rule: no two people may have the same first and last names. This is checked before the write to display a clear message;
  • lines 33–49: the update. Additional rule: the optimistic lock (lines 38–40). The update form retrieved the record’s version as it was when the form was opened. If it has changed in the meantime (another user has modified the same record), the update is rejected rather than silently overwriting the user’s work;
  • lines 61–67: [BeginTransactionAsync] opens a transaction ([START TRANSACTION]), and [CommitAsync] commits it ([COMMIT]). [await using] closes the transaction upon exiting the block, no matter what happens: if closed without [COMMIT], it is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]). Thus, an exception thrown by [work] (including a [BusinessException]) rolls back everything that has been done;
  • lines 70–73: the version check mentioned earlier is not always sufficient: two users can save the same record at the same time, and both pass the check. The second user’s [UPDATE ... WHERE id = ... AND version = ...] then does not modify any lines; EF Core detects this and raises a [DbUpdateConcurrencyException], which becomes the same [BusinessException];
  • Lines 75–79: Similarly, two simultaneous additions by the same person pass the homonym check, but the database’s uniqueness constraint does not allow them to be added. The error [MySQL] (code [DuplicateKeyEntry], No. 1062) occurs nested within a [DbUpdateException] (property [InnerException]); its message includes the name of the constraint. The clause [when] intercepts the exception only if the condition is true. [is MySqlException { ErrorCode: ... } sqlError] is a pattern filter: it tests the type and value of a property and stores the object in a variable.

docs.title: 9.1.7. The Web Layer
docs.text:
The file [Models/PersonForm.cs]:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace Example28.Models;

// the form fields and their constraints (see example 19)
public class PersonForm
{
    private string? firstName;
    private string? lastName;

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "The first name is required.")]
    [MaxLength(30, ErrorMessage = "30 characters at most.")]
    public string? FirstName { get => firstName; set => firstName = value?.Trim(); }

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "The last name is required.")]
    [MaxLength(30, ErrorMessage = "30 characters at most.")]
    public string? LastName { get => lastName; set => lastName = value?.Trim(); }

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "The age is required.")]
    [Range(0, 150, ErrorMessage = "The age must be between 0 and 150.")]
    public int? Age { get; set; }

    // the version of the record, carried by a hidden field (edit only)
    public int? Version { get; set; }
}

// the model of the form view
public class FormView
{
    public required string Title { get; init; }  // "Add a person"...
    public required string Action { get; init; } // the address the form is sent to
    public PersonForm Values { get; init; } = new();
    public Dictionary<string, string> Errors { get; init; } = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
}

// the model of the _Field partial view
public record FieldModel(string Name, string Label, string Type, string? Value, string? Error);

The form and its constraints (see Example 19), including the record version (line 24); the form view template, used for adding and modifying records (different title and submission address, [Action]); the partial view template [_Field] (see Example 19).

The file [Controllers/PersonsController.cs]:

using Example28.Business;
using Example28.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example28.Controllers;

// the WEB layer: it only knows the business layer
public class PersonsController(PersonsBusiness business) : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Home() => RedirectToAction(nameof(List));

    [HttpGet("persons")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> List()
    {
        return View(await business.ListAsync());
    }

    [HttpGet("persons/add")]
    public IActionResult AddForm() => Form(BuildView("Add a person", "/persons/add", new()));

    [HttpPost("persons/add")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Add(PersonForm input)
    {
        var view = BuildView("Add a person", "/persons/add", input);
        if (!ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            return Form(view);
        }
        try
        {
            var person = await business.AddAsync(new PersonData(input.FirstName!, input.LastName!, input.Age!.Value));
            TempData["Success"] = $"{person.FirstName} {person.LastName} has been added.";
            return RedirectToAction(nameof(List));
        }
        catch (BusinessException e)
        {
            // a business rule refuses: we display the form again, the message at the bottom of the page
            return Form(view, e.Message);
        }
    }

    [HttpGet("persons/{id:int}/edit")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> EditForm(int id)
    {
        try
        {
            var p = await business.ReadAsync(id);
            var values = new PersonForm { FirstName = p.FirstName, LastName = p.LastName, Age = p.Age, Version = p.Version };
            return Form(BuildView("Edit a person", $"/persons/{id}/edit", values));
        }
        catch (BusinessException e)
        {
            TempData["Error"] = e.Message;
            return RedirectToAction(nameof(List));
        }
    }

    [HttpPost("persons/{id:int}/edit")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Edit(int id, PersonForm input)
    {
        var view = BuildView("Edit a person", $"/persons/{id}/edit", input);
        if (!ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            return Form(view);
        }
        try
        {
            var data = new PersonData(input.FirstName!, input.LastName!, input.Age!.Value);
            var person = await business.EditAsync(id, input.Version ?? 0, data);
            TempData["Success"] = $"{person.FirstName} {person.LastName} has been edited.";
            return RedirectToAction(nameof(List));
        }
        catch (BusinessException e)
        {
            return Form(view, e.Message);
        }
    }

    [HttpPost("persons/{id:int}/delete")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Delete(int id)
    {
        try
        {
            var person = await business.DeleteAsync(id);
            TempData["Success"] = $"{person.FirstName} {person.LastName} has been deleted.";
        }
        catch (BusinessException e)
        {
            // no form to display again: the error also travels in TempData
            TempData["Error"] = e.Message;
        }
        return RedirectToAction(nameof(List));
    }

    // the model of the form view, with the ModelState errors sorted by field
    private FormView BuildView(string title, string action, PersonForm values) => new()
    {
        Title = title,
        Action = action,
        Values = values,
        Errors = ModelState
            .Where(c => c.Value!.Errors.Count > 0)
            .ToDictionary(c => c.Key, c => c.Value!.Errors[0].ErrorMessage, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase),
    };

    private ViewResult Form(FormView view, string? error = null)
    {
        ViewData["Error"] = error;
        return View("Form", view);
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 8: the controller only knows the business layer;
  • line 11: the site root redirects to the list;
  • lines 14–16: an asynchronous action: it returns a [Task<IActionResult>] and waits ([await]) for the list to be read from the database;
  • lines 23–39: the addition, in three steps: form validation (errors: page reload), call to the business layer (success: message in [TempData] and redirection, see Example 20), [BusinessException] (re-display with the message at the bottom of the page). Another exception is not caught: this is an anomaly that will result in a 500 error;
  • lines 44–55: the update form, pre-filled with the record retrieved from the database, including its version;
  • lines 60–76: same process as for adding; the version returned by the form is passed to the business layer;
  • lines 81–93: deletion. There is no form to redisplay: any errors are also passed through [TempData];
  • lines 97–104: the form view template, with the errors from [ModelState] sorted by field (see Example 19).

The file [Views/Persons/Form.cshtml]:

@model FormView
@{
    string? Error(string field) => Model.Errors.GetValueOrDefault(field);
}
<h1 class="h3">@Model.Title</h1>
<form method="post" action="@Model.Action" novalidate>
  @* the version of the record read: it will come back with the form *@
  <input type="hidden" name="version" value="@Model.Values.Version">
  <partial name="_Field" model='new FieldModel("firstName", "First name", "text", Model.Values.FirstName, Error("firstName"))' />
  <partial name="_Field" model='new FieldModel("lastName", "Last name", "text", Model.Values.LastName, Error("lastName"))' />
  <partial name="_Field" model='new FieldModel("age", "Age", "number", Model.Values.Age?.ToString(), Error("age"))' />
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Save</button>
  <a class="btn btn-link" href="/persons">Cancel</a>
</form>
  • line 8: the hidden field that carries the record version. The view is used for adding and modifying records: its title and the submission URL ([action]) are provided by the controller.

The [Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml] file:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Persons</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    @* the success message (TempData, after a redirect): at the top *@
    @if (TempData["Success"] is string success)
    {
      <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">@success</div>
    }
    @RenderBody()
    @* the error: from the current request (ViewData) or from before the redirect (TempData) *@
    @if ((ViewData["Error"] ?? TempData["Error"]) is string error)
    {
      <div class="error-area" role="alert">@error</div>
    }
  </div>
  <partial name="_Confirmation" />
  <script src="/js/app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • line 12: the success message, at the top of the page;
  • line 18: the error message, at the bottom of the page: either the one for the current request ([ViewData]) or the one displayed before a redirect ([TempData]).

The views [List.cshtml] and [_Field.cshtml], and the confirmation script, are the same as those in Examples 19 and 21.

docs.title: 9.1.8. Execution
docs.text:
If the values in [appsettings.json] are unsuitable (a password for [root], for example), they can be replaced—without modifying the file—with environment variables: the section separator [:] is written as [__] (two underscores). Under [Windows] ([PowerShell]):

$env:ConnectionStrings__DbPersons="server=localhost;database=dbpersons;user=root;password=secret"; dotnet run

The list, starting with URL http://localhost:5000/:

An invalid form:

A homonym: the business rule detects it. [MySQL], which compares based on the database’s collation, would also reject [marie pelissier]—written in lowercase and without accents:

A successful addition:

With logging level [Information] set for [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command], the console then displays, for each SQL request, the request text, its parameters (hidden by default, as a precaution), and its execution time: We can see the transaction, the homonym search ([SELECT ... LIMIT 1]), the [INSERT] followed by the reading of the assigned identifier, the [COMMIT], and then, after the redirection, the reading of the list ([SELECT ... ORDER BY]).

The optimistic lock: two forms are open on the same record; the first is saved (the version increases to 2); the second, which still has version 1, is rejected:

Deletion, with confirmation:

docs.title: 3. The Action Model
docs.text: An action requires information sent by the browser: the parameters from URL ([?name=martin&age=42]), form fields, and route parameters. The source course refers to all of this information as the action model. This chapter shows how [ASP.NET Core] provides this information to the action, converts it to the correct type, and validates it. This process is called model binding ([model binding]).

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: URL Parameters
docs.text:
The [Controllers/ParametersController.cs] file:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example07.Controllers;

[Route("parameters")]
public class ParametersController : Controller
{
    // /parameters/action01?name=martin: the [name] URL parameter -> the [name] action parameter
    [HttpGet("action01")]
    public string Action01(string? name)
    {
        return $"name = [{name}], of type {name?.GetType().Name ?? "null"}";
    }

    // /parameters/action02?age=42: the value is CONVERTED to the parameter type
    [HttpGet("action02")]
    public string Action02(int age)
    {
        return $"age = [{age}], of type {age.GetType().Name}, ModelState.IsValid = {ModelState.IsValid}";
    }

    // /parameters/action03?age=42: int? distinguishes a missing parameter (null) from a zero
    [HttpGet("action03")]
    public string Action03(int? age)
    {
        return $"age = [{age?.ToString() ?? "null"}], ModelState.IsValid = {ModelState.IsValid}";
    }

    // /parameters/action04?page=2: a default value if the parameter is missing
    [HttpGet("action04")]
    public string Action04(int page = 1)
    {
        return $"page = [{page}]";
    }

    // /parameters/action05?q=nest: [FromQuery(Name = ...)] when the names differ
    [HttpGet("action05")]
    public string Action05([FromQuery(Name = "q")] string? search)
    {
        return $"search = [{search}]";
    }

    // /parameters/action06?name=martin&age=42: all the parameters at once
    [HttpGet("action06")]
    public Dictionary<string, string> Action06()
    {
        return Request.Query.ToDictionary(p => p.Key, p => p.Value.ToString());
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • Lines 10–12: The model binding associates the action’s parameters with the query data by name: the action’s parameter [name] receives the value of the parameter [name] from URL (the part following [?], called the query string or [query string]). The type [string?] indicates that the value may be missing; in that case, it is [null]. [name?.GetType().Name ?? "null"]: the name of the value type, or the string ["null"] if the value is [null] (the operator [??] provides a replacement value);
  • lines 17–19: the parameter is declared as type [int]: the template binding converts the received string (["42"]) to a number. If the conversion fails ([?age=abc]), the action is still executed, using the type’s default value (0 for a [int]), and the failure is logged in [ModelState]; the status of the model binding—[ModelState.IsValid]—then becomes [false];
  • lines 24–26: with type [int?] (a “nullable” integer), a missing parameter is represented as [null], not 0: this allows distinguishing between “no age” and “age 0”;
  • lines 31–33: a default value of [C#] replaces a missing parameter;
  • Lines 38–40: The attribute [[FromQuery(Name = "q")]] specifies where to look for the value (in URL) and under what name: The [search] parameter of the action receives the [q] parameter from the URL;
  • Lines 45–47: [Request.Query] provides access to all parameters of URL, without any mapping or conversion. [ToDictionary] ([LINQ]) creates a dictionary from it, serialized in JSON.

The results:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action01?name=martin"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

name = [martin], of type String

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action01"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

name = [], of type null

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action02?age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

age = [42], of type Int32, ModelState.IsValid = True

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action02?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

age = [0], of type Int32, ModelState.IsValid = False

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action02"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

age = [0], of type Int32, ModelState.IsValid = True

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action03?age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

age = [42], ModelState.IsValid = True

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action03"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

age = [null], ModelState.IsValid = True

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action03?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

age = [null], ModelState.IsValid = False

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action04"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

page = [1]

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action04?page=2"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

page = [2]

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action05?q=aspnet"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

search = [aspnet]

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action06?name=martin&age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"name":"martin","age":"42"}

The quotation marks around URL are necessary when it contains the character [&], which has a specific meaning for the console. Note that:

  • a parameter is bound by its name, regardless of case ([?NAME=martin] is also valid);
  • its value is converted to the declared type. This is an important difference from [NestJS], where a parameter’s type was merely a declaration ([TypeScript]) that was removed at compile time;
  • an impossible conversion does not cause an error: the action is executed with a default value, and it is up to the action to check [ModelState.IsValid]. A “nullable” type ([int?]) prevents a missing or invalid value from being confused with 0.

Accented characters and spaces are encoded in a URL ([%C3%A9] for [é], etc.): [ASP.NET Core] decodes them before binding.

docs.title: 3.2. Example 08: An action template described by a class
docs.text:
When an action has multiple parameters, they are described by a class. Each property of the class carries validation attributes provided by the standard namespace [System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations]. This is equivalent to the decorators in the [class-validator] library of [NestJS].

The [Models/PersonModel.cs] file:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace Example08.Models;

// the action model: a class whose every property carries its constraints
public class PersonModel
{
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "the name is required")]
    [StringLength(20, MinimumLength = 2, ErrorMessage = "the name must have 2 to 20 characters")]
    public string? Name { get; set; }

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "the age is required")]
    [Range(0, 150, ErrorMessage = "the age must be between 0 and 150")]
    public int? Age { get; set; }

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "the title is required")]
    [AllowedValues("Mr", "Mme", "Melle", ErrorMessage = "unknown title")]
    public string? Title { get; set; }

    // optional: no [Required]
    [EmailAddress(ErrorMessage = "invalid email address")]
    public string? Email { get; set; }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 1: the namespace for validation attributes;
  • line 10: each expected parameter is a public property ([{ get; set; }]: it can be read and written). The model binding creates a [PersonModel] object, then populates each property with the parameter of the same name;
  • lines 8–9: the name is required ([[Required]]) and must be between 2 and 20 characters long ([[StringLength]]). Each attribute accepts a custom error message ([ErrorMessage]). The properties are declared “nullable” ([string?], [int?]): a parameter may be omitted from a query, and [[Required]] enforces this requirement;
  • lines 12–14: age is converted to an integer, which is required and must be between 0 and 150 ([[Range]]);
  • Line 17: The title must be part of a list of values ([[AllowedValues]], introduced with [.NET] 8);
  • Line 21: The email address is optional (no [[Required]]); if included, it must be valid.

The [Controllers/PersonsController.cs] file:

using Example08.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example08.Controllers;

// [ApiController]: a request whose model is invalid is rejected
// AUTOMATICALLY (400 error), even before the action runs
[ApiController]
[Route("persons")]
public class PersonsController : Controller
{
    // /persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr
    [HttpGet("action01")]
    public object Action01([FromQuery] PersonModel person)
    {
        return new { person, ageType = person.Age?.GetType().Name };
    }
}
  • line 6: the [[ApiController]] attribute directs the controller to a JSON server (a API). It changes several behaviors, including this one: a request with an invalid template is automatically rejected with a 400 error before the action is even executed. This is equivalent to the global [ValidationPipe] of [NestJS];
  • Line 14: The action receives a [PersonModel], populated from the parameters of the URL. With [[ApiController]], a class-type parameter is searched for by default in the request body (in JSON): [[FromQuery]] specifies that it should be searched for in URL;
  • Line 16: The action returns the person received and their age type.

A valid query with a [pirate] parameter that does not correspond to any property:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr&pirate=1"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"person":{"name":"martin","age":42,"title":"Mr","email":null},"ageType":"Int32"}

The age is indeed a number, and the parameter [pirate] was ignored: the binding populates only the properties of the class. An invalid request (the response JSON has been formatted for readability):

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=m&age=abc&title=Dr&email=xx"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8

{
  "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.1",
  "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "status": 400,
  "errors": {
    "Age": [
      "The value 'abc' is not valid for Age."
    ],
    "Name": [
      "the name must have 2 to 20 characters"
    ],
    "Email": [
      "invalid email address"
    ],
    "Title": [
      "unknown title"
    ]
  },
  "traceId": "00-ea340e76f456fbefae537611139be71b-2db7a84085adc345-00"
}

[[ApiController]] rejected the request with a 400 error; its body, JSON, in the standard format [Problem Details] (RFC 9110), lists the errors by field. The action was not executed. The age conversion error has a message in English, provided by [ASP.NET Core]; we’ll see how to replace it. The same applies without any parameters:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/persons/action01

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8

{
  "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.1",
  "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "status": 400,
  "errors": {
    "Age": [
      "the age is required"
    ],
    "Name": [
      "the name is required"
    ],
    "Title": [
      "the title is required",
      "unknown title"
    ]
  },
  "traceId": "00-af1f22e662507d8f360028f71752ded1-4ff5a136398590da-00"
}

This behavior is appropriate for a JSON server, queried by a [JavaScript] client that displays errors in its own way. For a HTML application, an error code like JSON makes no sense: we want to redisplay the form along with its errors. The following example shows how to take control.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 09: Validation Performed by the Action
docs.text:
Example 09 does not use [[ApiController]]. The [PersonModel] class is identical; only the controller changes. The [Controllers/PersonsController.cs] file:

using System.Net;
using Example09.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example09.Controllers;

// no [ApiController]: the action is ALWAYS executed, and it is the action that
// decides what to do with an invalid model
[Route("persons")]
public class PersonsController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("action01")]
    public ContentResult Action01(PersonModel person)
    {
        // ModelState: the result of the binding AND of the validation of the model
        if (ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            return Page($"<p>Welcome {person.Title} {person.Name} ({person.Age} years old)</p>");
        }
        // the errors, field by field
        var items = ModelState
            .Where(field => field.Value!.Errors.Count > 0)
            .Select(field => $"<li>{field.Key}: {string.Join(", ", field.Value!.Errors.Select(e => e.ErrorMessage))}</li>");
        return Page($"<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul>{string.Join("", items)}</ul>");
    }

    // an HTML page (code 200 in both cases)
    private ContentResult Page(string html) => Content(html, "text/html; charset=utf-8");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 9: without [[ApiController]], the action is always executed, regardless of whether the model is valid or not. A class-type parameter is searched for everywhere: in URL, in form fields, and in the route;
  • line 13: the model binding and validation were performed before the action was executed: the [person] object is populated, and [ModelState] contains any errors;
  • lines 16–18: no errors: a welcome page;
  • lines 21–23: otherwise, the list of errors. [ModelState] is a dictionary in which each key is the name of a field ([Name], [Age]...) and each value is the status of that field, along with its list of errors ([Errors]). The methods [LINQ], [Where] (filter), and [Select] (transform) retain the fields with errors and generate one line HTML per field. [!] informs the compiler that a value is not [null];
  • line 24: a page listing the errors;
  • line 28: in both cases, the response is a HTML page, with status code 200.

A conversion error appears in [ModelState] as a validation error:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=martin&age=abc&title=Mr"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 92
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul><li>Age: The value 'abc' is not valid for Age.</li></ul>

This is the technique that all forms in the case study will use (see Example 19): the action checks [ModelState.IsValid] and redispays the form if there are any errors.

docs.title: 3.4. Example 10: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
A single parameter can appear multiple times in a query: this is the case with checkboxes on a form or a multiple-selection list ([?color=red&color=green]).

The [Controllers/ArraysController.cs] file:

using Example10.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example10.Controllers;

[Route("arrays")]
public class ArraysController : Controller
{
    // /arrays/action01?color=red&color=green: a simple parameter
    [HttpGet("action01")]
    public object Action01(string? color)
    {
        return new { color };
    }

    // /arrays/action02?color=red&color=green: an array
    [HttpGet("action02")]
    public object Action02(string[] color)
    {
        return new { color, count = color.Length };
    }

    // /arrays/action03?color=red: a list, validated by ChoiceModel
    [HttpGet("action03")]
    public object Action03(ChoiceModel choice)
    {
        return new
        {
            colors = choice.Color,
            valid = ModelState.IsValid,
            errors = ModelState.Values.SelectMany(v => v.Errors).Select(e => e.ErrorMessage),
        };
    }
}

The [Action01] action (lines 11–13) shows what a single parameter receives:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action01?color=red"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"color":"red"}

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action01?color=red&color=green"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"color":"red"}

A parameter of type [string] receives only the first value. An array-type parameter ([Action02], lines 18–20) receives all of them, whether there are zero, one, or more:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action02?color=red"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"color":["red"],"count":1}

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action02?color=red&color=green"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"color":["red","green"],"count":2}

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action02"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"color":[],"count":0}

[ASP.NET Core] thus avoids a common pitfall found in [NestJS] ([Express]), where the same variable was a string for a single value and an array for multiple values. The list still needs to be validated. The file [Models/ChoiceModel.cs]:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace Example10.Models;

// IValidatableObject: a validation written in C#, for what the attributes
// cannot express (here: EACH element of the list)
public class ChoiceModel : IValidatableObject
{
    private static readonly string[] Colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];

    [MinLength(1, ErrorMessage = "choose at least one color")]
    public List<string> Color { get; set; } = [];

    public IEnumerable<ValidationResult> Validate(ValidationContext context)
    {
        foreach (var color in Color.Where(c => !Colors.Contains(c)))
        {
            // yield return: the method returns the errors one by one
