            yield return new ValidationResult($"unknown color: {color}", [nameof(Color)]);
        }
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 7: the class implements the [IValidatableObject] interface: a validation written in [C#] for what the attributes cannot express;
  • line 11: [[MinLength(1)]]: the list must have at least one element;
  • lines 14–18: the method [Validate], called by the validation after the attributes, checks each color. It returns an error ([ValidationResult]) for each unknown color, indicating the relevant field. [yield return] returns errors one by one, without creating a list.

The controller’s [Action03] action receives a [ChoiceModel] and returns its contents along with the validation status:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action03?color=red&color=green"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"colors":["red","green"],"valid":true,"errors":[]}

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action03?color=red&color=black"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"colors":["red","black"],"valid":false,"errors":["unknown color: black"]}

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action03"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"colors":[],"valid":false,"errors":["choose at least one color"]}

docs.title: 3.5. Example 11: Parameters of a POST request
docs.text:
A HTML form sent using the POST method places its fields in the request body, not in the URL. The [Controllers/PostController.cs] file:

using System.Text.Json;
using Example11.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example11.Controllers;

[Route("post")]
public class PostController : Controller
{
    // the fields of an HTML form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded body)
    [HttpPost("action01")]
    public object Action01()
    {
        return new
        {
            receivedType = Request.ContentType,
            fields = Request.Form.ToDictionary(c => c.Key, c => c.Value.ToString()),
        };
    }

    // a JSON body: [FromBody] deserializes it
    [HttpPost("action02")]
    public object Action02([FromBody] JsonElement body)
    {
        return new { receivedType = Request.ContentType, body };
    }

    // a single field of the form: [FromForm]
    [HttpPost("action03")]
    public string Action03([FromForm] string? name)
    {
        return $"name = [{name}]";
    }

    // the form fields, bound and validated by the PersonModel class
    [HttpPost("action04")]
    public object Action04([FromForm] PersonModel person)
    {
        return new
        {
            person,
            valid = ModelState.IsValid,
            errors = ModelState.Values.SelectMany(v => v.Errors).Select(e => e.ErrorMessage),
        };
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • lines 12–17: [Request.Form] contains the fields of a HTML form (body type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded]), without any binding or conversion. [Request.ContentType] is the body type;
  • lines 23–25: [[FromBody]] instructs the system to read the request body as a JSON document (this is what a [JavaScript] client sends). [JsonElement] represents any JSON document; a class could have been declared;
  • lines 30–32: [[FromForm]]: a field in the form;
  • lines 37–43: the entire form, bound and validated by the [PersonModel] class from Example 08.

The [-d] option of [curl] sends a POST request with a body in the format of a HTML ([application/x-www-form-urlencoded]):

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42" http://localhost:5000/post/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"receivedType":"application/x-www-form-urlencoded","fields":{"name":"martin","age":"42"}}

The same content in JSON format:

curl -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"martin","age":42}' http://localhost:5000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"receivedType":"application/json","body":{"name":"martin","age":42}}

(for [Windows], enter [-d "{\"name\":\"martin\",\"age\":42}"] at the command prompt). The age is a string in the first case (a HTML form carries only text) and a number in the second. A [[FromBody]] action rejects a body that is not in the JSON format, returning a 415 error ([Unsupported Media Type]):

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42" http://localhost:5000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type
Content-Length: 0

The other two actions:

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42" http://localhost:5000/post/action03

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

name = [martin]

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42&title=Mme" http://localhost:5000/post/action04

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"person":{"name":"martin","age":42,"title":"Mme","email":null},"valid":true,"errors":[]}

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=200" http://localhost:5000/post/action04

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"person":{"name":"martin","age":200,"title":null,"email":null},"valid":false,"errors":["the age must be between 0 and 150","the title is required","unknown title"]}

An action POST returns a 200 status code, just like an action GET ([NestJS], on the other hand, returned a 201 by default). For a HTML application, a POST action responds either with a page (the form redisplayed) or with a redirect (see Example 20).

docs.title: 3.6. Example 12: Custom Binding and Validation
docs.text:
You can extend the template binding and validation. The case study makes moderate use of these features, but understanding them helps you grasp how [ASP.NET Core] works.

12-custom-binding/
├── Binding/
│   ├── DateFrBinder.cs
│   ├── LanguageBinder.cs
│   └── NoSpaceAttribute.cs
├── Controllers/
│   └── ExamplesController.cs
├── appsettings.json
├── Example12.csproj
└── Program.cs

docs.title: 3.6.1. A model binder: DateFrBinder
docs.text:
A model binder is the object that constructs a parameter’s value from the request. [ASP.NET Core] provides them for all common types; you can write your own. The file [Binding/DateFrBinder.cs]:

using System.Globalization;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ModelBinding;

namespace Example12.Binding;

// a "model binder": turns a French date "23/09/2026" into a DateOnly
public class DateFrBinder : IModelBinder
{
    public Task BindModelAsync(ModelBindingContext context)
    {
        // the raw value, found in the URL, the form, the route...
        var raw = context.ValueProvider.GetValue(context.ModelName).FirstValue;
        if (DateOnly.TryParseExact(raw, "dd/MM/yyyy", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out var date))
        {
            // success: the value the action will receive
            context.Result = ModelBindingResult.Success(date);
        }
        else
        {
            // failure: an error in ModelState ("31/02/2026" is rejected too)
            context.ModelState.AddModelError(context.ModelName, $"[{raw}] is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date");
        }
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
  • line 7: a model binder implements the [IModelBinder] interface;
  • line 9: its method [BindModelAsync] receives the binding context: the parameter name ([ModelName]), the value sources ([ValueProvider]: URL, the form, the route...), [ModelState]...;
  • line 12: the raw value of the parameter ([FirstValue]: the first one, if there are multiple);
  • lines 13–16: [DateOnly.TryParseExact] converts a string in the [dd/mm/yyyy] format to [DateOnly] (a date without a time), and returns [false] if this is impossible, including for a date that does not exist (31/02/2026). If successful, [ModelBindingResult.Success(date)] provides the value that the action will receive;
  • line 21: if the operation fails, an error is added to [ModelState];
  • line 23: the method is asynchronous by nature ([Task]), but there is nothing to wait for: it returns a task that has already completed.

docs.title: 3.6.2. A second model binder: LanguageBinder
docs.text:
A parameter may come from somewhere other than URL or the form. The file [Binding/LanguageBinder.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ModelBinding;

namespace Example12.Binding;

// the browser's preferred language, read from the header
// "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8" -> "fr"
public class LanguageBinder : IModelBinder
{
    public Task BindModelAsync(ModelBindingContext context)
    {
        var header = context.HttpContext.Request.Headers.AcceptLanguage.ToString();
        var first = header.Split(',')[0].Trim();
        var language = first.Length >= 2 ? first[..2].ToLowerInvariant() : "fr";
        context.Result = ModelBindingResult.Success(language);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
  • line 11: the [Accept-Language] header, which specifies the user’s preferred languages;
  • lines 12–13: the first two letters of the first language. [first[..2]] is a range ([range]): the characters with indices 0 and 1.

docs.title: 3.6.3. A validation attribute: [NoSpace]
docs.text:
The file [Binding/NoSpaceAttribute.cs]:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace Example12.Binding;

// a "home-made" validation attribute: [NoSpace]
public class NoSpaceAttribute : ValidationAttribute
{
    public NoSpaceAttribute() : base("the {0} field must not contain any space")
    {
    }

    public override bool IsValid(object? value)
    {
        // null is accepted: requiring it is the job of [Required]
        return value is not string text || !text.Contains(' ');
    }
}
  • line 6: a validation attribute inherits from [ValidationAttribute]. By convention, the name of an attribute class ends with [Attribute], which is omitted in practice: [[NoSpace]];
  • line 8: the default error message, passed to the parent class. [{0}] will be replaced by the field name;
  • Lines 12–15: The rule. [value is not string text]: If the value is not a string ([null], for example), it is accepted; otherwise, it is assigned to the variable [text], which must not contain any spaces. The case study has an attribute of this type: [[OneOf]].

docs.title: 3.6.4. The controller
docs.text:
The file [Controllers/ExamplesController.cs]:

using Example12.Binding;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example12.Controllers;

[Route("examples")]
public class ExamplesController : Controller
{
    // /examples/schedule?day=23/09/2026: a custom model binder
    [HttpGet("schedule")]
    public IActionResult Schedule([ModelBinder(typeof(DateFrBinder))] DateOnly day)
    {
        if (!ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            return BadRequest(ModelState[nameof(day)]!.Errors[0].ErrorMessage);
        }
        return Ok($"schedule for the day [{day:yyyy-MM-dd}]");
    }

    // /examples/hello: a parameter that does not come from the URL, but from a header
    [HttpGet("hello")]
    public string Hello([ModelBinder(typeof(LanguageBinder))] string language)
    {
        return language == "en" ? "Hello!" : "Bonjour !";
    }

    // /examples/search?keyword=aspnet: a custom validation attribute
    [HttpGet("search")]
    public IActionResult Search([NoSpace] string? keyword)
    {
        if (!ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            return BadRequest(ModelState[nameof(keyword)]!.Errors[0].ErrorMessage);
        }
        return Ok($"search for [{keyword}]");
    }
}
  • line 11: the attribute [[ModelBinder]] specifies the model binder to be used for this parameter;
  • line 15: an invalid date results in a 400 error, with the message from the model binder;
  • line 22: the parameter [language] is provided by the second model binder;
  • line 29: A validation attribute can also be applied directly to an action parameter.

The results:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/schedule?day=23/09/2026"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

schedule for the day [2026-09-23]

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/schedule?day=2026-09-23"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

[2026-09-23] is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/schedule?day=31/02/2026"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

[31/02/2026] is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date

curl -i -H "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9" http://localhost:5000/examples/hello

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Bonjour !

curl -i -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9" http://localhost:5000/examples/hello

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Hello!

(The [-H] option of [curl] adds a header to the request)

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/search?keyword=aspnet"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

search for [aspnet]

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/search?keyword=asp%20net"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

the keyword field must not contain any space

([%20] encodes a space in a URL)

docs.title: 3.6.5. Conclusion
docs.text: The action template is constructed by the template binding based on the request: route parameters, URL, form fields, JSON body, and headers. The values are converted to the parameter types and then validated against the attributes. The result of these two steps is stored in [ModelState]. For a server JSON, [[ApiController]] automatically rejects an invalid model; for a HTML application, the action itself tests [ModelState.IsValid] (example 09) so that the form can be redisplayed. This is the subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: 7. The lifecycle of a request
docs.text:
Between the arrival of a request and the execution of the action, [ASP.NET Core] involves several types of objects, each with a specific role. We have already encountered some of them: middleware ([UseStaticFiles], [UseRequestLocalization], the middleware from Example 23), and the model binding ([IModelBinder], Example 12). The MVC component adds filters that run around the action. The case study uses each of them:

ObjectRoleIn the case studymiddlewarePrepares the request; does not yet know the actionstatic files, language, authentication (reading the token), error pagesauthorization filterallow or deny access to the action[[Authorize]], [[Authorize(Roles = ...)]]Template bindingConvert and validate parametersforms, [ModelState]action filterCode before and after the action(not used: services and the view parent class are sufficient)exception filterConvert an exception into a responseSession expired: redirect to /login

docs.title: 7.1. Example 24: The steps in processing a request
docs.text:
Example 24 has an action that calculates the square of a number, and one object of each type. Each writes a line to the console, so we can see the order in which they are executed.

24-lifecycle/
├── Controllers/
│   ├── CalcController.cs
│   └── ErrorController.cs
├── Filters/
│   ├── BlockAttribute.cs
│   ├── ErrorPageFilter.cs
│   ├── IntegerBinder.cs
│   ├── LoggerMiddleware.cs
│   └── TimingAttribute.cs
├── Views/
│   ├── Calc/
│   │   └── Result.cshtml
│   ├── Shared/
│   │   ├── _Layout.cshtml
│   │   └── Error.cshtml
│   └── _ViewStart.cshtml
├── appsettings.json
├── Example24.csproj
└── Program.cs

The file [Filters/LoggerMiddleware.cs]:

namespace Example24.Filters;

// a middleware written as a class: it receives the rest of the pipeline
// (next) in its constructor, and handles each request in InvokeAsync
public class LoggerMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        Console.WriteLine();
        Console.WriteLine($"--- {context.Request.Method} {context.Request.Path}{context.Request.QueryString}");
        Console.WriteLine("1. middleware (before)");
        await next(context); // the whole rest: routing, filters, action, view
        Console.WriteLine($"8. middleware (after: code {context.Response.StatusCode})");
    }
}
  • Line 5: A middleware can be a class. Its constructor takes a [RequestDelegate]: the rest of the pipeline (the subsequent middlewares, followed by MVC);
  • line 7: the [InvokeAsync] method is called for each request;
  • line 12: the middleware calls the rest of the pipeline and waits for it to finish. If it did not call it, the request would stop there (it would then have to generate the response itself). The code placed before this call executes on the outbound request, and the code placed after it executes on the return: the middleware “wraps” everything else and sees the final status code of the response.

The file [Filters/BlockAttribute.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Controllers;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters;

namespace Example24.Filters;

// an AUTHORIZATION filter: it decides whether the action can be executed.
// It is also an attribute: it is set on a controller or an action.
public class BlockAttribute : Attribute, IAuthorizationFilter
{
    public void OnAuthorization(AuthorizationFilterContext context)
    {
        // the filter knows the targeted action, unlike the middleware
        var action = (ControllerActionDescriptor)context.ActionDescriptor;
        Console.WriteLine($"2. authorization filter (targeted action: {action.ActionName})");
        if (context.HttpContext.Request.Query.ContainsKey("block"))
        {
            // setting Result short-circuits the rest: no binding, no action
            context.Result = new StatusCodeResult(StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden);
        }
    }
}
  • line 9: an authorization filter implements [IAuthorizationFilter]. The class also derives from [Attribute]: it can be applied, in square brackets, to a controller or an action;
  • lines 14–15: Unlike middleware, the filter knows the target action ([ActionDescriptor]). This is what allows the [[Authorize(Roles = "ADMIN")]] attribute (see the next chapter) to protect only certain actions;
  • lines 16–19: A filter rejects the request by setting [context.Result]: the sequence (binding, action) is not executed, and this result becomes the response. Here, a 403 response (access denied), with no content.

The file [Filters/IntegerBinder.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ModelBinding;

namespace Example24.Filters;

// the model binding of an integer parameter (see example 12)
public class IntegerBinder : IModelBinder
{
    public Task BindModelAsync(ModelBindingContext context)
    {
        var value = context.ValueProvider.GetValue(context.ModelName).FirstValue;
        Console.WriteLine($"3. model binding (received value: \"{value}\")");
        if (int.TryParse(value, out var integer))
        {
            context.Result = ModelBindingResult.Success(integer);
        }
        else
        {
            context.ModelState.AddModelError(context.ModelName, $"\"{value}\" is not an integer.");
        }
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

A custom template binding, like those in Example 12. An invalid value does not stop anything: the error is logged in [ModelState], and the action determines the outcome (line 18).

The file [Filters/TimingAttribute.cs]:

using System.Diagnostics;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters;

namespace Example24.Filters;

// an ACTION filter: code before and after the action.
// ActionFilterAttribute: a framework class, whose useful methods we override
public class TimingAttribute : ActionFilterAttribute
{
    private const string Key = "timing";

    public override void OnActionExecuting(ActionExecutingContext context)
    {
        // the action parameters are already bound: the filter can read them
        Console.WriteLine($"4. action filter (before; parameters: {string.Join(", ", context.ActionArguments.Values)})");
        context.HttpContext.Items[Key] = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    }

    public override void OnActionExecuted(ActionExecutedContext context)
    {
        var timer = (Stopwatch)context.HttpContext.Items[Key]!;
        // context.Exception: the exception possibly thrown by the action
        var outcome = context.Exception is null ? "" : $", exception {context.Exception.GetType().Name}";
        Console.WriteLine($"6. action filter (after, {timer.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms{outcome})");
    }
}
  • line 8: an action filter. [ActionFilterAttribute] is a framework class that already implements the necessary interfaces: we override ([override]) the relevant methods;
  • Lines 12–16: [OnActionExecuting] runs before the action. Model binding has already taken place: the action parameters are available ([ActionArguments]). A timer is started ([Stopwatch]), stored in [HttpContext.Items] (query scope; see Chapter 6);
  • lines 19–24: [OnActionExecuted] runs after the action. If the action threw an exception, it is available in [context.Exception]. An action filter can also override the result of the action ([context.Result]).

The file [Filters/ErrorPageFilter.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ModelBinding;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ViewFeatures;

namespace Example24.Filters;

// an EXCEPTION filter: it turns an exception into a response
public class ErrorPageFilter(IModelMetadataProvider metadata) : IExceptionFilter
{
    public void OnException(ExceptionContext context)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"x. exception filter ({context.Exception.GetType().Name}: {context.Exception.Message})");
        // instead of the default error page, our Error view, with the 500 code
        context.Result = new ViewResult
        {
            ViewName = "Error",
            StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError,
            ViewData = new ViewDataDictionary(metadata, context.ModelState) { Model = 500 },
        };
        context.ExceptionHandled = true; // the exception is handled: it goes no further
    }
}
  • Line 9: An exception filter implements [IExceptionFilter]. It receives exceptions thrown by the model binding, the action filters, and the action. This is a service: it receives the [IModelMetadataProvider] object via injection, which is necessary to construct the [ViewData] dictionary for a view;
  • lines 15–20: instead of the default error page, the filter generates a HTML page: the [Error] view, with status code 500. This is what the [View] method of a controller does, written here by hand;
  • Line 21: The exception is marked as handled; it does not propagate further up the chain.

The file [Program.cs]:

using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Example24.Filters;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews(options =>
{
    // a GLOBAL filter: it applies to all the actions of the application
    options.Filters.Add<ErrorPageFilter>();
});
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));

var app = builder.Build();

// the middlewares run in the order in which they are added
app.UseMiddleware<LoggerMiddleware>();
// an error response WITHOUT content (400, 403, 404...): the request is
// re-executed with the /error/{code} address, which builds a page
app.UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/error/{0}");
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
  • line 10: a global filter is applied to all actions in the application. It is added to the options of MVC;
  • line 17: a class-based middleware is added via [UseMiddleware]. Middlewares execute in the order they are added: this one is first, so it processes all requests;
  • line 20: a framework middleware. When an error response (codes 400–599) has no content, it re-executes the request using the address [/error/{code}] (where [{0}] is replaced by the code), and returns the resulting page while retaining the error code. This is how 403 responses from the authorization filter, 400 responses from the action, and 404 responses from routing become HTML pages.

The [Controllers/CalcController.cs] file:

using Example24.Filters;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example24.Controllers;

// two filters set on the controller: they apply to all its actions
[Block]
[Timing]
public class CalcController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("square/{n}")]
    public IActionResult Square([ModelBinder(typeof(IntegerBinder))] int n)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"5. action Square({n}); valid model: {ModelState.IsValid}");
        if (!ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            return BadRequest(); // a 400 without content: see UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute
        }
        if (n == 13)
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException("13 brings bad luck"); // an "unexpected" error
        }
        return View("Result", n * n);
    }
}
  • lines 7–8: two filters applied to the controller; they apply to all of its actions (they can also be applied to a single action);
  • line 12: the custom parameter binding;
  • lines 15–17: an invalid parameter: a 400 response with no content;
  • lines 19–21: an “unexpected” error, to see the exception filter in action.

The file [Controllers/ErrorController.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example24.Controllers;

public class ErrorController : Controller
{
    // [Route] without an HTTP method: the re-executed request keeps its original method
    [Route("error/{code:int}")]
    public IActionResult Display(int code)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"7. error page {code} (re-executed request)");
        Response.StatusCode = code; // the page keeps the error code
        return View("Error", code);
    }
}
  • line 8: the action for the error page. [[Route]], without a method; HTTP, accepts all methods: a re-executed POST request remains a POST request;
  • Line 12: The page retains the original error code.

The file [Views/Shared/Error.cshtml]:

@* the error page; its model: the error code *@
@model int
@{
    var message = Model switch
    {
        400 => "Bad request.",
        403 => "Access denied.",
        404 => "Page not found.",
        _ => "Internal server error.",
    };
}
<div class="alert alert-danger">
  <h1 class="h4">Error @Model</h1>
  <p class="mb-0">@message</p>
</div>
  • Lines 4–10: a switch expression [C#]: it returns the value of the first branch whose pattern matches the template. [_] corresponds to everything else. The view is in [Views/Shared]: it is found regardless of the controller ([CalcController] for the exception filter, [ErrorController] otherwise).

Five requests: a normal calculation (http://localhost:5000/square/7), an invalid parameter ([/square/abc]), a request blocked by the authorization filter ([/square/7?block=1]), an unexpected error ([/square/13]), and an unknown address ([/unknown]). The server console:

--- GET /square/7
1. middleware (before)
2. authorization filter (targeted action: Square)
3. model binding (received value: "7")
4. action filter (before; parameters: 7)
5. action Square(7); valid model: True
6. action filter (after, 0 ms)
8. middleware (after: code 200)

--- GET /square/abc
1. middleware (before)
2. authorization filter (targeted action: Square)
3. model binding (received value: "abc")
4. action filter (before; parameters: )
5. action Square(0); valid model: False
6. action filter (after, 0 ms)
7. error page 400 (re-executed request)
8. middleware (after: code 400)

--- GET /square/7?block=1
1. middleware (before)
2. authorization filter (targeted action: Square)
7. error page 403 (re-executed request)
8. middleware (after: code 403)

--- GET /square/13
1. middleware (before)
2. authorization filter (targeted action: Square)
3. model binding (received value: "13")
4. action filter (before; parameters: 13)
5. action Square(13); valid model: True
6. action filter (after, 0 ms, exception InvalidOperationException)
x. exception filter (InvalidOperationException: 13 brings bad luck)
8. middleware (after: code 500)

--- GET /unknown
1. middleware (before)
7. error page 404 (re-executed request)
8. middleware (after: code 404)

This log shows:

  • the order of the steps: middleware, authorization filter, model binding, action filter (before), action, action filter (after), and then the middleware again, which sees the final response code;
  • the authorization filter that rejects the request bypasses the rest of MVC (no binding, no action);
  • an invalid parameter does not prevent the action from executing: the action itself decides, based on [ModelState] (see example 09);
  • an exception from the action is handled by the exception filter, which generates the response;
  • an empty error response (400, 403, 404) is converted into a page by re-executing the request (step 7). For an unknown address, MVC does not even come into play: no route matches.

The resulting pages:

Let's check that the error code is preserved:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/square/7?block=1

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Lifecycle</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    <div class="alert alert-danger">
  <h1 class="h4">Error 403</h1>
  <p class="mb-0">Access denied.</p>
</div>

  </div>
</body>
</html>

The case study combines these mechanisms: [UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/error/{0}")] and a controller ([ErrorController]) for 400, 403, and 404 pages; the [UseExceptionHandler("/error/500")] middleware, which similarly re-executes any request that ends with an unhandled exception; and an exception filter ([Web/HtmlExceptionFilter.cs]) for a specific case: an expired session does not display an error page but redirects to the login page.

docs.title: 4. The View and Its Model
docs.text: Up to this point, actions have generated their own responses. In a MVC application, this is the role of a view: a file that describes the page HTML, with placeholders for the data passed to it by the action—the view’s template. [ASP.NET Core MVC] uses the [Razor] view engine: A view is a [.cshtml] file, derived from HTML, into which [C#] code is inserted, preceded by the character [@]. [Razor] is part of the framework: there is nothing to install.

docs.title: 4.1. Example 13: An Initial View
docs.text:
The [Program.cs] file:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// the MVC services: controllers AND Razor views
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews();

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
  • Line 4: [AddControllersWithViews] replaces [AddControllers] from the previous examples. It adds view services to the controller services: the [Razor] engine, view file search, and Tag Helpers (Example 15).

The view template is a simple class. The file [Models/PageModel.cs]:

namespace Example13.Models;

// the view model: the data the action passes to the view
public record PageModel(string Title, string Message, string Time);
  • line 4: a [record] is a class whose properties are set by the constructor; here, three strings: [Title], [Message], and [Time]. This is a concise way to define a class that simply carries data.

The file [Controllers/ViewsController.cs]:

using Example13.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example13.Controllers;

public class ViewsController : Controller
{
    // View(model): the view that bears the name of the action (Views/Views/Index.cshtml)
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Index()
    {
        var model = new PageModel(
            "My first view",
            "This page was built by Razor, on the server.",
            DateTime.Now.ToString("HH:mm:ss"));
        return View(model);
    }

    // View(name, model): the view is chosen by the action
    [HttpGet("hello/{name}")]
    public IActionResult Hello(string name)
    {
        if (name == "unknown")
        {
            Response.StatusCode = 404;
            return View("Unknown", name);
        }
        var model = new PageModel(
            $"Hello {name}",
            "This time, the action designated the view by its name.",
            DateTime.Now.ToString("HH:mm:ss"));
        return View("Index", model);
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 6: The controller derives from class [Controller], rather than [ControllerBase]: [Controller] adds to [ControllerBase] everything related to views (methods [View], [ViewData], [TempData], etc.);
  • lines 12–15: the action generates the view template: a title, a message, and the current time;
  • line 16: [View(model)] returns a [ViewResult]: the action no longer generates the response; instead, it designates a view and passes a template to it. If no view name is specified, the view with the same name as the action is used: [Index];
  • lines 23–26: When the view depends on the request, the action selects the view. Here, the name [unknown] displays the view [Unknown], with status code 404. The template for this view is a simple string;
  • line 32: the action [Hello] explicitly specifies the view [Index] by name: two actions share the same view, with different templates.

Where does [ASP.NET Core] look for the view [Index] for action [ViewsController.Index]? By convention, in two folders, in this order:

  • [Views/Views/Index.cshtml]: the folder named after the controller (without the suffix [Controller]);
  • [Views/Shared/Index.cshtml]: the folder containing views shared by all controllers (see Example 15).

If the view is not found anywhere, an exception lists the paths that were checked. The project files:

13-first-view/
├── Controllers/
│   └── ViewsController.cs
├── Models/
│   └── PageModel.cs
├── Views/
│   ├── Views/
│   │   ├── Index.cshtml
│   │   └── Unknown.cshtml
│   └── _ViewImports.cshtml
├── appsettings.json
├── Example13.csproj
└── Program.cs

The file [Views/_ViewImports.cshtml]:

@* the "using" directives shared by all the views of the Views folder *@
@using Example13.Models
  • Line 1: [@* ... *@] is a comment [Razor]: it does not appear on the generated page (unlike a comment HTML [<!-- -->]);
  • Line 2: The directives in the [_ViewImports.cshtml] file apply to all views in its folder and subfolders. [@using Example13.Models] allows you to write [PageModel] instead of [Example13.Models.PageModel] in the views.

The [Views/Views/Index.cshtml] file:

@* the type of the model of this view *@
@model PageModel
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>@Model.Title</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>@Model.Title</h1>
  <p>@Model.Message</p>
  <p>Page built at @Model.Time.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • line 2: the directive [@model] declares the type of the view template. In the view, the property [Model] is then of type [PageModel], and the compiler verifies that [Model.Title] exists;
  • Lines 7–12: Each expression [@Model.Title] is replaced by the corresponding value from the template. [Razor] recognizes the end of an expression on its own: in [@Model.Time.], the period is followed by a tag, so it is not a property access.

A view is a [C#] file in disguise: when the project is compiled ([dotnet build]), each [.cshtml] file is translated into a [C#] class, which is compiled along with the rest of the application. An error in a view ([@Model.Titl]) is therefore reported during compilation. The result, in the URL http://localhost:5000/:

The source code of the page received by the browser no longer contains any trace of [Razor]:

curl http://localhost:5000/

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>My first view</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>My first view</h1>
  <p>This page was built by Razor, on the server.</p>
  <p>Page built at 12:12:36.</p>
</body>
</html>

Note that accented characters inserted by an [@] expression would be encoded (this page contains none): a French title such as [Ma première vue] would be sent as [Ma première vue], [è] being the code for the character [è], whereas accented text typed directly into the view would remain unchanged. The browser displays both correctly, but the code HTML is difficult to read. We’ll see in Example 15 how to avoid this. The URL http://localhost:5000/hello/martin displays the same view using a different template:

and http://localhost:5000/hello/unknown displays a different view:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/hello/unknown

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [unknown] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>

The file [Views/Views/Unknown.cshtml]:

@* the model of this view is a simple string: the requested name *@
@model string
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [@Model] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>
  • Line 2: The template for this view is a string;
  • line 10: [@Model] is the string itself.

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: The Razor language
docs.text:
[Razor] is not a “logic-free” template language like [Handlebars]: you can write [C#] code within a view (conditions, loops, variables, method calls). This freedom requires discipline: the view must remain purely for formatting; calculations and decisions belong to the action and the services. Example 14 provides an overview of the syntax. The template, file [Models/BasicsModel.cs]:

namespace Example14.Models;

public record Product(string Name, decimal Price, bool InStock);

public record Address(string Street, string City);

public class BasicsModel
{
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public string? Nickname { get; set; }
    public string Html { get; set; } = "";
    public bool LoggedIn { get; set; }
    public string Currency { get; set; } = "";
    public List<Product> Products { get; set; } = [];
    public List<Product> Cart { get; set; } = [];
    public Address Address { get; set; } = new("", "");
}

The file [Controllers/BasicsController.cs]:

using Example14.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example14.Controllers;

public class BasicsController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Index()
    {
        var model = new BasicsModel
        {
            Title = "Razor basics",
            Name = "Martin",
            Nickname = null,
            Html = "<b>this is HTML</b>",
            LoggedIn = true,
            Currency = "€",
            Products =
            [
                new Product("Keyboard", 25m, true),
                new Product("Mouse", 12.5m, false),
                new Product("Screen", 149m, true),
            ],
            Cart = [],
            Address = new Address("12 rue des Lilas", "Angers"),
        };
        return View(model);
    }
}
  • Lines 11–26: The action populates the template: a few strings, a Boolean, a list of three products, an empty shopping cart, and an address. [Nickname] is intentionally the same as [null].

The view, file [Views/Basics/Index.cshtml]:

@model BasicsModel
@* a C# code block: it produces nothing in the page *@
@{
    var total = Model.Products.Sum(p => p.Price);
    var count = Model.Products.Count;
}
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>@Model.Title</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>@Model.Title</h1>
  @* 1. display a value of the model; a null value displays nothing *@
  <p>1. Name: @Model.Name - nickname: [@Model.Nickname]</p>
  @* 2. @ escapes HTML, @Html.Raw inserts it as is *@
  <p>2a. @Model.Html</p>
  <p>2b. @Html.Raw(Model.Html)</p>
  @* 3. a condition *@
  @if (Model.LoggedIn)
  {
    <p>3. You are logged in.</p>
  }
  else
  {
    <p>3. You are not logged in.</p>
  }
  @* 4. a loop; the loop variables are C# variables *@
  <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>
    @for (var i = 0; i < Model.Products.Count; i++)
    {
      var product = Model.Products[i];
      <li>no. @i: @product.Name, @product.Price @Model.Currency
        @(product.InStock ? "(in stock)" : "(sold out)")
        @if (i == 0) { <text>- the first one</text> }
        @if (i == Model.Products.Count - 1) { @:- the last one, seen by @Model.Name
        }
      </li>
    }
  </ul>
  @* 5. the empty list *@
  <p>5. Your cart:
    @if (Model.Cart.Count == 0)
    {
      <text>it is empty.</text>
    }
    else
    {
      foreach (var p in Model.Cart) { <span>@p.Name</span> }
    }
  </p>
  @* 6. an explicit expression @( ... ), and the variables of the @{ } block *@
  <p>6. @count products, for a total of @(total) @Model.Currency; average price: @((total / count).ToString("0.00")) @Model.Currency</p>
  <p>7. Address: @Model.Address.Street, @Model.Address.City.ToUpper()</p>
  <p>8. An email address: contact@example.com</p>
</body>
</html>

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 2–5: A block of code named [@{ ... }] contains instructions named [C#]. It does not produce anything on the page. The variables it declares ([total], [count]) can be used later in the view;
  • line 16: a value [null] ([@Model.Nickname]) displays nothing, with no error;
  • Lines 18–19: An expression [@...] escapes the special characters in HTML ([<] becomes [<]...): the text is displayed as-is. [@Html.Raw(...)] inserts it without escaping: it is interpreted as HTML. [Html.Raw] is used only for HTML generated by the application, never for data entered by a user: the user could inject HTML, or even [JavaScript], into the page (an attack known as [XSS], [cross-site scripting]);
  • Lines 21–27: a condition. After [@if (...)], the content within the curly braces is HTML: [Razor] recognizes the start of a tag and reverts to HTML mode. We return to [C#] via [@];
  • lines 32–40: a loop from [for] to [C#]. [var product = ...] is an instruction [C#], [<li>] of HTML: [Razor] alternates between the two without any specific marker;
  • Line 36: an explicit expression [@( ... )]. Parentheses are required whenever the expression contains spaces or operators (in this case, the conditional operator [? :]);
  • line 37: To write unformatted text within a [C#] block, enclose it in the special tag [<text>], which does not appear on the page;
  • line 38: [@:] does the same thing for the rest of the line;
  • lines 45–51: An empty list is simply [if]. In the [else] block, already in [C#] mode, [foreach] is written without [@];
  • line 55: the variables of the [@{ }] block and explicit expressions, including a method call: [ToString("0.00")] formats a number with two decimal places;
  • line 56: a pointed path [@Model.Address.Street], and a method call [ToUpper()];
  • line 57: [Razor] recognizes that a [@] placed between two alphanumeric characters is not code: [contact@example.com] is an email address. To write a [@] that would be ambiguous, we duplicate it: [@@].

The result, URL, is http://localhost:5000/:

The code HTML produces:

curl http://localhost:5000/

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Razor basics</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Razor basics</h1>
  <p>1. Name: Martin - nickname: []</p>
  <p>2a. <b>this is HTML</b></p>
  <p>2b. <b>this is HTML</b></p>
    <p>3. You are logged in.</p>
  <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>
      <li>no. 0: Keyboard, 25 €
        (in stock)
- the first one      </li>
      <li>no. 1: Mouse, 12.5 €
        (sold out)
      </li>
      <li>no. 2: Screen, 149 €
        (in stock)
 - the last one, seen by Martin
      </li>
  </ul>
  <p>5. Your cart:
it is empty.  </p>
  <p>6. 3 products, for a total of 186.5 €; average price: 62.17 €</p>
  <p>7. Address: 12 rue des Lilas, ANGERS</p>
  <p>8. An email address: contact@example.com</p>
</body>
</html>

Note the spaces and blank lines left by the [C#] instructions: they have no effect on the display. We also see the encoding of accented characters derived from expressions ([€] for [€]), which is corrected in the following example.

docs.title: 4.3. Example 15: Template, Partial Views, Static Files
docs.text:
The pages of a website share a common template (header, navigation bar, footer). [Razor] refers to this template as a “layout”: each view is inserted into it. Reusable page components are partial views. Finally, pages require static files (style sheets, images, scripts), which are served as-is, without going through a controller. The files in the example:

15-layout/
├── Controllers/
│   └── PagesController.cs
├── Views/
│   ├── Pages/
│   │   ├── Home.cshtml
│   │   ├── Raw.cshtml
│   │   └── Team.cshtml
│   ├── Shared/
│   │   ├── _Card.cshtml
│   │   ├── _Layout.cshtml
│   │   └── _Navbar.cshtml
│   ├── _ViewImports.cshtml
│   └── _ViewStart.cshtml
├── wwwroot/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
├── appsettings.json
├── Example15.csproj
└── Program.cs

The file [Program.cs]:

using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews();
// Razor writes accented characters as is (and not "é");
// < > & " ' remain escaped
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));

var app = builder.Build();

// 1. the static files of the wwwroot folder: wwwroot/css/styles.css is served as /css/styles.css
app.UseStaticFiles();
// 2. Bootstrap, shared by the examples: the examples/common/bootstrap folder is served under /bootstrap
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 9: the [HtmlEncoder] service is the one used by [Razor] to escape the expressions in [@]. By default, it only allows characters from the basic Latin alphabet to pass through: this is what encodes [é] as [é] (and [€] as [€]). We replace this service with an encoder that allows all characters to pass through ([UnicodeRanges.All]). The dangerous characters ([<], [>], [&], ["], [']) remain escaped: the protection against injection in HTML remains intact. All of the following examples, as well as the case study, include this line;
  • line 14: a middleware component (see Chapter 7) that serves files from the [wwwroot] folder of the project: the file [wwwroot/css/styles.css] is served to URL and [/css/styles.css]. If the file does not exist, the request continues on to the controllers;
  • Lines 16–19: A second static file service. The CSS [Bootstrap] framework is common to all examples: it is stored only once, in the [examples/common/bootstrap] folder, and served under the prefix [/bootstrap]. [PhysicalFileProvider] refers to a folder on the disk; [ContentRootPath] is the project folder. Thus, [examples/common/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css] is served to URL and [/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css]. The case study, on the other hand, places [Bootstrap] in its own folder, [wwwroot].

Let’s check:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/css/styles.css

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 430
Content-Type: text/css

/* a few settings on top of Bootstrap */
body {
  background-color: #f5f7fa;
}

/* the footer of the layout */
.footer {
  margin-top: 2rem;
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #6c757d;
}

/* the error messages, at the bottom of the page, on a light pink background */
.error-area {
  margin-top: 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background-color: #fdecef;
  border: 1px solid #f5c2c7;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
  color: #842029;
}

The file [Views/_ViewStart.cshtml]:

@* executed before every view: all the views use the _Layout layout *@
@{
    Layout = "_Layout";
}
  • Line 3: The file [_ViewStart.cshtml] is executed before each view in its folder and subfolders. It sets the [Layout] property: all views use the [_Layout] template, which is searched for in the view’s folder and then in [Views/Shared].

The file [Views/_ViewImports.cshtml]:

@* the ASP.NET Core Tag Helpers: "enriched" HTML tags, such as <partial> *@
@addTagHelper *, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.TagHelpers
@using Example15.Controllers
  • Line 2: Enables the Tag Helpers provided by [ASP.NET Core]: HTML tags or attributes processed by the server. The [<partial>] tag is one such example. [*] means “all Tag Helpers in the assembly” [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.TagHelpers];
  • Line 3: The type [Member] is declared in the controllers namespace.

The file [Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml]:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  @* ViewData["Title"]: a value set by the view, read by the layout *@
  <title>@ViewData["Title"] - My site</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    <partial name="_Navbar" />
    @* the view requested by the action is inserted here *@
    @RenderBody()
    @* Context: the current request (HttpContext), available to every view *@
    <footer class="footer">Page [@Context.Request.Path] - © @DateTime.Now.Year</footer>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 7: [ViewData] is a dictionary shared by a view and its template (and by the action, which can also store values in it). The view stores its title there, and the template displays it;
  • lines 8–9: the style sheets, served by [UseStaticFiles];
  • line 13: insertion of the partial view [_Navbar], searched for in the view’s folder and then in [Views/Shared];
  • line 15: the location where [Razor] inserts the view requested by the action;
  • line 17: [Context] is the [HttpContext] object of the current request (see Example 05), accessible to any view: the template displays the requested path without each action having to pass it along.

The file [Views/Shared/_Navbar.cshtml]:

<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">My site</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    <a class="nav-link" href="/">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/team">Team</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/raw">Page without layout</a>
  </div>
</nav>

The file [Views/Shared/_Card.cshtml]:

@* a Bootstrap "card"; its model: a Member (name, role) *@
@model Member
<div class="card">
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">@Model.Name</h5>
    <p class="card-text">@Model.Role</p>
  </div>
</div>

By convention, the name of a partial view or template begins with [_]: these are not complete pages. The partial view [_Card] has its own template (line 2), a name, and a role. The type [Member] is declared in the controller. The file [Controllers/PagesController.cs]:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example15.Controllers;

public record Member(string Name, string Role);

public class PagesController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IActionResult Home()
    {
        return View();
    }

    [HttpGet("team")]
    public IActionResult Team()
    {
        List<Member> members =
        [
            new Member("Marie Pélissier", "Director"),
            new Member("Jacques Bromard", "Developer"),
            new Member("Philippe Jandot", "Graphic designer"),
        ];
        return View(members);
    }

    [HttpGet("raw")]
    public IActionResult Raw()
    {
        return View();
    }
}
  • line 5: the type of team members;
  • line 12: the action [Home] has no template: [View()] with no arguments;
  • lines 18–24: the action [Team] passes a list of members.

The partial view is used in two ways. The file [Views/Pages/Home.cshtml]:

@{
    ViewData["Title"] = "Home";
}
<h1>Welcome</h1>
<p>This page only contains its own content: the header, the navigation
  bar and the footer come from the <code>_Layout.cshtml</code> layout.</p>
<partial name="_Card" model='new Member("A partial view", "inserted with a model built on the spot")' />
  • line 2: the view places its title in [ViewData], for the template;
  • Line 7: The [model] attribute of the [<partial>] tag provides the template for the partial view: in this case, an object created on the fly. This is a [C#] expression: it is enclosed in apostrophes so that quotation marks can be used within it.

The file [Views/Pages/Team.cshtml]:

@model List<Member>
@{
    ViewData["Title"] = "Our team";
}
<h1>Our team</h1>
<div class="row g-3">
  @foreach (var member in Model)
  {
    <div class="col-md-4">
      @* the partial view receives the current member as its model *@
      <partial name="_Card" model="member" />
    </div>
  }
</div>
  • Line 11: The partial view receives the current loop iteration as its template.

The file [Views/Pages/Raw.cshtml]:

@* Layout = null: this view does not use the layout, it is a complete page *@
@{
    Layout = null;
}
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Raw page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>This page does not use the layout: no Bootstrap, no navigation bar.</p>
  <p><a href="/">Back to home</a></p>
</body>
</html>
  • Line 3: Setting [Layout] to [null] in a view cancels the selection of [_ViewStart.cshtml]: The view [Raw] is a complete HTML page. You could also specify a different template ([Layout = "_Other"]).

The resulting pages, at URL http://localhost:5000/, http://localhost:5000/team, and http://localhost:5000/raw:

The template, partial views, and [ViewData] are exactly what the case study uses: a [_Layout.cshtml] template, partial views for the navigation bar, messages, and confirmation windows.

docs.title: 4.4. Example 16: Helpers
docs.text:
A view often requires small formatting functions: formatting a date or a price, capitalizing text, creating a badge HTML... With [Razor], these are simple methods [C#], called within an expression [@]. [ASP.NET Core] also offers Tag Helpers: [C#] code that acts on a HTML tag when the page is rendered.

The [Helpers/Formats.cs] file:

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Html;

namespace Example16.Helpers;

// ordinary C# functions, callable from the views: @Formats.Money(...)
public static class Formats
{
    // "keyboard" -> "KEYBOARD"
    public static string Uppercase(string? text) => (text ?? "").ToUpperInvariant();

    // an amount in a currency, in the format of the current language (CultureInfo.CurrentCulture)
    // "C" = currency; the NumberFormatInfo object sets the currency symbol
    public static string Money(decimal amount, string currency = "EUR")
    {
        var format = (NumberFormatInfo)CultureInfo.CurrentCulture.NumberFormat.Clone();
        format.CurrencySymbol = currency == "USD" ? "$" : "€";
        return amount.ToString("C", format);
    }

    // a date in full words, in the current language: "Wednesday, September 23, 2026"
    public static string Date(DateTime when) => when.ToString("D", CultureInfo.CurrentCulture);

    // a helper that builds HTML: it returns an IHtmlContent, which Razor does not escape.
    // It is then up to the helper to escape the data it inserts (HtmlEncoder)
    public static IHtmlContent Badge(int stock)
    {
        var cssClass = stock > 0 ? "text-bg-success" : "text-bg-danger";
        var text = HtmlEncoder.Default.Encode(stock > 0 ? $"{stock} in stock" : "sold out");
        return new HtmlString($"<span class=\"badge {cssClass}\">{text}</span>");
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 8: a static class—its methods are called without creating an object, [Formats.Uppercase(...)];
  • line 11: capitalization. [ToUpperInvariant] is independent of the user’s language;
  • lines 15–19: an amount in a currency. The format ["C"] ([currency]) formats an amount according to the current locale ([CultureInfo.CurrentCulture]): decimal separator, thousands separator, and currency symbol position. The locale rules are copied ([Clone]) to change the currency symbol;
  • line 23: a date written out in full (format ["D"]), in the language of the current culture;
  • lines 27–31: a helper that generates HTML. The output of a [@] expression is escaped, unless it is a [IHtmlContent]: pre-generated HTML. [HtmlString] is the simplest implementation of this. The helper must then escape the data it inserts into its HTML ([HtmlEncoder.Default.Encode]) itself.

The [TagHelpers/ActiveTagHelper.cs] file:

using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.TagHelpers;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Razor.TagHelpers;

namespace Example16.TagHelpers;

// a Tag Helper: it applies to the <a> tags that carry the "active-path" attribute
// <a href="/products" active-path="/products"> gets the "active" class if the
// current page is under this path
[HtmlTargetElement("a", Attributes = "active-path")]
public class ActiveTagHelper(IHttpContextAccessor accessor) : TagHelper
{
    // the value of the active-path="..." attribute
    public string ActivePath { get; set; } = "";

    public override void Process(TagHelperContext context, TagHelperOutput output)
    {
        var path = accessor.HttpContext?.Request.Path.Value ?? "/";
        var isActive = ActivePath == "/" ? path == "/" : path.StartsWith(ActivePath, StringComparison.Ordinal);
        if (isActive)
        {
            output.AddClass("active", HtmlEncoder.Default); // adds the class to the class attribute
        }
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 10: The Tag Helper applies to [<a>] tags that have the [active-path] attribute;
  • line 11: a Tag Helper derives from the [TagHelper] class. It is a service: it receives a [IHttpContextAccessor] via injection, which provides access to the current request;
  • line 14: the value of the [active-path="..."] attribute is assigned to the property of the same name ([ActivePath]);
  • Lines 16–22: The method [Process] is called for each relevant tag. If the page path begins with the value of the attribute, the class CSS [active] is added to the tag ([AddClass]). The [active-path] attribute itself does not appear in the generated page: the Tag Helper has consumed it.

The file [Program.cs]:

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews();
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));
// IHttpContextAccessor: gives access to the current request (used by ActiveTagHelper)
builder.Services.AddHttpContextAccessor();

var app = builder.Build();

// a middleware: the formatting language comes from the ?lang=fr parameter of the URL
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var language = context.Request.Query["lang"] == "fr" ? "fr-FR" : "en-US";
    CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = new CultureInfo(language);
    await next(context); // hand over to the next middleware
});

app.UseStaticFiles();
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
  • line 10: registers the [IHttpContextAccessor] service, used by the Tag Helper;
  • lines 15–19: middleware written directly into [Program.cs], executed for each request. It selects the culture based on the [lang] parameter from URL, then passes control to the next middleware ([next]). This is a simple way to test; the next chapter will cover it better.

The [Views/_ViewImports.cshtml] file:

@addTagHelper *, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.TagHelpers
@* our own Tag Helpers, those of the Example16 assembly *@
@addTagHelper *, Example16
@using Example16.Helpers
@using Example16.Controllers
  • Line 3: We enable the Tag Helpers for our own project (the [Example16] assembly);
  • line 4: views can write [Formats.Money(...)].

The [Views/Shared/_Navbar.cshtml] file:

<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Helpers</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    @* 1. a condition written in the view *@
    <a class="nav-link @(Context.Request.Path == "/" ? "active" : "")" href="/">Home</a>
    @* 2. our Tag Helper: the active-path="..." attribute *@
    <a class="nav-link" href="/products" active-path="/products">Products</a>
    @* 3. an ASP.NET Tag Helper: asp-action builds the URL of the action *@
    <a class="nav-link" asp-controller="Pages" asp-action="Products" asp-route-lang="fr">Produits (fr)</a>
  </div>
</nav>
  • Lines 4–5: First way to highlight the current page’s link: a condition written in the view;
  • line 7: second, more concise method: our Tag Helper. This is the one used in the case study;
  • line 9: a Tag Helper for [ASP.NET Core]. The attributes [asp-controller] and [asp-action] denote an action; the Tag Helper calculates its URL based on the routes (here, [/products]) and writes it to the [href] attribute. [asp-route-lang="fr"] adds a parameter, which is placed in URL ([?lang=fr]) since the route does not contain a [lang] parameter. If the action’s URL is changed, the link follows suit.

The code HTML in the navigation bar, from URL to [/products]:

<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Helpers</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    <a class="nav-link " href="/">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link active" href="/products">Products</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/products?lang=fr">Produits (fr)</a>
  </div>
</nav>

The file [Views/Pages/Products.cshtml]:

@model List<Product>
@{
    ViewData["Title"] = "Products";
}
<h1>Products</h1>
<table class="table table-sm w-auto">
  <thead><tr><th>Product</th><th>Price</th><th>Price in dollars</th><th>Stock</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    @foreach (var product in Model)
    {
      <tr>
        <td>@Formats.Uppercase(product.Name)</td>
        <td>@Formats.Money(product.Price)</td>
        <td>@Formats.Money(product.Price, "USD")</td>
        <td>@Formats.Badge(product.Stock)</td>
      </tr>
    }
  </tbody>
</table>
  • Lines 12–15: The helpers are called within [@] expressions. [Badge] returns HTML, inserted without escaping.

The resulting pages, in English (http://localhost:5000/, http://localhost:5000/products) and then in French (http://localhost:5000/products?lang=fr):

The prices change format depending on the language: [1 149,90 €] in French, [€1,149.90] in English.

docs.title: 4.5. Example 17: a GET form
docs.text:
A HTML form submitted using the GET method places its fields in the URL. This is the appropriate method for a search: it does not modify anything, and the resulting URL can be bookmarked or shared. The case study uses it to select a doctor and a date.

The [Models/Book.cs] file:

namespace Example17.Models;

public record Book(string Title, string Author, string Genre);

// the view model: the input (to display it again), the genres, the results
public record SearchModel(string Keyword, string Genre, string[] Genres, List<Book> Results);
  • Line 6: The view template contains the entered values ([Keyword], [Genre]), so that the form can display them again, along with the list of genres and the results.

The file [Controllers/BooksController.cs]:

using Example17.Models;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example17.Controllers;

public class BooksController : Controller
{
    private static readonly List<Book> Books =
    [
        new Book("Le Rouge et le Noir", "Stendhal", "novel"),
        new Book("Les Fleurs du mal", "Baudelaire", "poetry"),
        new Book("Madame Bovary", "Flaubert", "novel"),
        new Book("Alcools", "Apollinaire", "poetry"),
        new Book("Le Cid", "Corneille", "drama"),
    ];

    private static readonly string[] Genres = ["novel", "poetry", "drama"];

    // GET / and GET /search?keyword=...&genre=...: the form AND its results
    [HttpGet("/")]
    [HttpGet("search")]
    public IActionResult Search(string? keyword, string? genre)
    {
        var word = (keyword ?? "").Trim().ToLower();
        var results = Books
            .Where(b => word == "" || b.Title.ToLower().Contains(word) || b.Author.ToLower().Contains(word))
            .Where(b => string.IsNullOrEmpty(genre) || b.Genre == genre)
            .ToList();
        return View(new SearchModel(keyword ?? "", genre ?? "", Genres, results));
    }
}
  • lines 8–14: the books, in memory;
  • lines 20–21: two route attributes: the action processes [GET /] and [GET /search];
  • Line 22: The parameters [keyword] and [genre] are linked to the parameters of the same name in URL. On the first visit, the form has not yet been submitted: their values are [null];
  • lines 25–28: filtering, using [LINQ]. An empty keyword or an empty category does not filter anything;
  • line 29: the view template.

The file [Views/Books/Search.cshtml]:

@model SearchModel
<h1 class="h3">Book search</h1>
@* method="get": the fields are sent in the URL (?keyword=...&genre=...) *@
<form method="get" action="/search" class="row g-2 align-items-end mb-3">
  <div class="col-auto">
    <label class="form-label" for="keyword">Title or author</label>
    @* value="@Model.Keyword": the field displays again what was typed *@
    <input class="form-control" id="keyword" name="keyword" value="@Model.Keyword">
  </div>
  <div class="col-auto">
    <label class="form-label" for="genre">Genre</label>
    <select class="form-select" id="genre" name="genre">
      <option value="">(all)</option>
      @foreach (var genre in Model.Genres)
      {
        @* a boolean attribute: written if the condition is true, omitted otherwise *@
        <option value="@genre" selected="@(genre == Model.Genre)">@genre</option>
      }
    </select>
  </div>
  <div class="col-auto">
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Search</button>
  </div>
</form>
<p>@Model.Results.Count book(s) found.</p>
<ul>
  @foreach (var book in Model.Results)
  {
    <li><i>@book.Title</i>, @book.Author (@book.Genre)</li>
  }
</ul>
  • line 4: [method="get"] and [action="/search"]: submitting the form is a [GET /search?keyword=...&genre=...] request. The parameter names are the [name] attribute of each field;
  • Line 8: The [value] attribute re-displays the entry;
  • line 17: In the drop-down list, the option corresponding to the selected genre is assigned the attribute [selected]. [Razor] handles Boolean attributes in a specific way: if the value is [true], it writes [selected="selected"]; if it is [false], it does not write the attribute at all. This is exactly what HTML requires, for which the mere presence of the attribute [selected] is sufficient to select the option.

On the first display (http://localhost:5000/), and then after a search:

The address bar shows the parameters that were sent. Accented characters and spaces are encoded there ([%C3%A9]...): this is the URL encoding, which [ASP.NET Core] decodes before the template binding.

docs.title: 4.6. Example 18: Form Fields
docs.text:
Example 18 includes all types of HTML fields: text, password, date, radio buttons, checkboxes, drop-down list, multi-select list, text box, and hidden field. It shows how the server receives them and how the view displays them.

The [Services/ListsService.cs] file:

namespace Example18.Services;

public record Country(string Code, string Name);

// the lists offered by the form. In a real application, they would
// come from a database: we would read them ONCE, at startup,
// since they are the same for all users
public class ListsService
{
    public string[] Titles { get; } = ["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"];

    public Country[] Countries { get; } =
    [
        new Country("fr", "France"),
        new Country("be", "Belgium"),
        new Country("ch", "Switzerland"),
        new Country("ca", "Canada"),
    ];

    public string[] Hobbies { get; } = ["reading", "music", "sport", "cinema"];

    public string[] Languages { get; } = ["French", "English", "Spanish", "German"];
}

The lists offered by the form are provided by a service. They are the same for all users: a service instantiated only once (a singleton; see Chapter 6) is the natural place to store them. It is saved in [Program.cs]:

using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Example18.Services;
using Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews();
// Razor writes accented characters as is (and not "é");
// < > & " ' remain escaped
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));
// the lists of the form: the same for everyone, a single object (singleton)
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ListsService>();

var app = builder.Build();

// 1. the static files of the wwwroot folder: wwwroot/css/styles.css is served as /css/styles.css
app.UseStaticFiles();
// 2. Bootstrap, shared by the examples: the examples/common/bootstrap folder is served under /bootstrap
app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "..", "common", "bootstrap"))),
    RequestPath = "/bootstrap",
});

app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
  • line 12: a single instance of [ListsService], shared by all requests.

The file [Models/Input.cs]:

namespace Example18.Models;

// what the user typed: model binding fills each property
// with the field of the same name (the arrays receive all the checked values)
public class Input
{
    public string? Name { get; set; }
    public string? Password { get; set; }
    public string? Comment { get; set; }
    public string? Title { get; set; }
    public string[] Hobbies { get; set; } = [];
    public string? Country { get; set; }
    public string[] Languages { get; set; } = [];
    public DateOnly? BirthDate { get; set; }
    public string? Token { get; set; }
}

// an option of a list, and its state (checked / selected)
public record Option(string Value, string Label, bool Chosen);

// the view model
public class FormModel
{
    public required Input Input { get; init; }
    public required List<Option> Titles { get; init; }
    public required List<Option> Hobbies { get; init; }
    public required List<Option> Countries { get; init; }
    public required List<Option> Languages { get; init; }
    public string? Received { get; init; } // what the server received, to display it
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 5–15: the input. The template binding populates each property with the field of the same name. The checkboxes and the drop-down list are arrays ([string[]]): they receive all the values sent (see Example 10). The date of birth is converted to [DateOnly];
  • line 19: an option from a list: its value, its label, and a Boolean indicating whether it is checked or selected;
  • lines 22–29: the view template. The keyword [required] requires that the property be provided when the object is created; [init] prevents it from being modified afterward.

The [Controllers/FormController.cs] file:

using Example18.Models;
using Example18.Services;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace Example18.Controllers;

[Route("form")]
public class FormController(ListsService lists) : Controller
{
    // GET: the form, with initial values
    [HttpGet("")]
    public IActionResult Display()
    {
        var initial = new Input { Title = "Mme", Country = "fr", Languages = ["French"], Token = "A7X2" };
        return View("Form", Model(initial, null));
    }

    // POST: model binding fills [input]; we display the form again
    [HttpPost("")]
    public IActionResult Process(Input input)
    {
        // what the browser actually sent, field by field
        var received = string.Join("\n", Request.Form.Select(c => $"{c.Key} = [{string.Join(", ", c.Value.ToArray())}]"));
        return View("Form", Model(input, received));
    }

    // the view model: the lists, each option being marked checked /
    // selected according to the input. The view will only have to test a boolean.
    private FormModel Model(Input input, string? received) => new()
    {
        Input = input,
        Titles = lists.Titles.Select(t => new Option(t, t, t == input.Title)).ToList(),
        Hobbies = lists.Hobbies.Select(h => new Option(h, h, input.Hobbies.Contains(h))).ToList(),
        Countries = lists.Countries.Select(c => new Option(c.Code, c.Name, c.Code == input.Country)).ToList(),
        Languages = lists.Languages.Select(l => new Option(l, l, input.Languages.Contains(l))).ToList(),
        Received = received,
    };
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 8: the list service is injected;
  • lines 11–15: [GET /form] displays the form with initial values;
  • lines 19–24: [POST /form] receives the user input—populated by the model binding—and redraws the form. [Request.Form] also provides access to the fields as they were submitted: it converts them into text, one line per field, for display;
  • lines 29–36: the view template. For each list, the action calculates which options should be checked or selected: the view will then only need to test a Boolean.

The file [Views/Form/Form.cshtml]:

@model FormModel
<h1 class="h3">A complete form</h1>
<form method="post" action="/form" style="max-width: 40rem">
  @* hidden field: sent with the form, but invisible *@
  <input type="hidden" name="token" value="@Model.Input.Token">

  <div class="mb-2">
    <span class="form-label me-3">Title</span>
    @foreach (var title in Model.Titles)
    {
      @* radio buttons: same [name], a single value sent *@
      <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
        <input class="form-check-input" type="radio" name="title" id="title-@title.Value"
               value="@title.Value" checked="@title.Chosen">
        <label class="form-check-label" for="title-@title.Value">@title.Label</label>
      </div>
    }
  </div>

  <div class="row g-2 mb-2">
    <div class="col">
      <label class="form-label" for="name">Name</label>
      <input class="form-control" type="text" id="name" name="name" value="@Model.Input.Name">
    </div>
    <div class="col">
      <label class="form-label" for="password">Password</label>
      @* a password is NEVER sent back in the page *@
      <input class="form-control" type="password" id="password" name="password">
    </div>
    <div class="col">
      <label class="form-label" for="birthDate">Date of birth</label>
      @* a date field exchanges its values in the yyyy-mm-dd format *@
      <input class="form-control" type="date" id="birthDate" name="birthDate"
             value="@Model.Input.BirthDate?.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd")">
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="mb-2">
    <span class="form-label me-3">Hobbies</span>
    @for (var i = 0; i < Model.Hobbies.Count; i++)
    {
      var hobby = Model.Hobbies[i];
      @* checkboxes: same [name], several possible values *@
      <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
        <input class="form-check-input" type="checkbox" name="hobbies" id="hobby-@i"
               value="@hobby.Value" checked="@hobby.Chosen">
        <label class="form-check-label" for="hobby-@i">@hobby.Label</label>
      </div>
    }
  </div>

  <div class="row g-2 mb-2">
    <div class="col">
      <label class="form-label" for="country">Country</label>
      <select class="form-select" id="country" name="country">
        @foreach (var country in Model.Countries)
        {
          <option value="@country.Value" selected="@country.Chosen">@country.Label</option>
        }
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="col">
      <label class="form-label" for="languages">Spoken languages</label>
      @* multiple-selection list: several possible values *@
      <select class="form-select" id="languages" name="languages" multiple size="4">
        @foreach (var language in Model.Languages)
        {
          <option value="@language.Value" selected="@language.Chosen">@language.Label</option>
        }
      </select>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="mb-2">
    <label class="form-label" for="comment">Comment</label>
    @* a text area: the value is BETWEEN the tags *@
    <textarea class="form-control" id="comment" name="comment" rows="2">@Model.Input.Comment</textarea>
  </div>

  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

@if (Model.Received is not null)
{
  <h2 class="h5 mt-3">What the server received</h2>
  <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">@Model.Received</pre>
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 3: The form is submitted via POST: its fields are included in the request body;
  • Line 5: A hidden field is sent with the form but is not displayed. It is used to pass information from one page to the next (in the case study, for example, it contains the version of a record). Note: The user can modify it;
  • Lines 9–15: Radio buttons share the same [name]; only one can be selected, and only one value is sent. The Boolean attribute [checked="@title.Chosen"] selects the button (see [selected], Example 17);
  • line 28: a password is never sent back in a page: the field has no [value] attribute;
  • lines 33–34: a date field. The browser displays the date in the user’s format, but always sends and receives [yyyy-mm-dd];
  • lines 40–46: checkboxes with the same [name] attribute: each checked box sends its value; the parameter is therefore repeated;
  • lines 55–60: a drop-down list. The selected option has the attribute [selected];
  • line 65: the [multiple] attribute allows you to select multiple options;
  • line 77: the value of a text field is enclosed within its tags, not in a [value] attribute;
  • Lines 83–86: What the server received, displayed within a [<pre>] tag, which preserves line breaks.

The initial form (http://localhost:5000/form), then after submission:

Note that the text field re-displayed [Hello <b>everyone</b>] exactly as entered: thanks to the escaping of [@] expressions, the entered tags are not interpreted. The password was received but is not displayed. With [curl], we can see the difference when a checkbox is selected:

curl -d "token=A7X2&title=Mr&name=Martin&hobbies=sport" http://localhost:5000/form

token = [A7X2]
title = [Mr]
name = [Martin]
hobbies = [sport]

and two checked boxes:

curl -d "token=A7X2&title=Mr&name=Martin&hobbies=sport&hobbies=music" http://localhost:5000/form

token = [A7X2]
title = [Mr]
name = [Martin]
hobbies = [sport, music]

(only the content of the [<pre>] tag on the page is reproduced, as displayed by a browser). An unchecked box is not sent at all: [Request.Form] does not contain the field, and the [Hobbies] property of the input retains its initial value—the empty array.

docs.title: 4.7. Example 19: Form Validation
docs.text:
An invalid form must be redisplayed, showing the entered values and a message below each field with an error. Example 19 applies the technique from Example 09 (validation performed by the action, using [ModelState]) to a registration form.

The [Models/RegistrationModel.cs] file:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace Example19.Models;

// the form fields and their constraints
public class RegistrationModel
{
    // removes the superfluous spaces of an input (the "setter" is called by model binding)
    private string? name;

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "The name is required.")]
    [MaxLength(20, ErrorMessage = "The name must not exceed 20 characters.")]
    public string? Name
    {
        get => name;
        set => name = value?.Trim();
    }

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "The email address is required.")]
    [EmailAddress(ErrorMessage = "Invalid email address.")]
    public string? Email { get; set; }

    // everything that comes from a form is a string: "42" -> 42
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "The age is required.")]
    [Range(18, 120, ErrorMessage = "The age must be between 18 and 120 years.")]
    public int? Age { get; set; }
